clusters.settings: Bimanual mocap datasets (TACO, GigaHands, OakInk2, GazeHOI, HandX, BOTH2Hands, HUMOTO); multi-person collaboration (CORE4D); egocentric trajectory prediction (EgoDex, OpenEgo, SHOW3D, Ego4D, AssemblyHands); egocentric video generation (TASTE-Rob, HandsOnWorld, Glove2Hand); RGB-D handover video generation; piano motion (FurElise, PianoMotion10M); static grasp synthesis (OakInk, AffordPose).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Predictive versus generative forecasters; text and gaze conditioning; contact and penetration guidance in diffusion; physics-simulator post-processing (proposed); refinement stages; diffusion restorers for rendered hands; LLM planning with MCTS or staged decomposition; model and codebook scaling. Gains are partial and physical validity is not guaranteed.

clusters.name: Metrics miss absolute error, contact and physics
clusters.statement: Standard hand-object metrics (Procrustes-aligned joint error, geometric overlap, R-precision, per-frame F1, hidden leaderboard scores) do not verify absolute placement, true contact, physical plausibility or perceptual quality. Several benchmarks also lack ground truth for what they claim to measure: instantaneous contact, depth, in-the-wild 3D and novel views.
clusters.description: A survey states that evaluation is dominated by geometric metrics that do not establish correct contact or function, and that alignment protocols conceal absolute errors. Dataset papers report that R-precision sits at the real-data value for all methods, that F1 scores do not match perception, and that human-likeness metrics have no validated standard. Contact, depth, NVS and in-the-wild benchmarks fall back on accumulated contact, cross-pair consistency or 2D mask proxies because instantaneous or 3D ground truth is unavailable. Challenge rankings use hidden server metrics or historical submissions, and automated success judges such as VLM observers are unreliable. Cross-study comparison in handover is blocked by differing settings and metrics.

evidence_items.item: Evaluation is dominated by geometric metrics; contact, function, physics and state transitions are rarely assessed together, and Procrustes alignment conceals absolute errors.
Standard single-condition metrics such as R-precision are insensitive to multi-condition hand generation; metrics for hand, body and text alignment are missing.
There is no ground truth for per-frame contact; only accumulated contact is benchmarked.
Unscripted in-the-wild video has no 3D ground truth; only 2D mask proxies and stable contact area are measured.
Per-frame F1 may not match human auditory perception of the performance.
Musically meaningful evaluation beyond F1 is open.
No standardized criteria exist for choosing human-likeness metrics; many were introduced without comprehensive assessment.
There is no ground-truth depth; stereo is evaluated only by cross-pair consistency.
The VLM observer has low accuracy at detecting failures and localizing failure steps.
The official ranking score is a hidden server-side metric whose formula is not public.
Leaderboard scores come from historical submissions with different training settings, not the ablation checkpoints.
Strictly synchronized tactile-kinematic demonstrations and contact-aware metrics are lacking.
Different handover studies adopt different settings and metrics, making cross-study comparison difficult.
HOI datasets lack ground-truth views and protocols for novel view synthesis of handheld objects.

benchmark_evidence: BOTH57M / R-Precision Top-3: all methods 0.104-0.115 vs real data 0.109, so the metric cannot separate methods (8)
DyTact-21 / instantaneous contact: no per-frame ground truth; only accumulated contact (1535)
Ego-1K / stereo cross-pair agreement within 1 mm: 0.0-74.0 percent, evaluated without ground-truth depth (226)
RoboTwin 2.0 / VLM failure localization correct in 12 of 40 flagged failures (30 percent) (1176)
KIT bimanual retargeting / Spearman correlation MAD 0.126 across robots, metrics not invariant (734)
clusters.settings: Hand pose benchmarks reporting PA-MPJPE (surveyed in 1118); two-hand motion generation (BOTH57M); dynamic contact (DyTact); egocentric multiview depth (Ego-1K); handheld object NVS (NVS-HO); in-the-wild grasps (EPIC-Grasps); piano performance (FurElise, RP1M); retargeting (KIT); SHOW3D HANDS challenge leaderboards; tactile dexterous transfer (TactiDex); handover simulation (HandoverSim); simulated policy data generation (RoboTwin 2.0).
clusters.attempted_fixes: A unified human-likeness metric (which depends on the chosen metrics and robots), accumulated wet-paint contact ground truth, contact-aware and safety metrics (TactiDex), cross-pair stereo consistency, stable-contact-area proxies and perceptual user studies. Benchmarks that unify contact, function, physical plausibility and state transitions are proposed but not built.

clusters.name: Fine-grained hand-object action and kinematic reasoning
clusters.statement: Video models cannot reliably recognize fine-grained hand-object actions across views and subjects: verbs, simultaneous two-handed actions, grasp and release stages, object state changes, mistakes and skill level. Vision-language models also cannot reason about 3D hand and object kinematics, distances or timing.
clusters.description: Benchmarks report verb recognition far below noun recognition and roughly half accuracy for two-handed simultaneous actions and cross-view settings. State-change detection and interaction anticipation are near floor, and long-tail classes stay below 20 percent. VLMs answer 3D perception, object-motion and kinematics questions at 20-35 percent versus over 90 percent for humans, and they confuse left and right or opposite actions. Action segmentation learns action order rather than the current action. Better hand poses raise verb accuracy, which ties the gap to hand and object pose quality. Tried: hard-negative contrastive training, hand plus body pose input, gaze and multi-view fusion.

evidence_items.item: EgoVLMs fail to choose the correct caption among single-word substitutions; verb accuracy is much lower than noun accuracy due to object-centric feature spaces.
Models confuse left/right directions and fixtures in 3D and object-motion questions; Gemini Pro reaches 20.8 percent on object motion.
VLMs fail on context, distances, timings and kinematics; vision plus language is insufficient for precise kinematics.
Recognizing simultaneous, overlapping fine-grained actions of both hands is open; accuracy on the view split is roughly half that on the person split.
Frequent confusion between opposite actions (attach vs detach, open vs close) because of weak temporal reasoning.
Egocentric views score 16.2 percent lower than fixed views; mistake detection recall stays low even with ground-truth labels.
Fine-grained action segmentation models learn action order rather than perceiving the current action.
Objects cannot be recognized reliably in cluttered, occluded scenes, so ground-truth object labels are used.
Single-frame state-change object detection reaches only 8-14 percent AP.
Action recognition from predicted hand poses is lower than from annotated poses, showing pose quality matters.
Transitional manipulation stages (grasp, release) are hard to segment in uncontrolled multi-person third-person video.
Skill proficiency classification from egocentric video reaches only 0.53 top-1 accuracy.
Human action segmentation for handover failure detection stays low, and interpreting failure reasons from predicted human actions needs further work.
Action recognition accuracy drops sharply on novel tool-action-object triplets and novel tool categories.

benchmark_evidence: EgoHOIBench / verb accuracy 36.10-46.61 percent vs noun 63.40-74.33 percent (483)
HD-EPIC VQA / Gemini Pro 3D perception 32.5 and object motion 20.8 percent vs human 93.8 and 92.7 (1398)
ATTACH / view-split recognition 33.2 percent vs 57.4 percent person split (1189)
Assembly101 / segmentation MoF 39.2, F1@50 21.3; mistake recall 46.6 percent (1184)
AssemblyHands-X / zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Pro 30.9 percent on six verbs (1170)
HOI4D / Asformer 46.8 vs 85.6 on 50Salads (1119)
IndEgo / VLM QA 57.6-64.1 percent vs human 90.0 percent (476)
AssemblyHands-Val / G-HTT action top-1 34.79-36.74 percent even with ground-truth objects (1538)
EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30 / tail-class action top-1 at most 19.44 percent (461)
Ego4D / state-change object detection AP 8-14 percent; anticipation Top-5 mAP about 2 percent (1072)
ADL4D / hand action segmentation 55.04 percent frame accuracy, F1@50 33.78 (1192)
Ego-Exo4D demonstrator proficiency / top-1 accuracy 0.53 (1526)
HFD / human action segmentation F1@50 57.1 multimodal, 51.1 video-only (1165)
TACO S4 compound generalization / top-1 action accuracy: AIM 39.33 and CACNF 44.00 percent vs 83.08 and 86.15 on S1 (88)
clusters.settings: Egocentric video (Ego4D, EPIC, HD-EPIC, Assembly101, IndEgo, HOI4D, AssemblyHands, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen); multi-Kinect assembly (ATTACH); multi-view RGB-D daily living (ADL4D); ego-exo skilled activity (Ego-Exo4D); third-person in-the-wild video (ChildPlay-Hand); robot handover failure video (HFD); bimanual tool use (TACO); sign-language fingerspelling; event cameras.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hard-negative contrastive objectives (EgoNCE++), hand plus body pose sequences, multi-view and gaze fusion (late fusion and gaze can hurt), fine-tuned small VLMs, and temporal action models. Joint hand-object modelling is proposed but not done, and VLM kinematic reasoning stays near chance on 3D questions.

clusters.name: Bimanual robot policies fail coordinated tasks and handovers
clusters.statement: Learned bimanual and dexterous robot policies (imitation, RL and VLA) cannot reliably perform tightly coordinated two-arm tasks, handovers (arm-to-arm and human-to-robot), or long-horizon and sub-millimetre tasks. This holds even in noiseless simulation with perfect perception, and the policies collapse under realistic visual domain shift and sim-to-real transfer.
clusters.description: Simulation benchmarks report average success well below 50 percent and near zero on handovers, stacking and coordinated lifts. Real dual-arm results stay low on precise, asymmetric or deformable tasks. Policies that do well in clean simulation rely on perfect point clouds, segmentation or state observations and collapse under domain randomization. Human-to-robot handover benchmarks assume perfect perception or non-reactive simulated givers, and dynamic handover success collapses when alignment starts farther away. Failures are attributed to arm collisions from poor spatial awareness or timing, missing coordination design and noisy multimodal demonstrations. Tried: imitation learning at scale, generated simulation data, active perception and force sensing.

evidence_items.item: No method reaches a sufficiently high success rate; in handover the arms collide due to inadequate spatial awareness or timing errors.
DP and DP3 score 0 percent on Handover and Storage at all data sizes.
Imitation policies perform poorly on tasks requiring complex bimanual coordination, below 15 percent.
Non-pretrained policies collapse under randomized conditions; DP3's few-shot results rely on perfect point clouds available only in simulation.
Success rates collapse in Hard Mode of dynamic human-to-robot handover; RGB-only policy cannot handle occlusion and depth ambiguity.
The simulated human giver does not adapt to the robot; baselines assume perfect perception of hand and object states.
Bimanual hand-over is the hardest task: 45.5 percent seen, 26.6 percent unseen.
All baseline algorithms fail on long-horizon mobile bimanual tasks.
Policies use state-based observations unavailable in the real world, hindering sim-to-real transfer; multi-task RL largely fails.
There is a large performance gap between single-hand and bimanual tasks; the framework has no bimanual coordination design.
RT-1 baselines fail on fine tasks with small objects, and large deformables that fill the field of view break gaze-based prediction.
Sub-millimetre small-part handling stays low: M3 nut pick-and-place 44 percent, asymmetric bimanual unfolding 9/20 with pi0.5 and 0/20 with Diffusion Policy.
UMI-trained policies need multiple attempts under imperfect contact on insertion.
Out-of-distribution scores remain below in-distribution, and roughly 40 percent of complex-task trials still fail.

benchmark_evidence: TWIN/RLBench2 / handover success 0 percent for ACT, RVT-LF, PerAct-LF, 11 percent PerAct2; 13-task average 5.9-17.5 percent (758)
HGen-Bench / Handover and Storage 0 percent for DP and DP3 (469)
RoboTwin / Dual Shoes Place at most 12.0 percent; real Dual Bottle Pick Hard 11/50 (1160)
RoboTwin 2.0 Easy to Hard / ACT 29.7 to 1.7, DP 28.0 to 0.6, DP3 55.2 to 5.0 percent (1176)
BiGym / stack_blocks 0 percent for all seven algorithms; best average 46.3 percent (1163)
DexH2R Hard Mode / success MotionNet 26.6, DP 8.3, DP3 27.1 percent (257)
HandoverSim / best success 64.58 percent with ground-truth perception (1188)
EFM-10 / Charger-Plug best 23.3 percent; force sensing lifts Light-Plug only from 20.0 to 36.7 (843)
Bi-DexHands MT20 / multi-task PPO reward 8.9 vs 32.5 per-task (1191)
HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker / success 52.8 percent bimanual vs 76.2 percent single-hand (1533)
YUBI / M3 nut single-attempt success 44 percent (UMI 14 percent); unfold glasses 9/20 (1371)
DAA real-robot tests / 69.6 percent overall, 61.5 percent on new objects (907)
clusters.settings: Simulation (RLBench2, RoboTwin, ManiSkill3, Isaac Gym, Isaac Sim, BiGym, HandoverSim, HGen-Bench, Bi-DexHands, RoboPianist, DexGarmentLab); real dual-arm platforms (COBOT Magic, UR5 pairs, AgiBot G1, JAKA K-1, Franka); ShadowHand handover rigs; handheld bimanual grippers (HiFi-UMI, YUBI); gaze-attentive teleoperation.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy, DP3, RDT, Pi0); LLM-generated simulation data, on which DP3 plateaus; domain randomization; multi-task pretraining; active viewpoint perception; force sensing, with small gains; human-verified data; human video co-training and mixture-of-experts policies. Success on coordinated and handover tasks remains low.

clusters.name: Transferring human hand demonstrations to robot hands
clusters.statement: Human hand-object demonstrations cannot yet be turned reliably into robot-executable dexterous behaviour, especially bimanual behaviour. Functional correspondence across hand morphologies is undefined, kinematic retargeting is often infeasible, and trajectory imitation ignores contact and force. The noisy hand tracking in scalable human data also limits supervision quality.
clusters.description: Papers using human data for robot learning name the embodiment gap as prohibitive and the human-to-robot hand action mapping as open. Kinematic retargeting gives very low success on some robot hands. Trajectory-centric transfer reaches goals by air grasps or penetration because contact and force are ignored, and human data adds little in-distribution. Open-loop replay fails on shifting or articulated objects, and real deployment needs fingertip state tracking that is not available. Even in simulation with mocap references, bimanual tracking succeeds only about half the time. Tried: residual mixture-of-experts policies, contact-map transfer, co-training with unified state spaces, per-object RL and tactile-aware rewards.

evidence_items.item: Large performance gap between single-hand and bimanual tasks when transferring mocap to dexterous hands; the framework lacks a bimanual coordination design.
Human and robot grasps are paired only semantically; functional equivalence across morphologies is undefined; kinematic retargeting gives low success.
Retargeting fails when the robot hand cannot reach a feasible analog of the MANO pose; open-loop execution fails on objects that shift or articulate.
Trajectory-centric transfer ignores contact formation; the kinematic baseline achieves goals via air grasping or mesh penetration.
A prohibitive embodiment gap remains between humans and robots.
Separate state spaces let the policy shortcut embodiment, and human action speed mismatches teleoperation speed; human data has only a minor in-distribution effect.
Human-to-robot hand action space mapping remains open; robot experiments are mostly single-handed.
There is no validated, robot-independent standard for scoring how human-like a retargeted bimanual motion is.
Per-object RL policy training does not scale; cross-morphology retargeting that preserves contact dynamics is open.
Real-robot deployment needs state estimation including precise fingertip tracking; human fingering annotations may not fit robot morphologies.
Retargeting primitive demonstrations to heterogeneous robot hands and platforms is future work (same paper as 67).
The repository does not address transfer to multi-finger robot hands.
Human-operated gripper demonstrations do not capture the kinematic and dynamic constraints of real manipulators.
Imitation-learning robots driven by generated HOI videos need nearly identical environments to the demonstration, and only simulated robot results are reported.

benchmark_evidence: HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker / success 52.8 percent bimanual vs 76.2 percent single-hand; object translation error 0.728 vs 0.220-0.323 (1533)
HRDexDB / kinematic retargeting seed-level success Allegro 1.21 percent; cross-embodiment retrieval R@1 8.18 percent (1131)
HUG-Bench / 73.0 percent vs human-grasp oracle 94.0 percent in simulation; 66.7 percent tabletop, 62.0 percent in-the-wild real (1386)
DexCanvas / RL reproduction 80.15 percent nominal, 62.54 percent with object pose perturbation (1375)
TactiDex / tactile-aware success 39.35 percent kinematic baseline vs 64.64 percent best (1395)
Humanoid Policy / vertical grasping 28/90 robot-only vs 35/90 co-trained (650)
KIT bimanual retargeting / metric correlation MAD 0.126 across robots (734)
TASTE-Rob / Mujoco robot success 84 percent with coarse vs 96 percent with refined videos; real-robot results not reported (113)
clusters.settings: Mocap references replayed in Isaac Gym (OakInk2, GigaHands, DexCanvas, TactiDex, HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker); egocentric human video for VLA pretraining; Vision Pro and Aria human demonstrations (EgoDex, Humanoid Policy, HUG); multi-embodiment grasp capture (HRDexDB); handheld UMI-style grippers; affordance learning from human images (GLOVER++); simulated humanoid retargeting (KIT); robot piano (RP1M); generated HOI video for imitation (TASTE-Rob).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Residual mixture-of-experts imitation policies; contact-map rather than pose transfer; co-training with a unified state space and slowed human actions; VLA pretraining on reconstructed human hands; per-object RL policies, which do not scale; tactile-aware rewards with safety penalties; open-loop grasp transfer. Closed-loop tactile feedback and unified policies remain future work.

notes:

Papers are multi-assigned, so the n_papers counts sum to more than 116.

Not added: 103 (its occlusion item concerns objects, and its hand number is a domain gap, used in cross-domain), 1124 (object registration) and 1127 (contact deformation).

clusters.name: Unseen-object detection and segmentation bottleneck
clusters.statement: Two-stage 6D pose pipelines for novel objects depend on an upstream 2D detector or segmenter. In clutter, under heavy occlusion, among repeated instances, with reflections or in dark scenes, that detector trails seen-object detection by tens of AP points and becomes the limiting stage, while many benchmarks hide the stage by supplying ground-truth boxes or masks.
clusters.description: BOP 2023 and 2024 both name 2D detection of unseen objects as the main pipeline bottleneck. Given seen-object detections, the unseen-object method GenFlow comes within 5.9 AR of the best seen-object method. Zero-shot proposal generators built on SAM or FastSAM (CNOS, SAM-6D, NIDS-Net) and open-vocabulary segmenters (Grounded-SAM) lose much of their accuracy on industrial bins, dense piles, cluttered desktops and new capture conditions; they split instances wrongly and assign wrong object IDs among stacked identical parts. The IJCV survey notes that state-of-the-art pipelines need a separate pretrained detector and calls for end-to-end designs. Many dataset and method papers give baselines ground-truth masks, ground-truth boxes or an external detector crop, so their reported pose numbers leave out detection error.

evidence_items.item: 2D detection of unseen objects is the main bottleneck of 6D pipelines and lags seen-object detection by about 35%.

A large gap remains between unseen and seen object detection, especially amodal detection of occluded instances. Given seen-object detections, GenFlow reaches 79.2 AR, showing that detection is the limiting stage.

Unseen-object 2D detection degrades sharply under heavy occlusion, repeated instances and strong reflections (SAM6D drops more than 33% AP), detections get wrong object IDs in dense multi-instance scenes, and unseen-object pose depends on an upstream segmentation prior.
Foundation segmentation (Grounded-SAM) separates instances poorly in clutter, reaching 16.2 AP; adapting foundation segmentation to clutter is future work.
SAM6D's built-in segmentation and fixed thresholds do not generalize to cluttered backgrounds.
CosyPose-LS misses nearly 20% of objects; off-the-shelf pose pipelines need better object detection.
Removing the segmentation proposal network causes a dramatic drop (IADD AUC 3.1-4.4 versus 19.0-36.3).
Ground-truth masks are used because large-vocabulary semantic classification is unreliable.
State-of-the-art pipelines need a separate pretrained detector or segmenter; end-to-end methods that integrate detection are needed.
The RCNN detector from CosyPose failed on the dataset, and YOLOX detection recall drops by 39.7 points on the new sequences.
Gen6D matches instance-specific estimators on LINEMOD only when given ground-truth bounding boxes.
FFB6D segmentation fails in dark lighting; DenseFusion is given ground-truth segmentation masks at evaluation.
The tracker needs a given first-frame 2D mask, and segmentation masks become noisy late in sequences as the viewpoint departs from the first frame.
A separate object detector is still required; doing detection through local feature matching is future work.

BOP-H3 / 2D detection AP: MUSE 39.0 versus 52.0 on BOP-Classic-Core (1312)
BOP core 2023 / unseen detection mAP: CNOS-FastSAM 42.8, a 37 mAP gap to GDet2023 (1313)
BOP core 2023 / AR with seen-object detections: GenFlow 79.2, 5.9 behind GPose2023 (1313)
XYZ-IBD / unseen 2D detection AP: CNOS 0.275, SAM-6D 0.296, NIDS-Net 0.258, versus 0.36-0.49 on BOP-Core5 (402)
IndustryShapes Classic / segmentation mAP: CNOS 0.203, SAM-6D 0.345; CNOS bbox mAP 0.240 (837)
GraspClutter6D / instance segmentation AP: Grounded-SAM 16.2, best Mask2Former 43.5 (839)
YCB-Ev / YOLOX detection average recall: 50.1 versus 89.8 on YCB-V (1320)
HOPE / detection: CosyPose-LS fails to detect nearly 20% of objects (1315)
GraspNet-1Billion / IADD AUC without the segmentation proposal network: 3.1-4.4 versus 19.0-36.3 (1327)
clusters.settings: Single-image RGB and RGB-D pipelines, model-based and model-free, on BOP core and BOP-H3; industrial bins (XYZ-IBD), industrial workcells (IndustryShapes), dense piles (GraspClutter6D), moving-camera desktops (DynOPETs), event plus RGB-D captures (YCB-Ev) and dark long-range scenes (DTTD). Benchmarks or methods that supply ground-truth boxes or masks, or rely on an external detector: Omni6DPose, Omni6D, PACE, HouseCat6D, EgoXtreme, DTTD, DTTD-Mobile, 6D-Diff on LM-O, OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D, OmniPose6D (first-frame mask) and MessyKitchens (SAM 3 masks).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Zero-shot proposal generators (CNOS, SAM-6D, NIDS-Net, MUSE), including the default detector BOP 2023 gave to all entries, still trail seen-object detectors, by about 35% in BOP 2024 (1312, 1313, 402). Proposed directions: adapting foundation segmentation to clutter (839), end-to-end detection plus pose (1088), and detection through local feature matching (1325). Many dataset papers give baselines ground-truth masks or boxes (201, 347, 348, 350, 1316, 1318, 1319, 1321), which separates detection error from pose error but hides it.

clusters.name: Sim-to-real gap and dataset-specific bias
clusters.statement: 6D pose and related 3D perception models lose most of their accuracy on real captures that differ in sensor, range, scene arrangement or domain when they were trained on synthetic (PBR) data or tuned to one benchmark's capture distribution. Gains on standard benchmarks may reflect dataset-specific domain randomisation rather than generalisation.
clusters.description: Benchmark papers report steep transfer losses. GDRN falls from 0.827 to 0.266 AP on real industrial bins after synthetic training, and GDRNPP falls from 76.4 to 8.9 recall on recreated YCB-V arrangements of the same objects. On PACE, depth-input HS-Pose falls from 81.2 to 1.1 AP from sim to real. YCB-Ev argues that narrowing the synthetic-to-real gap does not remove dataset bias, and the monocular surveys say domain shift counts as solved only on standard low-variance datasets, with PBR-only training still trailing PBR plus real by up to 19.6%. Papers say synthetic generators lack realistic sensor, transparent-material and contact artifacts as well as realistic out-of-plane rotation and occlusion, that reconstructed meshes with baked lighting cannot yet give realistic synthetic data, and that synthetic-only training also fails for 3D point tracking, generative scene reconstruction and grasp detection.

evidence_items.item: Seen-object methods trained on synthetic bin-picking data fail on real scenes (GDRN 0.827 on BOP-Core5 falls to 0.266).

GDRNPP recall collapses from 76.4 to 8.9 on recreated YCB-V arrangements. Narrowing the synthetic-to-real gap does not reduce dataset bias, and BOP gains may reflect dataset-specific domain randomisation.
Depth-input category methods collapse from sim to real because of real depth noise (HS-Pose 81.2 to 1.1); advanced sim-to-real techniques are future work.
Claims that domain shift is solved hold only for standard datasets with limited variance in shapes, support planes, textures and illumination.
PBR-only training trails PBR plus real by up to 19.6% on YCB-V and TUD-L; the paper calls its domain-shift conclusions tentative.
Generative scene methods (MIDI, PartCrafter) trained on synthetic data fail to generalize to real captures.
Synthetic 3D tracking benchmarks have a significant domain gap; TAPIR-3D, trained only on synthetic video, scores below the static baseline.
Synthetic datasets lack realistic out-of-plane rotation and occlusion, and the tracker is trained on synthetic data only.
Synthetic transparent-object datasets lack realistic artifacts (a syn-to-real gap).
Synthetic grasp datasets suffer sim-to-real gaps from inaccurate sensor noise and contact dynamics.
Instant NGP meshes have poor texture and baked lighting, so realistic synthetic data cannot be generated from the reconstructions.
Synthetic-to-real transfer for models trained on synthetic data is listed as an open problem.
Prior models trained on limited real data fail to generalise in the wild, and a domain gap between synthetic and real data remains.
The synthetic-to-real domain gap is an open problem; synthetic-to-real adaptation and generalization are future work.

benchmark_evidence: XYZ-IBD / 6D detection AP: GDRN falls from 0.827 on BOP-Core5 to 0.266; SurfEmb from 0.758 to 0.247 (402)
YCB-Ev / average recall at 2 cm: GDRNPP 8.9 versus 76.4 on YCB-V; CosyPose 41.4 versus 82.5 (1320)
PACE sim-to-real / AP: HS-Pose falls from 81.2 to 1.1 (348, 1316)
BOP T-LESS, TUD-L, YCB-V / AR: PBR-only training trails PBR plus real by up to 19.6% (1328)
GraspClutter6D / grasp AP: EconomicGrasp falls from 51.63 on GraspNet-1B to 21.67 (839)
TAPVid-3D / 3D-AJ: TAPIR-3D trained on synthetic video averages 3.1, below the static baseline (444)
MessyKitchens / object-level IoU: synthetic-trained PartCrafter 0.071, MIDI 0.186 (405)
clusters.settings: Instance-level RGB and RGB-D pose trained on PBR renders and tested on real industrial bins (XYZ-IBD), real workcells (IndustryShapes), recreated YCB scenes with a new camera (YCB-Ev), longer-range AR captures (DTTD), clutter (PACE, GraspClutter6D) and transparent objects (ClearPose); category-level pose (Omni6DPose SOPE to ROPE, Wild6D, PhoCaL); synthetic-trained 3D point tracking (TAPVid-3D), single-image scene reconstruction (MessyKitchens), short-term RGB tracking (OmniPose6D) and grasp detection (GraspClutter6D).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Domain randomisation and large synthetic training sets (SOPE, Omni6D, OmniPose6D, BlenderProc/GSO renders) help on standard benchmarks but not on new real arrangements or sensors (1320, 402). Foundation-model pose methods (FoundationPose, SAM-6D) transfer better but stay below their BOP-Core5 scores (402). Mixing in real data helps (1328), but real data is expensive (347). Semi-supervised learning on real video (RePoNet) still trails full supervision (1323). Neural reconstruction for data synthesis is limited by baked lighting (1314). Proposed: advanced sim-to-real techniques and larger models (348, 1316), synthetic-to-real adaptation (1088) and synthetic event data (1320).

clusters.name: Saturated, constrained benchmarks hide real-world failure
clusters.statement: Standard rigid-object pose benchmarks are near saturation on controlled, opaque, household, static, near-range scenes and cannot reveal real-world failure. Methods that score well there lose large margins on realistic clutter, industrial parts, longer range, dynamic or egocentric capture, or new arrangements of the same objects.
clusters.description: XYZ-IBD calls household benchmarks near saturation, and BOP 2023 reports that seen-object accuracy saturates. PACE states that constrained sets such as NOCS-REAL275 (six categories, 18 videos) hide poor real-world performance. The monocular surveys describe standard datasets as opaque, diffuse, hand-sized objects on one support plane, centred in view, and say benchmark-driven research diverges from robotic needs. Dataset papers name specific coverage gaps: static cameras or stationary objects, range under one metre with fixed lighting, well-lit third-person views without blur or smoke, an upper-hemisphere viewpoint bias, fewer than ten categories, objects researchers cannot buy, no onboarding sequences, no mobile-AR depth, and (before TAPVid-3D) no real 3D point-tracking benchmark. Each paper answers with a new targeted dataset that covers one gap, and several of these remain small. This is an evaluation gap, separate from the training-domain gap.

evidence_items.item: Household 6D benchmarks are near saturation and do not reflect industrial complexity.
Seen-object accuracy saturates, but efficiency must improve.
Poor real-world performance is hidden by constrained benchmarks such as NOCS-REAL275 (six categories, 18 videos).
Standard datasets contain opaque, diffuse, hand-sized objects on a single support plane, centred in view; realistic benchmarks with natural clutter, backgrounds and material variety are needed.
Benchmarks exclude open-world robotics problems.
Most benchmarks remain limited in scale, diversity or realism; scalable benchmarks are needed.
BOP-style evaluation neglects capture effects such as noise, motion blur and lighting.
Existing 6D pose benchmarks are captured under controlled, well-lit, largely static third-person conditions and miss motion blur, extreme illumination, smoke and truncation.
Most real-world pose datasets assume either a static camera or stationary objects.
Existing 3D object tracking datasets target robot grasping at under one metre, under fixed lighting, with older noisy depth sensors.
Existing datasets have limited viewpoint coverage (an upper-hemisphere bias) and visible checkerboards.
Benchmark objects are not physically available to most researchers, and product appearance changes over time.
Existing datasets are limited to labs, bin-picking or household items, and novel-object onboarding sequences are underrepresented.
No real-world benchmark for 3D point tracking existed before this work.
Category-level datasets have few categories (typically under 10) and overlook occlusion and complex scenes.
Scarce, low-diversity annotated real data (REAL275: 13 scenes, 18 objects) keeps category-level pose in constrained environments.
Existing grasping benchmarks are simplistic, lightly occluded and low in diversity.
Prior datasets reflect robotic grasping with dedicated depth cameras, not mobile AR conditions.

benchmark_evidence: XYZ-IBD / unseen-object 6D detection AP: best SAM6D 0.578, FoundationPose 0.564, versus 0.70-0.73 on BOP-Core5 (402)
PACE Real2Real all categories / AR and AP: drops of 57-78 points versus single-instance fitting (348)
DTTD vs YCB-Video / ADD AUC (DenseFusion): spam_can 38.83 versus 79.94 on the same objects (1318)
YCB-Ev / YOLOX detection average recall: 50.1 versus 89.8 on YCB-V (1320)
BOP core / material coverage: six of seven datasets contain only opaque, diffuse objects (1020, 1328)
NOCS, DREDS / intra-category variation: little variation and overlapping categories (1020)
clusters.settings: BOP classic core, NOCS CAMERA25/REAL275, YCB-Video and LINEMOD, compared with new realistic sets: industrial bins (XYZ-IBD) and workcells (IndustryShapes), dense clutter (GraspClutter6D, PACE), longer-range AR (DTTD), mobile LiDAR (DTTD-Mobile), egocentric extreme conditions (EgoXtreme), moving-camera desktops (DynOPETs), event cameras (YCB-Ev), large vocabularies (Omni6D) and monocular 3D point tracking (TAPVid-3D).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Each paper responds with a new targeted dataset (industrial, clutter, transparent, long-range, mobile, event, egocentric, dynamic, large-vocabulary). Each new set covers one gap, and several remain small, for example 5 objects in IndustryShapes and 12 scenes in PhoCaL. The surveys call for realistic, scalable benchmarks with natural clutter, backgrounds and material variety (1020, 1088).

clusters.name: CAD-free onboarding of new objects lags far behind
clusters.statement: The 6D pose of a new rigid object cannot yet be estimated or tracked accurately without a CAD model when it is onboarded only from a casual or hand-manipulation video or a few posed reference images; accuracy stays well below model-based levels. Reference-based methods fail at viewpoints or scales the reference capture did not cover or with few references, and reconstruction-based onboarding fails at range or leaves artifacts.
clusters.description: BOP 2024 reports that model-free onboarding from static or dynamic hand-manipulation video is largely unaddressed: its model-free 6D detection track received no submissions. BOP 2023 still gave meshes to its unseen-object tasks. Where model-free variants are run, they fall far below the same method given a CAD model (FoundationPose AR 0.25 versus 0.67 on IndustryShapes), and model-free trackers stay under 13% 5deg5cm on PACE. Reference-based methods (OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D) need posed reference scans and fail at uncovered viewpoints, at extreme scale change or with few references. Reconstruction-based onboarding (BundleSDF, Instant-NGP) fails at distance or low resolution, or leaves texture and geometry artifacts. The surveys note that unseen-object, hand-object and render-and-compare methods still need CAD models, textured models or annotated reference views, and that accuracy falls from seen to novel objects even when the mesh is supplied.

evidence_items.item: Model-free onboarding of new objects from reference videos (static or dynamic hand manipulation) remains largely unaddressed; the model-free 6D detection track received no submissions.
Model-free FoundationPose onboarded from sequences falls far below the model-based version (AR 0.25 versus 0.67 on the classic split).

Unseen-object methods still need CAD models or annotated reference views, and hand-object interaction pose methods depend on object CAD models that are hard to obtain in daily scenes. Novel-view reconstruction priors suffer generative artifacts and view inconsistency.
Poses from viewpoints the reference images do not cover cannot be predicted accurately (Prj-5 falls from 82.64 to 35.56 with half-space coverage), and accuracy drops with few references.
High-quality CAD models of everyday objects are often inaccessible, and extreme scale change between the scan video and the test sequence is hard to handle.
BundleSDF fails to reconstruct objects at large distance, at low resolution or with too few frames per viewpoint, yielding no tracking.
Instant NGP meshes have poor texture and baked lighting.
Unseen-object methods were still given 3D mesh models for onboarding; onboarding from reference images only is left to future work.
Render-and-compare refinement depends on textured 3D models and realistic rendering, which fail for novel and reflective or refractive objects.
Accuracy falls from seen to similar to novel objects even with the mesh supplied, and registering a partial-view cloud to a full mesh fails at low overlap.
Novel-object pose estimation is open; reviewed methods mostly assume rigid objects with known models.
Labelling requires a scanned CAD model for every object; marker-free annotation without CAD models or mocap is what the field cannot yet do.
The model-free tracker BundleTrack reaches 1.3 at 5deg5cm with 46.9 deg rotation error on ROPE.
All evaluated egocentric pose methods require object CAD models.

benchmark_evidence: IndustryShapes Classic / BOP AR: FoundationPose model-free 0.25 versus model-based 0.67; Extended split model-free 0.33, FoundPose 0.28 (837)
BOP-H3 / model-free 6D detection: no submissions (1312)
GenMOP / Prj-5: 35.56 with references in one half-space versus 82.64 with even coverage; ADD-0.1d falls from 50.39 to 27.55 with 8 references (1326)
LINEMOD / ADD(S)-0.1d: CAD-free OnePose++ 76.9 versus instance-level CDPN 91.4; OnePose 63.6 (1325)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD AUC: BundleSDF 0.00 on cereal_box and all three markers (1319)
PACE / tracking: best model-free under 13% 5deg5cm (CAPTRA 12.9) versus best model-based ICG 38.1 ADD(-S) AUC (348, 1316)
ROPE tracking / 5deg5cm: model-free BundleTrack 1.3 with Rerr 46.9 deg (347)
GraspNet-1Billion / IADD AUC with mesh supplied: 36.3 seen, 29.2 similar, 23.7 novel (1327)
clusters.settings: Monocular RGB and RGB-D on novel rigid objects onboarded from reference video or images: OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D/GenMOP, the BOP 2023/2024 model-free tasks, IndustryShapes onboarding sequences and BundleSDF on DTTD-Mobile. Also unseen-object RGB-D pose with the mesh supplied (GraspNet-1Billion benchmark), model-free tracking (PACE, Omni6DPose ROPE, OmniPose6D), and CAD-assumed baselines in 6D-Diff, EgoXtreme, DynOPETs labelling and TAPVid-3D's note on model-based 3D tracking.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Methods tried so far: SfM-based one-shot pose (OnePose), detector-free and keypoint-free matching (OnePose++), generalizable reference matching (Gen6D), neural reconstruction for onboarding (BundleSDF; Instant-NGP in HANDAL), model-free trackers (BundleTrack, CAPTRA), and template matching with a mesh. Each fails on low texture, distance, few or poorly covering references, or reconstruction artifacts, or still needs a mesh. Proposed: 3DGS and neural-rendering CAD-free priors and sparse-reference methods (1088), template-free and training-free novel-object pose (1020, 1328), and onboarding from reference images only (1313).

clusters.name: Textureless objects defeat correspondence-based pose
clusters.statement: Pose estimators, model-free trackers and pseudo-labelers that rely on local feature correspondences or keypoint-based SfM fail on texture-poor objects, especially combined with large out-of-plane rotation, because they cannot find repeatable keypoints.
clusters.description: CAD-free one-shot methods name textureless objects as their main failure. OnePose cannot build SfM models without repeatable keypoints, and even keypoint-free OnePose++ reaches only 16.8 percent 1cm-1deg on low-texture objects. Feature-based model-free trackers such as BundleTrack fail on weak textures, and OmniPose6D fails when limited texture combines with large out-of-plane rotation or when coplanar keypoints give too little geometry. Pseudo-labelers remain poor on textureless bowls even after smoothing, and annotation pipelines cannot find keypoints on textureless objects. Industrial benchmarks highlight texture-less metal parts as a core difficulty.

evidence_items.item: Reliance on local feature matching causes failure on textureless objects that lack repeatable keypoints.
OnePose fails on low-textured objects whose complete point clouds cannot be reconstructed with keypoint-based SfM; strict 1cm-1deg success on low-textured objects stays at 16.8 percent.
Failures occur on textureless regions and on limited texture combined with large out-of-plane rotation; coplanar keypoints give too little geometry for SfM.
Weak-texture objects defeat feature-based tracking (BundleTrack).
After EKF/RTS refinement, FoundationPose pseudo-labels remain poor for symmetric or textureless objects such as bowls.
Correspondence-based methods degrade on texture-less objects that lack distinctive local descriptors.
Accuracy is lowest on small or texture-poor LM-O objects.
Highly reflective, texture-less, geometrically symmetric parts are an open problem.
Industrial objects are textureless, metallic or reflective, which makes pose estimation hard.
Annotating the 6D pose of textureless, reflective and transparent objects, where keypoints cannot be found, is open.

benchmark_evidence: OnePose-LowTexture / 1cm-1deg, 3cm-3deg, 5cm-5deg: best 16.8 / 57.7 / 72.1; OnePose 12.4 / 35.7 / 45.4 (1325)
ROPE tracking / 5deg5cm and rotation error: BundleTrack 1.3 with Rerr 46.9 deg (347)
LM-O / ADD(-S): ape 60.6, cat 63.2, duck 67.2 versus 97.9 for can (3)
clusters.settings: Monocular RGB CAD-free pose from reference scans (OnePose, OnePose-LowTexture); short-term RGB tracking of hand-held objects (OmniPose6D on HO3D, YCBInEOAT, DexYCB); RGB-D feature-based tracking (BundleTrack on ROPE); pseudo-label annotation (DynOPETs); texture-less industrial parts (XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes); annotation of textureless objects (PhoCaL).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Detector-free, keypoint-free matching (OnePose++) raises low-texture accuracy, but strict success stays at 16.8 percent (1325). EKF/RTS smoothing does not fix pseudo-labels for textureless bowls (825). Proposed: better keypoint sampling and joint refinement of keypoints and pose (1286).

clusters.name: Accurate real 6D labels do not scale
clusters.statement: Real-world 6D pose datasets are either large but inaccurate or accurate but small. Millimetre-level ground truth needs pre-scanned meshes, robot arms or tracking systems, markers, anti-reflection spray and manual alignment, which caps object count, categories, sizes and viewpoints and keeps learning dependent on scarce, dense real labels.
clusters.description: Dataset papers repeatedly describe a trade-off between scale and accuracy in real annotation. Robot-arm or IR-tracker acquisition is accurate but limits viewpoints and backgrounds. SfM, ARKit or COLMAP poses with manual alignment scale better but leave centimetre errors and manual bottlenecks. Large-vocabulary real annotation is called monumental, so Omni6D and Omni6DPose train on rendered data. Physical limits also apply: scanners cap object size near 20 cm, specular parts need anti-reflection coating, large or valuable objects are missing, and exhaustive annotation of cluttered configurations is impractical. Semi-supervised learning on unlabeled real video narrows the gap to full supervision but does not close it, and the surveys call for label-efficient and self-supervised learning.

evidence_items.item: Existing category-level datasets are either large but inaccurate or accurate but small with limited viewpoints; robot-based annotation limits viewpoints and backgrounds.
Real large-vocabulary annotation is described as monumental, so Omni6D is rendered and its real set has only 1k images of 73 instances.
Large real datasets are too expensive to collect at sufficient diversity, so training relies on simulated data; annotation uses SfM with manual keypoint alignment over keyframes.
The annotation pipeline still has manual bottlenecks: mesh alignment by oriented bounding box and XMem segmentation supervision.
Exhaustive annotation of all object configurations in complex scenes is impractical.
Existing datasets tolerate annotation errors up to a centimetre without per-frame refinement.
Existing benchmarks have limited registration accuracy, inaccurate contacts or poor scalability because they rely on mocap or robot-based capture; object scans take 6-10 minutes each.
The scanner could not handle objects larger than about 20 cm, and the depth-annotation and PnP tools carry noise or error along the projection ray.
Ground truth needs temporary anti-reflective coating and robot-arm repeated viewpoints over 50 calibrated views; accurate ground truth for specular objects is open.
Annotating 6D object pose is challenging and costly, and the limited number and diversity of annotated real data restricts category-level generalisation.
Reference poses need ARKit plus manual 3D boxes and bundle adjustment, and obtaining masks for instance-level training requires time-consuming dense reconstruction.
The robot workspace limits camera view angles, and only 12 scenes (24 trajectories) were captured.
Annotations are aligned on fused point clouds from 13 views with crowd-sourced manual alignment.
Dependence on labor-intensive real-world labeled data is an open problem; label-efficient learning is needed to remove the need for dense 6D annotations.
GenMOP reference poses come from COLMAP plus manual keypoint alignment.

benchmark_evidence: REAL275 / 5deg2cm: semi-supervised RePoNet 30.7 versus fully supervised SGPA 35.9 (1323)
REAL275 / IoU0.75: RePoNet-semi 51.8 versus fully supervised upper bound 63.2 (1323)
IndustryShapes / annotation depth error: under 12 mm on the classic split and about 5 mm on the extended split (837; dataset accuracy, not a method score)
clusters.settings: Static tabletop and bin scenes annotated with robot arms (PhoCaL KUKA, XYZ-IBD FANUC), IR tracking (HouseCat6D), calibrated multi-camera rigs with markers (PACE, GraspClutter6D) and SfM, ARKit or COLMAP plus manual alignment (Omni6DPose, HANDAL, IndustryShapes, OnePose, GenMOP). Also structured-light scanners limited to objects under about 20 cm (HOPE), scanned meshes plus scene scans (MessyKitchens), and category-level video annotation (Wild6D).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Semi-supervised learning on unlabeled real video (RePoNet, 1323) still trails full supervision. SfM/COLMAP camera localisation (1314, 347) and crowd-sourced alignment (839) reduce manual work but do not remove it. Synthetic data replaces real labels at the cost of a domain gap (347, 350). Proposed: LLM/LVM-guided weak and self-supervised learning (1088, 1020, 1328), fully automatic segmentation (1314), and annotating videos of scanned objects (350).

clusters.name: No scalable ground truth for moving manipulated objects
clusters.statement: Accurate 6D ground truth cannot be obtained at scale for objects that move during capture (hand-manipulated objects, simultaneous camera and object motion, fast motion). Markers cannot be used on moving objects, mocap confines capture to instrumented indoor spaces, and tracker or pseudo-label propagation drifts and needs manual correction.
clusters.description: PACE annotates moving objects with BundleTrack because markers cannot be used, and has to correct its drift by hand every ten frames. DynOPETs uses mocap for the camera and smoothed FoundationPose pseudo-labels, which stay poor for symmetric or textureless objects, and still removes bad poses manually. HANDAL calls dynamic-scene object pose extremely hard to annotate and relies on BundleSDF plus ICP with manual inspection. Mocap ground truth confines EgoXtreme and DTTD to indoor rooms, and DTTD's moving-camera sync depends on interpolation and Kalman smoothing. Other capture pipelines break under motion: YCB-Ev's camera tracking fails under fast motion and low light with event-RGB sync limited to 33 ms, and PhoCaL uses stop-and-go robot capture to avoid blur. OmniPose6D states that real datasets lack large-scale precise ground truth for dynamic object tracking and focus on hands with little object variety.

evidence_items.item: Marker-based annotation cannot be used on moving objects; BundleTrack is used instead but drifts and needs manual fixes every ten frames.

Pose annotation in dynamic scenes relies on labor-intensive manual work or expensive mocap; pseudo-labels remain poor for symmetric or textureless objects, and bad absolute poses must be removed by hand.
Dynamic-scene object pose is extremely hard to annotate; HANDAL uses BundleSDF plus averaged ICP and manual inspection.
OptiTrack ground truth confines capture to specialised indoor spaces and prevents outdoor evaluation; labelling hand articulation under extreme blur and speed is itself unsolved.
Camera tracking used for annotation degrades with motion blur and fails under fast motion and low light; RGB-event synchronisation is limited to 33 ms.
Real datasets lack large-scale precise ground truth for dynamic object pose tracking and focus on hands with little object variety.
In a freely moving rig, motion-induced camera pose error remains after time synchronisation, so bundle-adjustment post-processing is needed.
Automatic annotations from multi-sensor sources are imperfect, with flickering visibility flags and ground-truth noise.
Ground truth needs an OptiTrack room, and camera-mocap synchronisation relies on ArUco/mocap pose matching, interpolation and Kalman smoothing, which the paper describes only as generally good.
Stop-and-go robot capture is used to avoid motion blur, and annotation errors accumulate across sequences in marker or depth-based pipelines.

benchmark_evidence: DynOPETs (175 sequences) / ATE: dynamic-SLAM style trackers MaskFusion 0.320 m and DROID-SLAM 0.173 m versus FoundationPose 0.037 m; annotation accuracy is validated against mocap on only 10 additional sequences (825)
clusters.settings: Hand-held and moving objects with moving cameras: PACE moving objects, DynOPETs desktop sequences with a mocap-tracked camera, HANDAL dynamic RGB-D videos, EgoXtreme Aria glasses with OptiTrack, DTTD cart-mounted Azure Kinect with OptiTrack, YCB-Ev event plus RGB-D, the HouseCat6D handheld rig, PhoCaL robot stop-and-go capture, and TAPVid-3D on Aria Digital Twin.
clusters.attempted_fixes: BundleTrack or BundleSDF propagation with ICP and manual correction (1316, 1314). EKF/RTS smoothing of FoundationPose pseudo-labels combined with point-tracking relative poses, which drift (825). Mocap with hand-eye calibration, indoor only (825, 201, 1318). Marker inpainting (1316), bundle-adjustment post-processing (1321) and stop-and-go capture (1322). Proposed: pose estimation directly on events plus synthetic event data (1320), and hand labels from mocap combined with parametric hand models (201).

clusters.name: Pose accuracy collapses under heavy occlusion in clutter
clusters.statement: In dense real clutter (piles, bins, cluttered tabletops), detection and 6D pose accuracy of every method family fall steeply as the visible fraction of the object shrinks, and learned instance-level networks fall below classical point-pair matching. No current method is reported to handle severe occlusion, and how specific occlusion patterns affect accuracy has not been studied systematically.
clusters.description: Clutter benchmarks show accuracy falling steadily with occlusion level: on GraspClutter6D, MegaPose goes from 77.9 to 42.3 ADD(-S) between low and high occlusion. In PACE clutter, deep instance-level methods score below 10 AR even with ground-truth detections, while geometric PPF reaches 52.2. BOP 2023 names amodal detection of occluded unseen objects as open. The surveys state that no method handles severe occlusion, that occlusion-specific methods do not beat general ones, and that no systematic study of occlusion patterns and part visibility exists. Category-level datasets are criticised for overlooking occlusion, and Gen6D says it is not designed for it. The occlusion here comes from other objects in static scenes; occlusion by the holding hand is a separate cluster.

evidence_items.item: All pose methods degrade as occlusion increases; MegaPose ADD(-S) falls from 77.9 at low occlusion to 42.3 at high occlusion, and FFB6D to 13.2.
No method handles severe occlusion, which leaves incomplete texture and geometry features.
No systematic study exists of how specific occlusion patterns and part visibility affect pose accuracy; occlusion-specific methods do not outperform general methods on LM-O.
Deep instance-level methods (CosyPose, SurfEmb, GDRNPP) score far below geometric PPF in clutter.
Current methods handle occlusion weakly; cluttered, occluded scenes depress all baselines (VI-Net IoU50 12.7 on box, 17.1 on remote).
Gen6D is not designed for occlusion, and its accuracy may degrade under severe occlusion.
Category-level datasets overlook real-world challenges such as occlusion and complex scenes.
Occlusion, clutter and changing environments remain challenges; small occluded LM-O objects score lowest.
Detection of occluded objects, especially amodal detection of occluded unseen instances, is open.
High-density stochastic stacking with multi-instance ambiguity and heavy occlusion is open.
Heavy occlusion, translucent covers and opaque distractors break transparent-object pose.
Heavy occlusion depresses RGB-D method performance.

benchmark_evidence: GraspClutter6D high occlusion / ADD(-S): FoundationPose 55.0, MegaPose 42.3 (77.9 at low occlusion), GDR-Net 27.7, FFB6D 13.2 (839)
PACE instance-level / AR with ground-truth detections: PPF 52.2 versus CosyPose 4.4, SurfEmb 9.0, GDRNPP 7.0 (1316)
LM-O / ADD(-S): 6D-Diff mean 79.6 with ape 60.6, cat 63.2, duck 67.2 (3)
HouseCat6D / 3D IoU50: VI-Net box 12.7, remote 17.1 (1321)
LM vs LM-O / ADD(-S): occlusion-specific methods do not outperform general methods (1020)
ClearPose Opaque Distractor / ADD<10cm accuracy: FFB6D variants 0.5-2.4% (1317)
MessyKitchens / object-level IoU: best 0.445 in contact-rich clutter (405)
clusters.settings: Static cluttered tabletops, piles and industrial bins with RGB or RGB-D: LM-O, GraspClutter6D, PACE, HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, ClearPose, XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes and MessyKitchens; BOP amodal detection; instance-level, category-level and unseen-object pose, plus single-image object-level scene reconstruction.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Occlusion-specific methods do not beat general ones on LM-O (1020, 1328). Keypoint diffusion denoising (6D-Diff) still leaves small occluded LM-O objects at 60-67 ADD(-S) (3). Geometric PPF beats deep methods in PACE clutter but stays near 52 AR (1316). New clutter-heavy datasets (GraspClutter6D, PACE, XYZ-IBD, HouseCat6D) document the drop without fixing it. Occlusion-robust pose and better amodal detection are listed as future work (1088, 1313).

clusters.name: Transparent, reflective and thin objects break depth sensing
clusters.statement: Instance- and category-level 6D pose estimation and tracking fail on transparent, reflective, metallic and thin dark objects. Commodity RGB-D sensors return missing or biased depth on them and their RGB appearance varies with light and background; depth completion does not fix this, and even ground truth for them needs anti-reflection or vanishing spray.
clusters.description: Structured-light, active-stereo, ToF and mobile LiDAR sensors return invalid or biased depth on glass, cutlery, polished metal and thin dark markers. As a result, depth-based fitting, NOCS lifting and feature-based trackers such as BundleTrack break, even with perfect segmentation and NOCS maps. The RGB appearance of these objects changes with light, viewpoint and background, and render-and-compare refinement fails because realistic rendering of refractive or reflective surfaces is not available. Benchmarks largely avoid the problem: six of seven BOP core datasets are opaque and diffuse, GraspClutter6D excludes such objects from accuracy evaluation, TAPVid-3D evaluates only opaque solids, and ground-truth scanning needs spray. Depth completion gives little benefit for pose, and polarization has been added as a modality, but no method using it is yet shown to close the gap.

evidence_items.item: Raw sensor depth on transparent objects drops pose accuracy sharply, and depth completion (TransCG) gives little benefit for pose estimation.

Commodity structured-light, stereo and ToF sensors fail on reflection and refraction; the ToF sensor gives invalid depth on reflective objects and misses glassware, and NOCS lifting is sensitive to these depth artifacts even with accurate segmentation and NOCS maps.
Commodity depth sensing breaks down on specular metal, so the dataset needs anti-reflection spray for ground truth; depth sensors are biased on specular surfaces.
Structured-light depth noise on transparent and reflective objects impairs depth-based fitting, and BundleTrack fails on transparent or specular objects.

Metallic and transparent objects change appearance with light and viewpoint; handling them is largely unsolved even at instance level, and render-and-compare refinement fails for reflective or refractive objects.
Metallic and transparent surfaces are poorly handled; most BOP core datasets are opaque and diffuse.
The reflective, thin-structured Object 5 gets very low AR (EPOS 0.00, DOPE 0.00, FoundationPose model-based 0.31).
State-of-the-art pseudo-labelers struggle with symmetric, transparent and reflective objects, so many labels still need manual refinement.
Reflective and transparent objects cause depth sensor artifacts and are excluded from accuracy evaluation.
Sensor depth makes 2D-to-3D lifting inaccurate even with perfect NOCS maps; glass and tube suffer most, and the meshes needed vanishing spray.
Only solid, opaque objects are evaluated in the 3D point tracking benchmark.
Thin dark markers with high depth error (black_marker depth-ADD 0.769 m) remain poor even for DTTDNet (ADD AUC 44.08).
Glare and reflective, perforated and thin objects make category-level detection and pose hard.

benchmark_evidence: ClearPose Translucent Cover / accuracy: all methods 4.5-14.4% (1317)
ClearPose New Background / ADD(-S): best about 58 versus about 90 on opaque datasets (1317)
PhoCaL seen objects / 3D IoU25 and IoU50 (NOCS): glassware 4.00 / 0.06, cutlery 4.89 / 0.01, teapot 0.00 / 0.00 (1322)
IndustryShapes Classic / BOP AR on reflective thin Object 5: EPOS 0.00, DOPE 0.00, FoundationPose model-based 0.31 (837)
HouseCat6D / mean IoU75 with ground-truth NOCS maps and sensor depth: 22.6 percent; NOCS* IoU50 tube 29.1 and glass 68.0, the two worst categories (1321)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD AUC: DTTDNet black_marker 44.08 (1319)
BOP core / material coverage: six of seven core datasets contain only opaque, diffusely reflecting objects (1020, 1328)
clusters.settings: RGB-D tabletop clutter and industrial scenes with structured-light (RealSense D415), active-stereo, ToF (RealSense L515) and iPhone LiDAR sensors: ClearPose, PhoCaL, HouseCat6D, Omni6DPose ROPE, XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes, GraspClutter6D, HANDAL and DTTD-Mobile. Covers instance-level and category-level pose, model-free tracking (BundleTrack), pseudo-label annotation (DynOPETs) and monocular RGB surveys.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Depth completion before pose estimation (TransCG) gives little benefit (1317). Polarization cameras are added as a modality (1321, 1322), but no method using them is reported to close the gap. For ground truth, objects are sprayed with anti-reflection or vanishing spray (402, 839, 1321, 1322) or left out of accuracy evaluation (839, 444), which avoids the sensing problem rather than solving it. Proposed: comparing RGB-only and RGB-D methods on transparent objects (1020, 1317), neural rendering with lighting context (1317), and transparent-object pose as a research direction (1088).

clusters.name: Category-level pose does not scale across vocabularies
clusters.statement: Category-level and multi-object pose networks lose most of their accuracy as the number of categories or instances grows, and they do not generalize to unseen categories or high intra-class variation, because they rely on fixed per-category shape priors, per-category training and few real training categories.
clusters.description: Large-vocabulary benchmarks show sharp declines. HS-Pose falls from 62.52 to 14.42 percent 5deg2cm as fine-tuning grows from 3 to 48 categories, and the best method reaches 8.28 percent on 166 categories and 3.24 percent on unseen ones. Training one network on all PACE instances causes underfitting, with drops of 57-78 points, and NOCS scores 0.0 on Omni6DPose's hundreds of categories. Shape-prior methods (SPD, SGPA, CASS) generalize poorly in the wild, and category methods interpolate between object origins when an object lies between two categories. The surveys add that standard datasets (NOCS, DREDS) have little intra-category variation, that multi-object models still trail per-object models, and that training a network per category is unaffordable on mobile devices.

evidence_items.item: Accuracy declines as the category count grows (HS-Pose 5deg2cm 62.52% to 14.42%); rotation generalization fails on large vocabularies and unseen categories, and shape-prior methods generalize poorly.
Training on all instances causes underfitting (GDRNPP 88.2 for single instances, 9.7 for all instances).
RGB-only canonical-shape prediction (NOCS) scores 0.0 as category diversity grows, and GenPose++ leaves substantial room for improvement.
A pre-defined categorical mesh prior fixes the deformation model per category; RePoNet may not generalise to unseen categories, and CASS scores 0 on Wild6D pose metrics.

Category-level methods interpolate between object origins when an object lies between two categories; NOCS and DREDS have little intra-category variation; multi-object estimators trail per-object ones; comparisons use inconsistent train-test splits.
Category-level methods cannot generalize to unseen categories and need retraining with new data; few-shot category-level generalization is open.
High intra-class variance limits category-level generalisation.

Category-level methods need many annotated samples per category and generalise poorly to instances of very different shape or appearance; training and deploying a network per category is unaffordable for mobile AR.
Category-level generalisation to novel instances is open, especially for monocular methods that need large synthetic pretraining.

benchmark_evidence: Omni6D test (166 categories) / 5deg2cm: best 8.28 (DualPoseNet); unseen categories best 3.24 (350)
Omni6D fine-tuning from cls3 to cls48 / 5deg2cm: HS-Pose 62.52 to 14.42 (350)
ROPE / VUS@5deg2cm and AUC@IoU75: best GenPose++ 10.0 / 2.0; NOCS 0.0 (347)
PACE Real2Real all categories / AR and AP: drops of 57-78 points versus single-instance fitting; GDRNPP 88.2 to 9.7 (348, 1316)
PACE category-level / AP@0:20deg,0:5cm: best CPPF++ 9.9 on rigid objects (348)
Wild6D / 5deg2cm: best RePoNet-semi 29.5; Shape-Prior 2.6; CASS 0 (1323)
HouseCat6D / 10deg5cm: best VI-Net 29.1; NOCS 4.8 (1321)
PhoCaL mostly unseen objects / 3D IoU25 and IoU50: NOCS 22.70 / 0.17 (1322)
DynOPETs COPE-119 / 5deg2cm: AGPose 61.61, NOCS 11.57 (825)
clusters.settings: RGB-D category-level pose on household categories and large vocabularies: Omni6D (166 categories), Omni6DPose ROPE, PACE, Wild6D, HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, DynOPETs COPE-119 and HANDAL. Also multi-object instance-level training (PACE, BOP) and mobile AR deployment (OnePose).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Shape priors (SPD, SGPA), fine-tuning on growing category sets, diffusion pose (GenPose++), semi-supervised RePoNet and large synthetic sets (Omni6D, SOPE) all lose accuracy as diversity grows (350, 347, 1323). Proposed: representing shape as a deformation of a unit sphere instead of a category prior (1323), larger foundation models (348, 1316), few-shot category-level methods (1088), formal category taxonomies or ontologies (1020), and new training strategies for growing diversity (350).

clusters.name: Monocular RGB cannot fix depth and metric scale
clusters.statement: From RGB alone (smart glasses, monocular video), object translation along the viewing ray and metric scale are poorly constrained. RGB-only object pose and monocular 3D point tracking therefore trail RGB-D by a large and reportedly widening margin, and pose refinement without depth or textured models remains unsolved.
clusters.description: The surveys report that monocular category-level pose lags far behind RGB-D on CAMERA25/REAL275, that the gap appears to be widening, and that monocular methods are least accurate in translation. HOPE and Gen6D identify error along the projection ray as the main RGB-only error source, since for small, far objects a 1-2 pixel scale error becomes a large depth offset. HANDAL's RGB-only CenterPose needs ground-truth dimensions and halves its 3D IoU without depth, and BOP 2023 reports that RGB-only unrefined methods lose substantial accuracy against refined RGB-D pipelines. In 3D point tracking, accurate 2D tracks become poor 3D tracks because monocular depth is noisy, drifts in scale over time and is inconsistent across space. Smart-glass settings force RGB-only input, and evaluation often rescales predictions with ground-truth scale or depth, which hides the problem.

evidence_items.item: Monocular category-level pose lags far behind RGB-D on CAMERA25/REAL275, and the gap appears to widen; refinement without depth and without textured models is open.
Monocular methods are less accurate in translation than depth-based methods; monocular refinement without depth or ICP is open.
Errors along the projection ray are a significant source of error for RGB-only methods.
Without training on the object, depth along the viewing ray is poorly estimated for small, far objects, where a 1-2 pixel scale error causes a large depth offset.
Noisy monocular depth produces noisy 3D tracks even when 2D tracks are accurate; depth scale drifts over time and is inconsistent across space.
Baseline CenterPose needs ground-truth object dimensions, and its RGB-only 3D IoU and ADD AUC are much lower than with depth-based rescaling.
Large video datasets without depth (Objectron, CO3D) leave pose ambiguities, and COLMAP depth is too erroneous.
High-precision unseen-object pose from a single RGB image without depth is open; the survey proposes foundation-model monocular depth.
Evaluation is RGB-only because smart glasses lack depth, so RGB-D methods such as FoundationPose are excluded.
RGB-only unrefined methods lose substantial accuracy relative to refined RGB-D pipelines.

benchmark_evidence: TAPVid-3D full_eval / 3D-AJ: best 9.3 with median scaling (static baseline 4.9) and 20.6 with per-trajectory scaling, while the same trackers reach 2D-AJ 59.1 (444)
TAPVid-3D DriveTrack / 3D-AJ: ZoeDepth-based methods 5.0-5.4, near the static baseline 3.9 (444)
HANDAL / 3D IoU>50% and ADD AUC (CenterPose): 0.340 and 0.407 RGB-only versus 0.670 and 0.588 with depth (1314)
PhoCaL mostly unseen / 3D IoU25: monocular CPS 4.3 (1322)
ROPE / VUS@5deg2cm: RGB-only NOCS 0.0 (347)
CAMERA25 / REAL275: large and apparently widening gap between RGB-only and RGB-D category-level pose (1020; no single number given)
clusters.settings: Single RGB images and monocular RGB video: BOP RGB tracks, LINEMOD, HOPE, GenMOP, HANDAL, PhoCaL, Omni6DPose, CAMERA25/REAL275 and Wild6D; TAPVid-3D (Aria Digital Twin, DriveTrack, Panoptic Studio); egocentric smart-glass RGB (EgoXtreme); RGB tracking of hand-held objects (OmniPose6D on HO3D with depth discarded).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Evaluation rescales predictions to ground-truth scale (444) or uses ground-truth depth for rescaling (1314), which hides the problem. COLMAP and ZoeDepth combinations improve 3D tracks only slightly and fail on outdoor or dynamic content (444). RGB-D refinement closes the gap but is not available on glasses (201). Proposed: foundation-model monocular depth for single-RGB pose (1088), combining 2D tracking, monocular depth and SfM (444), and monocular depth or occupancy representations (1328).

clusters.name: Symmetry ambiguity needs known symmetries and lacks metrics
clusters.statement: Learned 6D pose estimators lose accuracy unless object symmetries are known in advance and handled during training. They output a single deterministic pose where symmetry or partial observation makes the answer multimodal, and no metric treats discrete and continuous symmetries consistently.
clusters.description: The surveys state that deep methods lose accuracy when symmetries are not handled at training time, and that symmetries usually must be known beforehand. Yet symmetry transformations were not even available for MegaPose's training objects in BOP 2023. Generative pose models do not solve this: GenPose's energy-based aggregation fails on the discontinuous multimodal distributions that discrete symmetries produce, and non-symmetry-aware evaluation drops sharply on Omni6D. The metrics are contested as well. ADD over-estimates and ADD-S under-estimates error for symmetric objects, the BOP symmetry definition depends on visual similarity, and no single metric covers both finite and infinite ambiguity. Symmetric industrial parts and bowls also defeat pseudo-labelers, and the surveys call for uncertainty modelling instead of single deterministic outputs.

evidence_items.item: Deep methods lose accuracy when visual symmetries are not considered at training time; symmetries often must be known beforehand, and uncertainty estimation for downstream decisions is open.
Symmetry handling without known symmetries is an open challenge.
Energy-based aggregation (GenPose) fails on discontinuous multimodal distributions from discrete symmetries; ambiguity from symmetry and partial observation remains.
ADD over-estimates and ADD-S under-estimates error for symmetric objects; the BOP symmetry definition requires visual similarity.
A unified metric for objects with finite and infinite pose ambiguity is missing; ADD-S is not comparable to ADD, and IADD for infinite axes falls back to center distance.
Models output a single deterministic pose, which limits robustness in ambiguous or occluded conditions.
Non-symmetry-aware evaluation drops sharply given widespread rotational symmetry; handling multi-axis rotational symmetry is open.
FoundationPose pseudo-labels remain poor for symmetric objects such as bowls after EKF/RTS refinement.
Symmetry transformations are not available for MegaPose training objects.
Highly reflective, texture-less, geometrically symmetric parts are an open problem.

benchmark_evidence: LINEMOD / ADD(S)-0.1d and Proj2D: OnePose++ on glue 48.0 and 51.8 (1325)
HOPE / BOP AR: evaluation needs MSSD/VSD/MSPD because ADD and ADD-S mis-estimate symmetric error (1315; no specific gap number)
clusters.settings: Rigid household and industrial objects with discrete or continuous rotational symmetry (bowls, cans, glue bottles, metal parts). Single-image RGB and RGB-D instance-, category- and unseen-object pose on LINEMOD, Omni6D, Omni6DPose ROPE, HOPE, the GraspNet-1Billion unseen benchmark, XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes and BOP 2023, plus pseudo-label annotation (DynOPETs).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Symmetry-aware losses and metrics (ADD-S, BOP MSSD/MSPD) need symmetry labels supplied in advance (350, 1315). A sampled IADD metric trades precision for efficiency (1327). Generative diffusion or energy-based pose models (GenPose, GenPose++) still fail on discrete symmetries (347). Proposed: keypoint-based symmetry handling and new pose representations (1020, 1328), and uncertainty modelling (1088).

clusters.name: Object pose trackers drift and cannot recover
clusters.statement: 6D object pose trackers, especially model-free ones, drift over long sequences, fail under large inter-frame displacement or simultaneous camera and object motion, and cannot re-acquire an object once they lose it. Most evaluations start from a ground-truth initial pose or score single images only.
clusters.description: PACE reports that the model-free tracker BundleTrack cannot recover once it loses the object. Model-free tracking stays under 13 percent 5deg5cm in clutter, and the best model-based tracker reaches 38.1 ADD(-S) AUC. EgoXtreme shows that propagating the previous pose fails under large inter-frame displacement, and that fusion strategies give initial poses the current frame cannot correct. DynOPETs reports drift in relative point-tracking poses and FoundationPose failures when camera and object move together. OmniPose6D handles only short offline windows and breaks when the object barely moves, and TAPVid-3D reports monocular depth scale drifting over time. BOP and several datasets score per image, Omni6DPose initialises tracking from a perturbed ground-truth pose, and no dedicated metric exists for short-term object tracking.

evidence_items.item: Model-free trackers cannot recover once the object is lost (BundleTrack); robust tracking in clutter and occlusion with recovery after loss is open.
Direct temporal propagation of the previous pose fails with large inter-frame displacement in fast motion, and fusion propagation gives poor initial poses that the current frame cannot correct.
The point-tracking relative pose branch drifts over long sequences, and FoundationPose has failure sequences under simultaneous camera and object motion.

The pipeline handles only short-term windows of a few keyframes and runs offline; small object translation and stationary frames break SfM assumptions, and no dedicated metric for short-term object pose tracking exists.
Tracking is initialized from a perturbed ground-truth pose; BundleTrack reaches 1.3 at 5deg5cm with 46.9 deg rotation error.
BOP evaluation is per image, not temporal tracking.
Uncertainty modelling and temporal consistency for dynamic scenes remain open; fast motion requires temporal consistency to avoid jitter.
Monocular depth scale drifts over time, and SfM pipelines fail on moving content.
Gen6D is a static per-frame estimator with no temporal tracking.

benchmark_evidence: PACE / ADD(-S) AUC (model-based tracking): best ICG 38.1 on rigid objects (348, 1316)
PACE / 5deg5cm (model-free tracking): best under 13% (CAPTRA 12.9); BundleTrack 6.4 (1316)
ROPE tracking / 5deg5cm: best 15.9; BundleTrack 1.3 with Rerr 46.9 deg (347)
EgoXtreme sports, golf and pingpong / ADD(-S) recall at 0.1d: per-frame 0.08 and 0.53; best temporal strategy below 1.6 percent (201)
DynOPETs / ATE: MaskFusion 0.320 m, DROID-SLAM 0.173 m versus FoundationPose 0.037 m (825)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD AUC: BundleSDF 0.00 (no tracking) on several objects (1319)
clusters.settings: RGB-D and RGB video of moving objects: PACE clutter tracking, Omni6DPose ROPE tracking, DynOPETs (moving camera plus moving object), EgoXtreme fast egocentric sports motion, OmniPose6D on HO3D/YCBInEOAT/DexYCB, DTTD-Mobile AR tracking, and TAPVid-3D long-range 3D point tracks. Per-image evaluation in BOP 2023/2024, Gen6D and the GraspNet-1Billion unseen benchmark.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Trackers tried: BundleTrack, BundleSDF, CAPTRA, ICG and FoundationPose tracking (1316, 347, 825). Also temporal propagation and fusion of the previous pose (201), EKF/RTS smoothing (825), and SfM over short windows (1286). Proposed: hybrid temporal strategies with dynamic quality assessment (201), integrated keypoint-and-pose refinement like DROID-SLAM (1286), and temporal consistency with uncertainty modelling (1088).

clusters.name: Hand-held object pose under hand occlusion
clusters.statement: Pose estimation of objects held and moved by hands (egocentric headset views, objects partly covered by the holding hand) is markedly less accurate than on static tabletop benchmarks. Most pose datasets contain no hands or no hand annotations, so this condition is barely measured and joint hand-object pose is left to future work.
clusters.description: BOP 2024 reports a clear accuracy drop on BOP-H3 (egocentric, hand-held AR/VR data) relative to BOP-Classic-Core, and its model-free hand-manipulation onboarding track drew no submissions. OmniPose6D attributes its weaker DexYCB results to heavy hand occlusion and small visible object area. EgoXtreme provides no 3D hand labels because labelling hands under blur and speed is itself unsolved. The IJCV survey notes that hand-object pose methods depend on CAD models and degrade when object features are occluded. Datasets either exclude hands (static bins, piles and kitchen scenes), mask them out (Aria Digital Twin in TAPVid-3D), or omit hand annotations (EgoXtreme, DynOPETs). Joint hand-object estimation and hand labels from mocap plus parametric hand models are listed only as future work.

evidence_items.item: Accuracy drops on BOP-H3 (egocentric, hand-held, AR/VR headset data) relative to BOP-Classic-Core; onboarding from dynamic hand-manipulation video remains largely unaddressed.
Heavy hand occlusion and far objects with small visible area degrade tracking on DexYCB; joint hand and object pose estimation is future work.
No 3D hand pose annotations are provided because labelling hand articulation under blur and speed is unsolved; hand-held object pose from egocentric RGB under fast motion is not yet usable.
Hand-object interaction pose methods depend on object CAD models that are hard to obtain, and they degrade when object features are missing or occluded.
Sequences have one dynamic object and no annotated hands; adding hand pose annotations is future work, and HOT3D-type egocentric datasets have limited object variety.
In existing RGB-D scan datasets, objects are heavily occluded by hands or only partially visible.
Operator hands are not modelled in the ADT digital replicas and are masked out for visibility.
Scenes are static with no humans or hands, a restrictive assumption shared by XYZ-IBD, MessyKitchens and IndustryShapes.
Gen6D models no hand-object interaction.

benchmark_evidence: BOP-H3 / model-based 6D detection AP: GigaPose+GenFlow 31.2 versus 50.4 on BOP-Classic-Core (1312)
BOP-H3 / 2D detection AP: MUSE 39.0 versus 52.0 on BOP-Classic-Core (1312)
BOP-H3 / model-free 6D detection: no submissions (1312)
EgoXtreme sports (hand-held golf club, pingpong) / ADD(-S) recall at 0.1d: below 1.6 percent for all strategies (201)
DexYCB (S3, subject 0) / pose tracking: below HO3D, attributed to heavy hand occlusion and distant objects (1286; no number given)
clusters.settings: Egocentric AR/VR headsets (BOP-H3 with HOT3D and HANDAL; EgoXtreme on Aria glasses); hand-held object video (DexYCB and HO3D in OmniPose6D); mocap-instrumented desktops (DynOPETs, Aria Digital Twin); and, for contrast, static benchmarks without hands (XYZ-IBD, MessyKitchens, IndustryShapes, GraspClutter6D).
clusters.attempted_fixes: BOP added the hand-held BOP-H3 datasets, which drew few submissions (1312). Hands are masked out of evaluation (444) or kept out of scenes (402, 405, 837, 839). OmniPose6D tracks hand-held objects with RGB SfM over short windows only and fails under hand occlusion (1286).
