Proposed: hand labels from mocap combined with parametric hand models (201), joint hand-object estimation (1286), hand pose annotations for AR/MR (825), and cross-modal tactile and contact cues (1088).

clusters.name: Articulated and deformable objects lack pose definitions
clusters.statement: Articulated and deformable objects are excluded or treated as rigid in a fixed default state, and every tested estimator and tracker nearly fails on movable parts. There is no common pose definition, canonical pose or metric for them.
clusters.description: PACE is the only paper in this group that measures articulated objects. There, model-based tracking accuracy falls from 38.1 to 10.1 ADD(-S) AUC, and category-level AP falls to about 1. HANDAL treats articulated tools as rigid in a default state, and PhoCaL reports that deformable surfaces break tip-based annotation and ICP refinement. MessyKitchens lists physically plausible reconstruction including deformations as open. The surveys state that deformable and articulated objects have no common pose definition, canonical pose or metric, and the IJCV survey names multiple degrees of freedom and self-occlusion as the obstacles. Most methods and benchmarks in the group assume rigid objects outright (6D-Diff, BOP 2023 and 2024, OmniPose6D, OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D, the unseen-object benchmark).

evidence_items.item: All methods struggle on articulated objects; category-level AP is near 0 on most strict metrics.
Model-based tracking reaches 38.1% ADD(-S) AUC on rigid objects versus 10.1% on articulated objects.
Deformable and articulated objects have no common pose definition or metric; most methods and datasets assume rigid objects.
Deformable and articulated objects need canonical poses and metrics.
Articulated objects are treated as rigid in a fixed default state; articulated-object research is future work.
Articulated object pose estimation (multiple DoF, self-occlusion) is an open problem.
Deformable surfaces such as empty boxes degrade tip-based surface measurement and ICP refinement; annotating deformable objects is open.
Physically plausible reconstruction, including deformations and other physical parameters, is open; scenes are static and rigid.
The unseen-object benchmark covers only rigid table-top objects in static single frames.

benchmark_evidence: PACE / ADD(-S) AUC (model-based tracking): ICG 38.1 rigid versus 10.1 articulated; RBOT 7.4 versus 0.5 (348, 1316)
PACE / 5deg5cm (model-free tracking): CAPTRA 12.9 rigid versus 4.4 articulated (348)
PACE / category-level AP@0:20deg,0:5cm: CPPF++ 9.9 rigid versus 1.1 articulated (348)
clusters.settings: PACE cluttered real scenes with articulated objects; HANDAL tools with movable parts; PhoCaL deformable boxes; MessyKitchens static rigid kitchenware. Rigid-only assumptions in BOP 2023/2024, 6D-Diff, OmniPose6D, OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D and the GraspNet-1Billion unseen benchmark.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Articulated objects are treated as rigid in a default state (1314). None of the tested rigid trackers or category methods handle them, and CAPTRA, which was designed for articulation, reaches 4.4% 5deg5cm on PACE (348, 1316). Proposed: formal pose definitions and metrics for deformable and articulated objects (1020, 1328), and articulated pose estimation as a research direction (1088, 1314).

clusters.name: Accurate unseen-object pose is far from real time
clusters.statement: The most accurate unseen-object and generative 6D pose methods take seconds to tens of seconds per image (template matching, multi-hypothesis refinement, iterative diffusion), and unseen-object estimators run below a few frames per second, so they cannot drive real-time tracking, AR or robot control.
clusters.description: BOP 2023 and 2024 report that the best unseen-object methods need 24.9-34.6 s per image, against 2.7 s for seen-object methods, and that faster entries such as SAM6D lose accuracy. DynOPETs measures every unseen-object estimator below 4 FPS, with FoundationPose at 0.98 FPS. Diffusion-based category pose (GenPose++) is slowed by iterative refinement, and OmniPose6D runs offline. The surveys note that template-matching runtime grows with template count up to minutes, raise the energy cost of per-object training, and call for lightweight models for mobile and robot use. OnePose notes that visual-localisation pipelines take seconds per frame and cannot track moving objects.

evidence_items.item: The most accurate unseen-object method is slow (24.9 s per image); even sub-second methods need further speed-up for real-time use.
Unseen-object pose estimation is slow (GenFlow-MultiHypo16 34.58 s per image), and efficiency must improve for real-time applications.
All unseen-object pose methods run below 4 FPS; FoundationPose runs at 0.98 FPS.
GenPose++ is slowed by iterative diffusion refinement; faster diffusion samplers are needed for real-time use.
Novel-object pose runtime grows with the number of templates, up to minutes, and per-object training and template matching carry an environmental cost.
Visual localization pipelines take seconds per frame and cannot track moving objects in real time.
Large models have inefficient runtime; lightweighting for mobile and robot deployment is needed.
The pipeline runs offline, and improving its speed is future work.

benchmark_evidence: BOP-Classic-Core / AR and time (unseen 6D localization): FreeZeV2.1 82.1 AR at 24.9 s per image versus seen-object 85.6 AR at 2.7 s (1312)
BOP core 2023 / AR and time: GenFlow-MultiHypo16 34.58 s per image; fastest, SAM6D, 3.87 s at 61.6 AR (1313)
DynOPETs UOPE-56 / FPS: all methods below 4 FPS, FoundationPose 0.98 (825)
ROPE tracking / FPS: GenPose++ 17.8 versus CATRE 38.5 (347)
OnePose / matching runtime: HLoc 618 ms versus OnePose 58 ms per frame (1324)
clusters.settings: Single-image unseen-object 6D localisation on BOP core (RGB-D); DynOPETs moving-camera sequences; Omni6DPose category-level tracking; OnePose mobile AR; offline SfM tracking (OmniPose6D); iterative diffusion keypoints (6D-Diff, no runtime reported); real-time pose with sparse depth at range (DTTD).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Sparse matching instead of full visual localisation (OnePose, 58 ms per frame), which then fails on textureless objects (1324). Fewer hypotheses and faster proposal generators (FastSAM in CNOS, SAM6D at 3.87 s), which trade accuracy for speed (1313). Proposed: faster diffusion samplers (347), model lightweighting (1088), template-free and training-free methods (1020), and faster pipelines (1286, 1312).

clusters.name: Real consumer depth noise collapses RGB-D pose
clusters.statement: RGB-D pose estimators and depth-based 2D-to-3D lifting degrade sharply on real sensor depth that is low-resolution, noisy at edges, holey or captured at long range (mobile LiDAR, stereo or structured light beyond one metre, passive stereo, real instead of simulated depth), even for opaque objects with segmentation given.
clusters.description: DTTDNet frames depth noise as the core gap. iPhone LiDAR depth is low resolution, has long-tail non-Gaussian errors at object edges and a mean error of about 0.25 m, and methods strong on YCB-Video lose 25 to 40 ADD-S AUC points on it. DTTD reports that stereo and structured-light depth is noisy beyond one metre and that hole filling adds error. HouseCat6D and PhoCaL show that NOCS lifting fails with real sensor depth even when the NOCS maps are ground truth, and PACE attributes the sim-to-real collapse of depth-input category methods to real depth noise. Point-cloud registration to a full mesh also fails on partial, noisy scene clouds, and scale from partial clouds is ambiguous. Event cameras force passive stereo depth, which lowers depth resolution.

evidence_items.item: RGB-D 6DoF pose methods degrade sharply under depth measurement inaccuracies; iPhone LiDAR depth is low resolution with long-tail non-Gaussian noise at object edges and a mean error around 0.25 m, which impairs MegaPose's coarse module.
Older stereo and structured-light depth sensors are noisy beyond one metre and leave holes; hole filling adds interpolation error at longer range and makes FFB6D results unstable.
Depth-input category methods collapse from sim to real because of real depth noise (HS-Pose 81.2 to 1.1).
Sensor depth makes 2D-to-3D lifting inaccurate even with perfect NOCS maps; mean IoU75 drops to 22.6 percent with ground-truth NOCS.
Partially observed, noisy scene point clouds degrade registration-style correspondence, and registering a partial-view cloud to a full mesh fails at low overlap.
Scale from partial, noisy point clouds is ambiguous.
Lifting from a NOCS map to a 6D pose is sensitive to depth artifacts even with accurate segmentation and NOCS maps.
Passive depth mode was forced because the active IR pattern corrupts events, reducing depth resolution.

benchmark_evidence: YCB-Video vs DTTD-Mobile / ADD-S AUC on overlapping objects: ES6D 85.67 to 45.20, MegaPose 88.18 to 63.99, MegaPose on tuna_can 91.03 to 22.11 (1319)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD AUC: ES6D 13.25, BundleSDF 46.86, MegaPose-RGBD 49.02, DenseFusion 69.67, DTTDNet 73.99 (1319)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD(1cm): best configuration 25.85 percent (1319)
DTTD (Azure Kinect, 1-2 m) / ADD AUC: FFB6D 14.33, and 11.56 without hole filling (1318)
HouseCat6D / mean IoU75 with ground-truth NOCS maps and sensor depth: 22.6 percent (1321)
PACE sim-to-real / AP: depth-input HS-Pose 1.1 (348, 1316)
GraspNet-1Billion / ADD AUC: registration baselines 1.5-13.5 (1327)
clusters.settings: Single RGB-D views from iPhone LiDAR (DTTD-Mobile), Azure Kinect at 1-2 m (DTTD), RealSense structured light and active stereo (PACE, HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, Omni6DPose), and passive stereo forced by event-camera interference (YCB-Ev). Covers instance-level RGB-D pose, category-level NOCS lifting and point-cloud registration to meshes.
clusters.attempted_fixes: DTTDNet adds depth-noise-robust fusion and Chamfer supervision and reaches 73.99 ADD AUC, but scores 44.08 on thin dark markers and about 25 percent ADD(1cm) (1319). Stereo hole filling helps little and adds error at range (1318). Proposed: advanced sim-to-real techniques for depth noise (348, 1316) and solutions compatible with inexpensive depth sensors (1319).

clusters.name: Pose metrics miss manipulation and AR tolerances
clusters.statement: Pose and reconstruction quality is judged by geometric metrics at centimetre tolerance (ADD, Chamfer, 5deg5cm) that poorly predict grasp success and fall short of the sub-millimetre accuracy industrial grasping needs or the millimetre accuracy at 1-2 m that AR needs. Errors are not traced through to the downstream task, and real grasp success in clutter stays low.
clusters.description: A simulated grasping benchmark finds that pose and reconstruction errors are evaluated in isolation and that 2D projection and pure rotation metrics poorly predict grasp success. Grasp success drops sharply once pose error passes a threshold, and reconstructed meshes with low Chamfer error can still produce colliding grasps. Industrial and AR papers state that centimetre-level errors acceptable on household benchmarks cause grasp failure at sub-millimetre tolerance, or miss the millimetre accuracy needed at room-scale distances. Under a strict 1 cm threshold, the best method on mobile depth reaches about a quarter of frames. Real-robot grasp trials succeed 33 to 68 percent of the time, and some failures come from open-loop approach motions even when the grasp pose is correct. The surveys ask for uncertainty estimates usable by downstream robot decisions, and HANDAL adds that functional grasps may need affordance labels and anthropomorphic hands.

evidence_items.item: Pose estimators and reconstructions are evaluated in isolation with geometric metrics; 2D projection and pure rotation error metrics poorly predict grasp success, success drops sharply once pose error exceeds a threshold, and a perfect pose cannot rescue grasps planned on a flawed mesh.
Centimeter-level errors acceptable for household objects cause grasp failure under industrial sub-millimeter tolerance.
AR digital twins need millimetre accuracy at 1-2 m, whereas centimetre accuracy is enough for grasping; existing datasets tolerate centimetre annotation errors.
Under the strict 1 cm threshold, DTTDNet reaches only about 24-26 percent ADD(1cm).
ADD and ADD-S mis-estimate error for symmetric objects, cuboids are less resistant to small rotation errors, and some benchmark items are unsuitable in size, shape or weight for grippers.
Uncertainty estimation for downstream robot decisions is open, as is the relation to generalist manipulation policies that act without explicit poses.
Open-loop approach trajectories collide or fail despite correct grasp poses; gripper-aware reactive grasping is needed.
Learning functional affordances (handles) for task-oriented grasping is open, and functional grasps may need anthropomorphic hands.
Real-world grasping with unseen objects, backgrounds and a different sensor succeeds only 33.3-60 percent of the time.

benchmark_evidence: YCB-V in PyBullet / grasp success: MegaPose poses 59.4% versus FoundationPose 89.9% (836)
YCB-V reconstructed meshes / grasp generation success: most reconstructions yield clearly fewer viable grasps than ground-truth CAD, dominated by collisions (836)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD(1cm): best 25.85 percent (1319)
HOPE / MeanSSD recall: CosyPose-LS 72% within 2 cm and 83% within 10 cm (1315)
Real-world 15-object pile / grasp success: best 67.9%, AnyGrasp 59.6% (839)
HouseCat6D real-world Franka grasping / success: 33.3-60 percent on remote and unknown objects (1321)
clusters.settings: Simulated parallel-jaw grasping on YCB-V objects (PyBullet), industrial bin picking (XYZ-IBD), AR digital-twin tracking at 1-2 m (DTTD, DTTD-Mobile), real robot grasping in piles (GraspClutter6D) and households (HouseCat6D), HOPE grocery objects, HANDAL handle affordances, and Omni6DPose downstream integration.
clusters.attempted_fixes: A simulation benchmark links pose and mesh error to grasp outcome, but only with open-loop execution and without physical validation yet (836). Existing remedies are the BOP MSSD/MSPD/VSD metrics and grasp-annotated datasets (GraspClutter6D, HouseCat6D); training on cluttered real data raises real grasp success to 67.9% (839). Proposed: physical validation and extension to placement and assembly (836), gripper-aware reactive grasping (839), uncertainty estimation (1020), integrating pose modules into downstream manipulation (347), and affordance annotations beyond handles (1314).

clusters.name: Small and distant objects get too few pixels
clusters.statement: Objects that are small or far from the camera (few pixels, low resolution, sparse depth) are posed much worse than large, near ones. Matching finds too few correspondences, one or two pixels of scale error become a large depth error, and reconstruction-based model-free trackers fail at range.
clusters.description: Several method and dataset papers report their lowest scores on small objects (LM-O ape, LINEMOD ape, the OnePose small set). Gen6D explains that for small, distant objects a 1-2 pixel scale error produces a large depth offset. Correspondence methods (SuperGlue with RANSAC, FCGF) fail when the target covers few pixels, and local matching suffers on very low-resolution images. AR-range datasets show methods that are strong on YCB-Video losing half their ADD AUC at 1-2 m with a wider field of view, and BundleSDF cannot reconstruct objects at large distance or low resolution. OmniPose6D also lists far objects with small visible area as a cause of its DexYCB failures.

evidence_items.item: For small, distant objects a 1-2 pixel scale error causes a large depth offset, so Gen6D trails instance-specific methods on LINEMOD.
SuperGlue+RANSAC fails on YCB-Video because the target is too small, and FCGF correspondences are poor, especially for small objects.
BundleSDF fails to reconstruct objects at large distance or low resolution, giving 0.00 AUC on several objects.
Longer average distance and a wider field of view make low-level geometric and appearance features hard to learn; DenseFusion ADD AUC drops sharply versus YCB-Video on the same objects.
Far objects with small visible area degrade tracking on DexYCB.
Local feature matching suffers on very low-resolution images, and small LINEMOD objects remain weak (ape ADD(S) 31.2).
Accuracy is lowest on small LM-O objects (ape 60.6 ADD(-S)) versus 97.9 for the can.
OnePose 1cm-1deg success is 0.405 for small objects versus 0.629 for medium objects.

benchmark_evidence: LM-O / ADD(-S): ape 60.6 versus can 97.9 (3)
OnePose / 1cm-1deg success: small 0.405, medium 0.629, large 0.471 (1324)
LINEMOD / ADD(S)-0.1d: OnePose++ ape 31.2 (1325)
YCB-Video without retraining / IADD AUC: best 19.0 (1327)
DTTD vs YCB-V / ADD AUC (DenseFusion): spam_can 38.83 versus 79.94; tomato_can 38.62 versus 87.76; mustard 57.62 versus 94.92 (1318)
DTTD-Mobile / ADD AUC: BundleSDF 0.00 on cereal_box and all three markers (1319)
clusters.settings: Monocular RGB and RGB-D on LM-O, LINEMOD, YCB-Video and OnePose; AR-range RGB-D at 1-2 m (DTTD with Azure Kinect, DTTD-Mobile with iPhone LiDAR); distant hand-held objects in DexYCB; novel-object RGB-D registration (GraspNet-1Billion benchmark).
clusters.attempted_fixes: No paper reports a targeted fix. Methods rely on external detector crops or ground-truth boxes (1326, 1324, 1325), and keypoint diffusion denoising (6D-Diff) still leaves small objects lowest (3).

clusters.name: Motion blur, low light and smoke break RGB pose
clusters.statement: RGB-based object detection, 6D pose estimation and the ground-truth pipelines behind them degrade strongly under motion blur, fast motion, low or extreme lighting and smoke. Image restoration preprocessing does not help and often hurts, and event cameras, which tolerate these conditions, have no established pose algorithms or accurate ground truth.
clusters.description: EgoXtreme shows that zero-shot RGB pose estimators (FoundPose, GigaPose, PicoPose) collapse under extreme lighting, smoke and the blur and cropping of fast sports motion. Sparse matching often finds too few correspondences for PnP, and deblurring, dehazing and low-light enhancement lower recall further by adding artifacts. YCB-Ev introduces event cameras but reports that no established pose algorithm works on event data, and its RGB-based annotation fails under fast motion and low light. DTTD reports segmentation failing in dark lighting at range, and the IJCV survey lists low light and fast motion as failure conditions of RGB pipelines. Dataset builders avoid the problem with stop-and-go capture, fixed lighting or static scenes, and industrial, mobile and handheld datasets list variable lighting, glare and motion blur as open robustness problems.

evidence_items.item: RGB-only zero-shot estimators (FoundPose, GigaPose, PicoPose) degrade strongly under extreme lighting and smoke; deblur, dehaze and low-light enhancement do not help and often hurt; FoundPose often fails to get the minimum correspondences for PnP-RANSAC under cropping and blur.
Fast camera motion and low light defeat RGB-based annotation, and no established algorithms exist for object pose estimation on event data.
FFB6D segmentation fails in dark lighting, and dark lighting makes detection at longer range harder to learn.
Low light degrades RGB-only pipelines, and fast motion requires temporal consistency to avoid jitter.
Occlusion, clutter and variable, unconstrained lighting degrade performance.
Glare and extreme lighting, along with reflective and perforated objects, make category-level detection and pose hard.
Robustness under varied lighting is listed as an open problem for mobile AR pose.
Timestamp offset and motion blur in freely moving camera rigs remain a problem.
Capture uses stop-and-go robot motion to avoid motion blur.
Real-world transparent-object datasets are small, with limited lighting variation.

benchmark_evidence: EgoXtreme sports / ADD(-S) recall at 0.1d/0.2d/0.3d (PicoPose): 2.81 / 8.80 / 23.02, lowered further by preprocessing to 2.58 / 8.22 / 20.99 (201)
EgoXtreme emergency (smoke) / ADD(-S) recall at 0.1d: PicoPose 15.12 falls to 4.74 with dehazing (201)
EgoXtreme maintenance / ADD(-S) recall at 0.3d: 63.32 without preprocessing, 53.28 with combined preprocessing (201)
YCB-Ev / per-object recall (GDRNPP): 025_mug 0.005, 009_gelatin_box 0.02 (1320)
clusters.settings: Egocentric head-mounted RGB (Aria glasses) in sports, emergency smoke and maintenance scenarios; event camera plus passive-stereo RGB-D (YCB-Ev); Azure Kinect at 1-2 m in dark lighting (DTTD); industrial workcells with variable lighting (IndustryShapes); hand-held captures with glare (HANDAL); iPhone LiDAR AR (DTTD-Mobile); freely moving and robot-mounted capture rigs (HouseCat6D, PhoCaL); transparent-object captures (ClearPose).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Deblurring, dehazing and low-light enhancement before pose estimation lower recall (201), and temporal propagation fails under large displacement (201). ICG local tracking with manual keyframes is the annotation fallback (1320). Stop-and-go capture and fixed lighting avoid the condition rather than solve it (1322, 1318). Proposed: pose estimation directly on events plus synthetic event data via vid2e (1320), hybrid temporal strategies with quality assessment and outdoor evaluation (201), restoration methods that actually help downstream pose (201), and cross-modal inertial cues (1088).

clusters.name: Multi-object reconstruction is not physically consistent
clusters.statement: Methods that reconstruct or pose several objects in a cluttered real scene treat each object independently, which yields inter-object penetrations, floating objects and wrong contacts. The field lacks methods and accurately registered benchmarks for contact-consistent multi-object pose and shape.
clusters.description: MessyKitchens reports that single-image scene reconstruction with SAM 3D treats objects independently. This produces inter-object penetrations and unstable floating poses, and object-level IoU stays below 0.45 on all four benchmarks even for the best method. Its MOD refinement corrects only pose and scale, so geometry errors remain, and evaluation still needs Sim(3) ICP alignment. Two monocular-pose surveys list scene-level consistency and physical plausibility (simulation verification, inverse rendering) as open. The IJCV survey calls for physically grounded estimation from tactile, contact and force cues. The cluster rests on one dataset paper plus the open-problem lists of three surveys.

evidence_items.item: SAM 3D treats objects independently, giving inter-object penetrations and unstable floating poses; absolute object-level IoU stays below 0.45 on all four benchmarks; prior benchmarks have inaccurate registration and penetrations.
Scene-level consistency of multi-object pose is open; the survey suggests simulation, reconstruction, inverse rendering or NeRF-like methods.
Geometric representations and physical plausibility, including verification through simulation, are open challenges.
Cross-modal, physically grounded estimation using tactile, inertial, contact and force cues, together with physics-aware simulation, is needed.

benchmark_evidence: MessyKitchens / object-level IoU: best MOD 0.445, SAM 3D 0.409, MIDI 0.186, PartCrafter 0.071 (405)
MessyKitchens / contact F1 (PhySIC contact graph): best MOD 66.1, SAM 3D 55.8, PartCrafter 21.2 (405)
GraspClutter6D / object-level IoU: MOD 0.340 versus SAM 3D 0.328 on the out-of-distribution high-clutter set (405)
clusters.settings: Single RGB image of static, contact-rich tabletop kitchenware with SAM 3 masks (MessyKitchens, the GraspClutter6D high-clutter set); multi-object monocular pose (survey and position papers).
clusters.attempted_fixes: MOD corrects only pose and scale on top of SAM 3D, is trained on synthetic scenes of 42 GSO objects, leaves geometry unchanged, and still needs Sim(3) ICP alignment for evaluation (405). Ground-truth fitting of thin concave objects needs a normal-aware registration term (405). Proposed: simulation and inverse-rendering consistency (1020, 1328) and physically grounded multimodal cues (1088).

- physical consistency

Finer cuts kept (each side has at least 3 papers):
1. Annotation. The bottom-up lens split static label scale from moving-object ground truth; the capability lens had one 22-paper cluster. I kept the split and reassigned the capability lens's extra papers after re-reading:
   - 402, 1324 and 1326 went to static labels (robot arm plus anti-reflective coating; ARKit or COLMAP with manual alignment).
   - 1318 and 1322 went to moving ground truth (mocap sync with Kalman smoothing; stop-and-go capture).
2. Training transfer versus evaluation. The bottom-up lens merged sim-to-real with benchmark realism; the capability lens split them. I kept the split into 'Sim-to-real gap and dataset-specific bias' and 'Saturated, constrained benchmarks hide real-world failure'.
   - 1313 moved to the benchmark cluster: its only relevant item is seen-object saturation.
   - 201 and 1319 were added to the benchmark cluster: both explicitly say prior benchmarks are controlled or unrepresentative.
   - 1314 was added to sim-to-real (baked lighting blocks synthetic data).
   - 1324 and 1326 were left out of sim-to-real: their items concern the need for synthetic pretraining or training-data volume, not transfer failure.
3. Textureless objects (10 papers) kept apart from CAD-free onboarding, where the capability lens had folded them in.
4. Small/distant objects (8 papers), which only the bottom-up lens had, kept as its own cluster.

Union additions confirmed by re-reading:
- 3 and 405 added to detection (external detector; SAM 3 masks).
- 1313 added to occlusion (amodal detection of occluded objects).
- 1319 added to transparent/thin (thin dark markers with high LiDAR depth error).
- 1324 added to category-level.
- 201 added to monocular (glasses lack depth).
- 1326 and 1327 added to tracking (per-frame only).
- 1326 added to hand-held.
- 405, 1324, 1325, 1326 and 1327 added to articulated (rigid-only assumptions).
- 1314 added to functional metrics.
- 1321, 1322 and 1317 added to blur/lighting.

Some papers support a cluster only through an assumption, so their n_papers counts are inflated by assumption-level support:
- Detection: 3, 201, 347, 348, 350, 1316, 1318, 1319, 1321 and 1326 support it mainly through ground-truth masks or boxes, or an external detector.
- Hand-held: 402, 405, 837 and 839 support it only through 'no hands in scenes'.
- Articulated: 3, 1286, 1312, 1313 and 1324-1327 support it only through 'rigid objects only'.
- CAD-free: 3, 201 and 825 support it partly through 'CAD model known'.

Counting caveats:
- 348 and 1316 are two digest records of the same PACE dataset, so any cluster citing both overstates its independent papers by one.
- 1020 and 1328 overlap in scope. 1328's v2 was withdrawn by its author.
- n_papers counts overlap across clusters and sum to far more than 32.

Items left out of every cluster:
- 6D-Diff's note that diffusion starts from random noise (3).
- The missing standard storage format for event data (1320).
- Gripper-specific failure types: small jaws fail by collision, wide jaws by slipping (836).

Relevance to a bimanual RGB-D hand-object thesis: hands and manipulation appear directly only in the hand-held, moving-object ground-truth and tracking-drift clusters. No paper in the group reports a causal tracker that recovers an object lost behind the holding hand.

clusters.name: Avatars from lightweight sensors need studio capture
clusters.statement: Photorealistic, driveable head, hand and body avatars cannot yet be built or driven for a new person from phone, VR-headset or monocular input; studio fidelity still needs per-subject capture in a calibrated dome of 16 to about 230 synchronized cameras, and paired high-end and lightweight captures exist for only four subjects.
clusters.description: Avatar dataset papers build their reference models on dense rigs: Multiface uses 40-160 cameras, ActorsHQ 160 cameras at 12 MP, Codec Avatar Studio about 170 and about 230, and NeRSemble 16 at 73 fps. Multiface shows reconstruction error rising as training cameras fall from 37 to 17. Codec Avatar Studio states that paired dome, headset and phone captures are unavailable outside industrial labs. It also says that headset driving relies on pseudo ground truth from personalized avatars, and that only four Goliath subjects carry the full paired set. SmartPortraits finds that casual handheld phone capture of near-static people does not yet give reliable 3D portraits. HumanRF and NeRSemble propose learning priors from high-end captures to drive monocular avatars, but leave this as future work.

evidence_items.item: The field cannot yet build relightable, multi-identity, full-body driveable avatars from commodity sensors without per-subject high-end dome captures; only the 4 Goliath subjects carry the full paired capture, which restricts research on converting low-quality captures to high quality.

Paired captures of the same subject on high-end and lightweight devices are unavailable outside industrial labs; headset-to-avatar driving depends on pseudo ground truth, and the paper calls a reliable mapping from headset images to face deformations a key challenge.
Reconstruction error rises as training cameras drop from 37 to 17 views; data-hungry neural face models need dense high-resolution multi-view captures (40 to 160 cameras).
HumanRF requires the high-end ActorsHQ capture (160 synchronized 12 MP cameras); future work is training on high-end recordings to build avatars driven from monocular-only test sequences.
Reconstruction is fit per sequence from 16 calibrated cameras; a learned prior over realistic 4D avatars for monocular dynamic head capture is future work.
The field cannot yet turn casual handheld smartphone captures of slightly moving people into high-quality 3D reconstructions reliably.

benchmark_evidence: Multiface (identity m-20180227), screen-space reconstruction error: joint novel view plus novel expression 1.088 with 37 training cameras rising to 1.272 with 17, versus 0.770 for novel view only at 37 cameras.
Goliath-4, number of subjects: only 4 subjects carry the full 8-modality paired capture (Codec Avatar Studio).
clusters.settings: Multi-view studio domes (Multiface 40-160 cameras, Codec Avatar Studio about 170-camera head and about 230-camera body domes, ActorsHQ 160 cameras, NeRSemble 16 cameras at 73 fps), contrasted with lightweight inputs (Quest Pro headset IR cameras, phone scans, handheld smartphone plus Azure Kinect in SmartPortraits). Tasks: avatar creation, headset driving, novel view and novel expression synthesis, 3D portrait reconstruction.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Codec Avatar Studio releases paired dome, headset and phone data (Ava-256, Goliath) and trains a headset driver on cycle-consistency pseudo ground truth. The driver works only for personalized avatars, and only four subjects are fully paired, at reduced quality. Multiface adds a spatial bias to its baseline, and the baseline still deteriorates with fewer cameras. HumanRF and NeRSemble propose learning priors from high-end data for monocular driving, and leave this as future work.

clusters.name: Per-identity fitting without cross-identity generalization
clusters.statement: Head and body avatar models are still optimized per identity or per sequence, and generalizable models trained on current data learn mean priors that fail on unseen identities, rare poses, complex garments and other long-tail appearance.
clusters.description: Most reference methods in these datasets are trained per subject or per sequence. Multiface needs about one day on eight V100 GPUs per identity, NeRSemble and HumanRF optimize each sequence, and Codec Avatar Studio trains personalized head, hand and body models. In RenderMe-360, unseen identities cause larger drops than unseen expressions, and generalizable methods learn mean-head priors that fail on long-tail cases. MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++ report that generalizable human NeRFs (IBRNet, GPNeRF) degrade on rare poses and complex garments and remain far from satisfactory on diverse cases. The survey adds that 3D-aware GANs cannot generate beyond their training data, and scaling datasets, the main attempted fix, has not closed the gap.

evidence_items.item: Unseen-identity NVS causes a larger performance drop than unseen-expression NVS; generalizable methods learn mean-head priors but fail on long-tail cases.
Generalizable NeRFs (IBRNet, GPNeRF) degrade on rare poses and complex garments with small training sets; human generalizable NeRFs still perform poorly on diverse cases.
Generalizable NeRFs remain far from satisfactory on diverse cases; LaRa is limited by its Gaussian volume representation and large input baselines.
Per-sequence optimization with no cross-sequence prior; future work is dynamic NeRFs that generalize over identities and expressions.
Per-identity training takes about one day on eight V100 GPUs; only 13 identities, with ablations on a single identity.
Personalized head, hand and body models are trained per subject; generalizable avatars built quickly for new users without expensive capture are listed as open.
Per-sequence offline optimization on the high-end ActorsHQ capture.
3D-aware GANs show artifacts and cannot generate beyond their training data.

benchmark_evidence: RenderMe-360 Generalizable NVS (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): the unseen-ID protocol shows a larger drop than the unseen-expression protocol for IBRNet, VisionNeRF and KeypointNeRF (the digest gives no single number).
clusters.settings: Head NVS (RenderMe-360 with 60 cameras, Multiface, NeRSemble), full-body free-viewpoint video (ActorsHQ), generalizable human NeRF and feed-forward reconstruction on MVHumanNet (48- and 24-camera rigs) and MVHumanNet++, personalized dome avatars (Codec Avatar Studio), avatar generation (survey).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Larger multi-view datasets (RenderMe-360, MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++) are used to train generalizable NeRFs (IBRNet, GPNeRF, KeypointNeRF, VisionNeRF) and feed-forward models. These still degrade on long-tail identities, poses and garments. Removing SMPL from generalizable NeRFs and scaling data further are proposed as future work.

clusters.name: Cross-dataset domain gap in human capture
clusters.statement: Human reconstruction models trained on one capture dataset do not transfer to another rig, camera-pose configuration or in-the-wild condition without fine-tuning, and saturated studio benchmarks hide the gap to real-world use.
clusters.description: MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++ both find that models trained only on their data show a domain gap on HuMMan, and need fine-tuning to beat HuMMan-only training. SmartPortraits reports that generalized NeRF methods (FVS, SVS) degrade on handheld captures because the camera-pose configuration differs from their training data. RenderMe-360 notes that performance saturates on existing head datasets, yet head avatar methods still fail in real-world scenarios. The only remedies reported are fine-tuning on target data or training on larger, more diverse sets.

evidence_items.item: Models trained only on MVHumanNet suffer a domain gap on HuMMan; fine-tuning is needed to beat HuMMan-only training; domain gap across human capture datasets is listed as open.
A domain gap to HuMMan persists for MVHumanNet++ until fine-tuning.
Generalized NeRF methods (FVS, SVS) degrade because the pose configuration differs from their training data.
Performance saturates on existing datasets while a gap to real-world scenarios remains; head avatar methods still face real-world obstacles.

benchmark_evidence: HuMMan cross-dataset (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): models trained only on MVHumanNet or MVHumanNet++ show a domain gap until fine-tuned.
clusters.settings: Generalizable human NeRF trained on MVHumanNet or MVHumanNet++ and tested on HuMMan, generalized NeRF on handheld smartphone trajectories (SmartPortraits), studio head avatar benchmarks (RenderMe-360).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Fine-tuning on the target dataset, and larger, more diverse training sets. No method is reported that transfers without target data.

clusters.name: Object-centric 3D models fail on humans
clusters.statement: 3D reconstruction and inverse-rendering methods that perform well on object-centric scenes (DUSt3R-style point maps, large reconstruction models, Gaussian inverse rendering) degrade on humans without human-specific training data, with depth ambiguity, missing detail and blur.
clusters.description: MVHumanNet++ finds that off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction performs poorly on humans until it is fine-tuned on human data, and DUSt3R shows depth ambiguity on human point maps. HumanOLAT reports that relighting methods which do well on object-centric scenes struggle on human captures, giving blurry renderings with hand and face artifacts. The survey says large reconstruction models fail to capture human detail and dynamics, and that HumanLRM does not beat implicit-function reconstruction. MVHumanNet attributes the lag of human 3D behind object-centric 3D to human data not having scaled.

evidence_items.item: Off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction is poor on humans without human training data; DUSt3R shows depth ambiguity on human point maps before fine-tuning.
Methods that do well on object-centric scenes face challenges on human captures, giving blurry renderings with hand and face artifacts.

Large reconstruction models fail to capture human detail and dynamics; HumanLRM does not surpass implicit-function reconstruction; robust feed-forward models for both general objects and humans are future work.
Human-centric 3D tasks have not seen the scale-driven progress of object-centric 3D, because high-fidelity human capture datasets remain mid-sized.

benchmark_evidence: HumanOLAT novel view plus novel light (PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM, Table 2, six captures): object-centric relighting methods give blurry human renderings with hand and face artifacts (the digest gives no single number).
clusters.settings: Feed-forward and point-map reconstruction on MVHumanNet++, relighting on HumanOLAT, large reconstruction models for humans (survey), generalizable human NeRF on MVHumanNet.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Fine-tuning DUSt3R and LRM-style models on human data (MVHumanNet++, HumanLRM) helps, but the result does not match human-specific methods.

clusters.name: Offline per-subject compute blocks real-time use
clusters.statement: Human reconstruction, avatar training and clinical kinematic pipelines run offline at high compute cost (about one day on eight GPUs per face identity, hours per text-to-avatar model, per-sequence and per-trial optimization, slow rendering), and baselines cannot train at full capture resolution, which blocks real-time and point-of-care use.
clusters.description: The reported pipelines fit each identity, sequence or trial offline. Multiface trains one identity in about a day on eight V100s and could not run sequential mesh tracking on all its data. NeRSemble and HumanRF optimize each sequence separately. HumanRF renders slowly and runs its comparisons at 4x downscaled resolution because the baselines fail at full resolution, and HumanOLAT downsamples to 1K to train its baselines. The survey reports hours-long, unstable SDS optimization per text-to-avatar model, and SmartPortraits calls the cost of reconstruction and rendering prohibitive. In the clinic, the monocular reachable-workspace study fits a MuJoCo model per trial offline and lists real-time point-of-care processing as open.

evidence_items.item: Per-identity training takes about one day on eight V100 GPUs; sequential mesh tracking is too costly to run on all data, so sentences were not processed by it.

Rendering is slow; comparisons run at 4x downscaled resolution because baselines fail at full resolution; real-time rendering is open, and conversion to a hybrid implicit-explicit representation (e.g. MobileNeRF) is future work.
SDS-based text-to-avatar optimization takes hours per model and suffers from stochasticity and initialization sensitivity; real-time 3D generation via 2D Gaussian parameter maps is future work.
The computational cost of reconstruction and rendering remains prohibitive.
Analysis is offline and post-hoc, with GPU optimization of a MuJoCo biomechanical model per trial; real-time point-of-care processing is open.
Images are downsampled to 1K for baseline training.
NeRSemble uses per-sequence optimization with no cross-sequence prior.
Personalized head, hand and body models are trained per subject from dome captures.

clusters.settings: Studio avatar training and rendering (Multiface, NeRSemble, ActorsHQ, HumanOLAT, Codec Avatar Studio), text-to-avatar generation (survey), handheld portrait reconstruction (SmartPortraits), clinical monocular reachable-workspace assessment with MuJoCo fitting.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hash-grid and 4D decomposed representations (NeRSemble, HumanRF) reduce cost but are still fit per sequence. Feed-forward large reconstruction models exist, but the survey says HumanLRM does not surpass implicit-function reconstruction. Hybrid representations, 2D Gaussian parameter maps and mobile point-of-care pipelines are proposed only as future work. In current practice, data is downsampled, only subsets are processed, or analysis runs offline.

clusters.name: Scarce, small and undistributable human capture data
clusters.statement: High-fidelity real 3D human capture data remains far smaller than object-centric 3D data and covers only a handful of identities for its richest modalities. At petabyte scale it cannot be distributed at full fidelity, and its creators cannot even use all of it.
clusters.description: MVHumanNet notes there is no human dataset comparable to Objaverse or MVImgNet, because high-fidelity capture is costly. Both MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++ train on only part of their own data (62 percent for MVHumanNet++) because of size, hardware and annotation limits. Codec Avatar Studio reports over 10 TB per dome capture and about 3 PB in total. Its release is therefore cut to about 80 cameras, 7.5 or 15 fps, lower resolution and lossy AVIF compression, and only four subjects carry the full paired capture. Multiface has 13 identities and could not run tracking on all its data. HumanOLAT cites scarce public full-body OLAT data, MVP-Human the lack of multi-pose scans with skinning weights, and the survey scarce high-quality 3D human training data; synthetic substitutes leave artifacts.

evidence_items.item: Human-centric 3D tasks lack large-scale data comparable to Objaverse or MVImgNet because high-fidelity capture is costly; experiments use only part of the data due to scale, hardware and annotation constraints.

Full-resolution data (over 10 TB per dome capture, over 3 PB total) cannot be distributed; the release is downsampled in resolution, camera count (about 80) and frame rate (7.5 or 15 fps) and lossily AVIF-compressed; only 4 Goliath subjects carry the full paired capture.
Full-resolution data is infeasible for academic labs to store; storage and distribution of petabyte-scale capture data is listed as open.
Experiments use 62% of the data due to size, hardware and annotation constraints.
Public full-body OLAT data is scarce, and reliance on synthetic data or learned priors yields artifacts.
Training needs multi-view, multi-pose images with T-pose shapes, and public multi-pose scan datasets with skinning weights are lacking.
Scarcity of high-quality 3D human training data is listed as an open problem.
Only 13 identities; sequential mesh tracking is too costly to run on all the data.

benchmark_evidence: Goliath-4, number of subjects: only 4 subjects carry the full 8-modality paired capture.
Ava-256 release: 2x or 4x downsampled resolution, about 80 of about 170 cameras, 7.5 or 15 fps instead of 30 fps, to fit 4 to 32 TB releases.
clusters.settings: Studio dome and light-stage human capture (Ava-256, Goliath, Multiface, MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++, HumanOLAT), scan-based avatar training (MVP-Human), avatar generation (survey).
clusters.attempted_fixes: MVHumanNet reaches scale by limiting capture to everyday clothing with no object interaction. Codec Avatar Studio releases tiered, downsampled and compressed data, and expects the higher-quality tiers to become usable as storage costs fall. HumanOLAT releases 21 subjects in static poses. Partial-data training and synthetic substitutes are used, and they leave artifacts.

clusters.name: Human-object interaction excluded from human capture
clusters.statement: Large-scale human and avatar capture leaves out people handling objects. Scaled datasets restrict subjects to everyday clothing with no object interaction, hands are captured separately without objects, generating human-object interaction motion is open, and clinical grasp assessments have no reliable finger or object tracking. The field therefore cannot yet reconstruct, generate or measure people while they manipulate objects.
clusters.description: MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++ limit capture to everyday clothing with no deliberate object interaction, because complex clothing and human-object interaction get in the way of scaling. Codec Avatar Studio captures left and right hands separately with no object interaction, not during whole-body activity. The avatar survey calls generating human-object interaction motion sequences a hard open problem. In clinical ARAT grasp assessment, the three-webcam setup tracks only upper-limb body kinematics, with no reliable finger or object tracking, even though the tasks are object manipulation. No paper in the group reports a fix.

evidence_items.item: The dataset focuses on everyday clothing because complex clothing and human-object interaction hinder scaling; the field cannot yet collect human capture data at scale that includes human-object interaction.
Complex clothing and human-object interaction are de-emphasized for scalability; scaling capture to them is listed as open.
Hands are captured separately (left and right) in a relightable dome with no object interaction.
Hands are captured separately in the head scanner, not during whole-body activity.
Human-object interaction motion sequence generation is a hard open problem.

The clinical setup captures upper-limb body kinematics only, with no reliable finger or object tracking; the field cannot yet capture reliable finger and hand-object kinematics during routine clinical grasp tasks.

clusters.settings: Multi-view studio human capture (MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++), dome hand capture (Codec Avatar Studio), text- and image-driven avatar generation (survey), clinical ARAT grasp tasks with three webcams (20 patients, 1,174 tasks).
clusters.attempted_fixes: None reported. The papers exclude interaction by design to stay scalable, capture hands in a separate session, or restrict measurement to arm and body kinematics.

clusters.name: Tight-fit body priors break on loose clothing
clusters.statement: Reconstruction and generation pipelines that depend on SMPL/SMPL-X priors and linear blend skinning cannot represent loose or skin-covering clothing, and they generalize poorly. Their fits twist, self-intersect or misalign, and no prior-free alternative is established.
clusters.description: Codec Avatar Studio reports that body models built from subjects in tight-fit clothing struggle with full-body captures in which clothing covers most of the skin. The survey states that reliance on SMPL/SMPL-X limits the generation and animation of loose clothing, and it proposes encoders that perceive depth, silhouette and semantics instead. MVHumanNet suggests that SMPL dependence hurts the generalization of human NeRFs and plans to remove it. MVHumanNet++ had to refit SMPL-X because earlier fits showed twisted ankles, self-intersection and misalignment. MVP-Human assumes rigid clothing reposed by linear blend skinning to a canonical T-pose.

evidence_items.item: Body models built from tight-fit clothing subjects are challenged by full-body captures in which clothing covers most of the skin.
Clothed full-body reconstruction is hard since body models come from tight-fit clothing.
Reliance on SMPL/SMPL-X priors limits loose clothing generation and animation; encoders perceiving depth, silhouette and semantics are proposed as an alternative.
Reliance on SMPL in generalizable NeRFs may hurt generalization; future work is to redesign them without the SMPL model.
Prior SMPL-X fits showed ankle twisting, self-intersection and misalignment.
Assumes a single clothed person with rigid clothing reposed via linear blend skinning to a canonical T-pose; SMPL-offset baselines miss fine geometry.

clusters.settings: Full-body dome capture (Codec Avatar Studio), generalizable human NeRF on everyday-clothing rigs (MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++), clothed avatar reconstruction from unconstrained frames (MVP-Human), monocular and generative avatar methods (survey).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Refined SMPL-X fitting (MVHumanNet++) and skinning-based canonicalization to a T-pose (MVP-Human) are still used. SMPL-free encoders and redesigned human NeRFs are proposed only as future work.

clusters.name: Camera and body-pose registration errors propagate
clusters.statement: Casual captures cannot be registered reliably: handheld phone video with an unsynchronized depth camera, unconstrained frames and sparse wide-baseline views all suffer. Visual-inertial odometry needs a static start, rolling shutter and small sensor time offsets degrade camera poses, and COLMAP is scale-ambiguous. Inaccurate SMPL/SMPL-X fits project 3D points to the wrong pixels, so reconstructions come out over-smooth, misaligned or incorrect.
clusters.description: SmartPortraits reports that several VIO methods (Kimera VIO, OpenVINS, MSCKF, ROVIO) cannot run without a static device at initialization, and that its rolling-shutter phone is calibrated with a global-shutter model. It also reports that small time offsets between the phone and the Azure Kinect degrade pose estimation, and that one visual-inertial trajectory produced an incorrect 3D reconstruction. MVP-Human relies on per-frame SMPL fitting for camera and body pose. When that fit is inaccurate, 3D points map to wrong image locations, background or irrelevant features are fused, and results are over-smooth. MVHumanNet++ had to refit SMPL-X because of misaligned earlier fits, and it reports that feed-forward reconstruction is limited under large input baselines.

evidence_items.item: Kimera VIO, OpenVINS, MSCKF and ROVIO cannot run because they require a static device at initialization; the rolling-shutter phone is calibrated with a global-shutter model; small time offsets between the independent smartphone and depth camera degrade pose estimation; one VI trajectory produced an incorrect 3D reconstruction; COLMAP trajectories are scale-ambiguous.
Inaccurate pose estimation maps 3D points to wrong image locations and fuses irrelevant or background features, yielding overly smooth results; failure cases occur when SMPL fitting is inaccurate.
Prior SMPL-X fits showed ankle twisting, self-intersection and misalignment; generalizable feed-forward human reconstruction under large view baselines is open.

benchmark_evidence: SmartPortraits ATE/RPE against pseudo ground truth: real-time visual-inertial methods are less accurate than visual-only methods, and only LDSO, OKVIS, PVIO, SVO2 and VINS can be ordered given the pseudo-ground-truth bound.

MVP-Human canonical shape Chamfer / P2S (cm): best method 1.72 / 1.34 versus ICON 3.96 / 3.96 and PIFu 4.96 / 6.19; the paper's failure cases occur when SMPL fitting is inaccurate (the digest gives no number for that subset).
clusters.settings: Handheld smartphone plus Azure Kinect semicircular trajectories around near-static people (SmartPortraits), unconstrained multi-pose frames with per-frame SMPL fitting (MVP-Human), SMPL-X annotation and sparse wide-baseline feed-forward reconstruction on MVHumanNet++.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Visual and visual-inertial SLAM are benchmarked against pseudo ground truth. Per-frame SMPL fitting supplies camera and body pose, and MVHumanNet++ refits SMPL-X. Better IMU initialization, and optimizing only the map under small pose perturbations, are proposed as future work.

clusters.name: Hair, mouth interior, eyes and accessories in head avatars
clusters.statement: Even with dense multi-view studio input, head avatar methods cannot yet reconstruct or render fast or curly hair, thin structures such as strands, hair bands and eyelashes, accessories, teeth and the occluded mouth interior, or view-dependent effects such as eye specularities and refraction.
clusters.description: The three head-capture dataset papers each name the same hard regions. Multiface reports poorly reconstructed teeth and eyelashes and a baseline that fails on high-frequency detail. It notes that mesh-based Codec Avatars fall short on thin structures and translucency. RenderMe-360 shows every static NVS method dropping as accessories get more complex and sharp drops on curly hair, with IM Avatar unstable on hair bands and strands and blur building up in dynamic hair. NeRSemble cannot capture fast hair motion, places teeth at the back of the mouth under occlusion (hollow-face artifacts), and shows eye-specularity artifacts; it does not model refraction.

evidence_items.item: Teeth and eyelashes are poorly reconstructed; the baseline fails on high-frequency details; prior mesh-based Codec Avatars fall short on thin structures, translucency and biological motion.

Hair rendering degrades sharply for curly hair; all static NVS methods drop as accessory complexity increases; IM Avatar struggles with thin structures like hair bands and strands; NR-NeRF blur accumulates across frames in dynamic hair.
The deformation field cannot capture fast hair motion; teeth are reconstructed at the back of the mouth under heavy occlusion; eye specular reflections cause artifacts; refraction is not modelled.

benchmark_evidence: RenderMe-360 Hair Rendering (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): the curls subset causes sharp drops under all metrics for static and dynamic NVS methods.
RenderMe-360 Single-ID NVS (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): Instant-NGP, NeuS, NV and MVP all drop with deformable and complex accessories.
NeRSemble (10 sequences, 4 held-out views, extreme viewing angles), PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS: 31.8 / 0.875 / 0.212 versus DyNeRF 30.6 / 0.860 / 0.254, with residual hair and mouth artifacts.
Neural 3D Video (PSNR): refraction of window panes and glass bottles is not captured.
clusters.settings: Dense multi-view studio head capture: Multiface (40-160 cameras), RenderMe-360 (60 cameras), NeRSemble (16 cameras at 73 fps). Tasks: static and dynamic head NVS, hair rendering, face avatar decoding.
clusters.attempted_fixes: NeRSemble combines a deformation field with multi-resolution hash ensembles; each alone is blurry or fails on mouth motion. It proposes optical-flow or differentiable-physics motion priors for hair and learned 4D priors for occluded regions. RenderMe-360 benchmarks NeRF, point-based and implicit avatars (PointAvatar, IM Avatar), and all of them fail on these regions.

clusters.name: Driving avatars beyond captured expressions and poses
clusters.statement: Avatars cannot yet be driven to expressions or poses outside those enacted during capture. Novel-expression methods fail on out-of-distribution expressions and on the long tail of expressivity, and joint novel-expression plus novel-view synthesis is much harder than either alone. Free-viewpoint human models have no articulation control outside training poses, and headset driving works only for personalized avatars.
clusters.description: RenderMe-360 reports that every novel-expression method fails on out-of-distribution expressions such as tongue out, and that point-based methods miss subtle motions such as a pout. In Multiface, joint novel-view and novel-expression error is far above novel-view error alone, and the baseline deteriorates quickly for novel expressions as cameras are removed. Codec Avatar Studio states that its datasets miss the long tail of expressivity (sweat, tiredness, blood flow), and lists headset driving for unseen subjects as future work. HumanRF has no articulation control outside its training poses, and the survey says text-to-3D methods cannot control motion. NeRSemble lists generalizing over expressions, rather than fitting each sequence, as future work.

evidence_items.item: All novel-expression methods (NeRFace, IM Avatar, PointAvatar) fail on out-of-distribution expressions such as tongue out; PointAvatar is limited on subtle motions such as pout by point granularity.

Joint novel view and novel expression synthesis is harder than either alone; the baseline with spatial bias deteriorates quickly for novel expressions with fewer training cameras; synthesis of expressions not enacted during capture is open.
The datasets miss the long tail of human expressivity (sweat, tiredness, blood flow); driving avatars from headset IR cameras for unseen subjects via generalizable encoders is future work.
No articulation control outside training poses; per-segment deformation networks or parametric models are future work.
Text-to-3D methods cannot control motion; realistic text-driven human motion generation and avatar animation remain open.
Future work: dynamic NeRFs that generalize over identities and expressions instead of per-sequence fitting.

benchmark_evidence: RenderMe-360 Novel Expression (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/L1): NeRFace, IM Avatar and PointAvatar all fail on OOD expressions such as tongue out.
Multiface screen-space error: joint novel view plus expression 1.272 (17 cameras) and 1.088 (37 cameras) versus 0.770 for novel view only (37 cameras).
clusters.settings: Studio head capture with scripted expression sets (RenderMe-360, Multiface, NeRSemble, Ava-256/Goliath), ActorsHQ full-body free-viewpoint video, text-driven avatar generation (survey), Quest Pro headset IR driving of Codec Avatars.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Expression-conditioned implicit and point avatars, cycle-consistency headset drivers for personalized avatars, and per-sequence free-viewpoint models are used, and they fail outside the training distribution. Parametric articulation control and generalizable encoders are listed as future work.

clusters.name: Full-body relighting and relightable data scarcity
clusters.statement: Humans cannot yet be relit photo-realistically: current methods miss subsurface scattering, self-shadowing, specular highlights and sharp shadows. Relightable training data exist only for a few subjects in static poses captured in costly light stages, and most avatar datasets sidestep relighting by capturing under uniform illumination.
clusters.description: HumanOLAT finds that the best Gaussian inverse-rendering methods stay blurry and miss specular highlights and sharp shadows. PRT-Gaussian shows ghosting, and IC-Light harmonization rarely produces self-shadows and loses eye color and mouth shape. Its own data cover 21 subjects in three static poses. Codec Avatar Studio has relightable captures for only four Goliath subjects, so multi-identity relightable head decoders are not supported, and that capture needs time-multiplexed group lighting. Multiface excludes relighting because its data were captured under uniform diffuse light, and lists relighting under unseen lighting as open.

evidence_items.item: Evaluated Gaussian inverse-rendering methods stay blurry and miss specular highlights and sharp shadows; IC-Light harmonization rarely produces self-shadows and fails to preserve eye color and mouth shape; PRT-Gaussian fails to reconstruct geometry from OLAT frames, producing ghosting.

The release is unlikely to support multi-identity relightable head decoders since relightable data exist only for the four Goliath subjects; relightable capture needs time-multiplexed group-light illumination.
Multi-identity relightable head decoders remain hard with the release.
Relighting is excluded because data were captured under uniform diffuse illumination; relighting under unseen lighting configurations is listed as open.

benchmark_evidence: HumanOLAT novel view plus novel light (PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM, Table 2, six captures): methods that do well on object-centric scenes give blurry renderings with hand and face artifacts (the digest gives no single number).
HumanOLAT illumination harmonization (qualitative): IC-Light lacks subsurface scattering and self-shadowing and loses facial details.
clusters.settings: Light-stage OLAT full-body capture (HumanOLAT, 21 subjects, 3 static poses, 11-second sequences), relightable head dome (Goliath, 4 subjects), uniform-light face dome (Multiface).
clusters.attempted_fixes: HumanOLAT adapts PRT-Gaussian, IntrinsicAvatar and IC-Light and applies optical-flow motion compensation for sway, and all of these fall short. New OLAT datasets are the main contribution, but they remain small and static.

clusters.name: Hands and faces under-resolved at full-body scale
clusters.statement: Full-body capture, relighting and generation cannot resolve hands and faces at the fidelity of dedicated captures. Full-body rigs give too little pixel density on them, Gaussian methods cull too many points there, and generators distort faces or drop hands and feet.
clusters.description: Codec Avatar Studio reports insufficient pixel density on the head and hands in full-body multi-view captures, which forces separate high-density captures. HumanOLAT finds that Gaussian methods cull many initial points, leaving too few Gaussians for hands and faces, and the renderings show artifacts there. The survey notes that text-to-3D methods often miss hands or feet, and that prior-based implicit reconstruction (PaMIR) fails when hands come close to clothing in motion. MVHumanNet++ reports faces distorting in latent-diffusion multi-view generation.

evidence_items.item: Full-body multi-view captures have insufficient pixel density on head and hands, requiring separate high-density captures.
Gaussian methods cull many initial points, leaving too few Gaussians for hands and faces; renderings show hand and face artifacts.
Text-to-3D methods often miss hands or feet; PaMIR fails when hands and clothes are close together in dynamic motion.
Faces distort in latent-diffusion multi-view human generation; face fidelity in multi-view human generation is open.

benchmark_evidence: HumanOLAT novel view plus novel light (PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM, Table 2, six captures): even the best relightable Gaussian method stays blurry with hand and face artifacts.
clusters.settings: Full-body dome capture (Codec Avatar Studio, about 230 cameras), full-body OLAT relighting (HumanOLAT), multi-view diffusion generation trained on MVHumanNet++, text-to-3D and implicit reconstruction (survey).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Codec Avatar Studio captures the head and hands separately at high density. No method-level fix is reported.

clusters.name: Long, fast or involuntary subject motion
clusters.statement: Neural human reconstruction assumes static subjects or short sequences with limited motion. It degrades under long sequences, fast hair or body motion and topology changes, and it produces temporally inconsistent masks. It fails even under the involuntary sway of subjects asked to hold still.
clusters.description: HumanRF reports that deformation-field baselines struggle on long sequences with complex motion and topology changes. Its own PSNR falls as sequences grow from 20 to 1000 frames, and per-frame masks cause silhouette flicker. NeRSemble notes that dynamic NeRFs work only on short, limited-motion sequences, blur under fast hair motion, and that a baseline's preprocessing (landmarks, masks, normals) failed on complex-motion sequences. RenderMe-360 shows NeRFace failing on dynamic motion and blur accumulating in dynamic hair, and the survey says video-diffusion 4D methods cannot represent large movements. Nominally static captures are not static either: HumanOLAT subjects sway during the 11-second OLAT sequence, and SmartPortraits volunteers cannot stay still.

evidence_items.item: Deformation-field baselines struggle on long sequences with complex motion and rapid topology changes; per-frame Instant-NGP lacks temporal stability; inconsistent per-frame masks cause silhouette-edge flicker; scaling dynamic representations to long sequences under memory budgets is open.
Dynamic NeRFs work on short sequences with limited motion; extremely fast hair motion yields blurry canonical hash-grid output; NHA preprocessing failed on 3 complex-motion sequences.
NeRFace cannot robustly model dynamic motion; NR-NeRF blur accumulates across frames in dynamic hair.
Video-diffusion 4D methods cannot represent complex poses or large movements; 4D animation of large movements is open.
Subjects sway during the 11-second OLAT capture, blurring image-based relighting and requiring optical-flow motion compensation; the dataset covers static humans only.
Volunteers cannot stay perfectly still, making the nominally static capture non-static.

benchmark_evidence: ActorsHQ (4x downscaled, 8 actors), PSNR/LPIPS: HumanRF PSNR falls from 30.30 at 20 frames to 29.05 at 1000 frames; LPIPS rises from 0.095 to 0.107.
clusters.settings: Full-body free-viewpoint video (ActorsHQ, 160 cameras), dynamic head capture (NeRSemble at 73 fps, RenderMe-360), OLAT light stage (HumanOLAT), handheld smartphone portraits of near-static people (SmartPortraits), 4D human generation (survey).
clusters.attempted_fixes: HumanRF uses 4D feature decomposition with temporal partitioning, and quality still drops with sequence length. NeRSemble's hash ensembles with deformation blur on fast hair, and the paper proposes optical-flow or physics priors. HumanOLAT applies optical-flow motion compensation, while the methods it evaluates still assume static subjects. Temporally consistent matting is future work.

clusters.name: Finger and hand kinematics lost in compact clinical setups
clusters.statement: Markerless capture in compact clinical rooms with one to three ad-hoc cameras cannot yet deliver reliable 3D finger and hand kinematics, because occlusion and limited viewpoints push errors above laboratory standards; lab-grade accuracy still needs a large calibrated multi-camera space.
clusters.description: TULIP obtains usable 3D hand and body kinematics only with six GPIO-synchronized cameras at 80 fps, in a 6.3 x 3 m room calibrated before and after each session, unlike a typical clinic. It still reports keypoints occluded from some viewpoints, and lists adapting the hardware to small rooms as future work. The ARAT study's three-webcam clinical setup has reprojection error above the laboratory standard, more occlusion and no reliable finger kinematics, which caused a longitudinal mismatch for one patient on the grip task. The monocular reachable-workspace study shows the torso or reaching arm hiding the hand and wrist on cross-body reaches, and finds no single viewpoint that suits multi-planar motion. All three use off-the-shelf keypoint detectors without clinical fine-tuning.

evidence_items.item: Reprojection error 12.5 px exceeds the 5-10 px laboratory standard, attributed to three cameras and more frequent occlusion in clinic; the three-camera setup lacks reliable finger kinematics, causing a longitudinal mismatch for patient P10 on the grip task.

Capture used a large 6.3 x 3 m room with six synchronized calibrated cameras, unlike a typical clinical exam space; keypoints can be occluded in specific viewpoints; future work is adapting hardware to smaller clinical spaces; MediaPipe and MMPose were used without fine-tuning.

Cross-body reaches where the torso or reaching arm occludes the hand and wrist force the model to infer distal joints; no single viewpoint is optimal for dynamic multi-planar motion; a static calibrated camera is assumed.

benchmark_evidence: Clinical ARAT recordings (20 patients, 1,174 tasks), reprojection error: 12.5 +/- 3.0 px versus the 5-10 px lab standard; Score 0 trials 13.9 px median.
TULIP pose tracking versus manual annotation, mean error: 21 mm for finger tapping and 56 mm for gait (reprojection 22 and 16 px).
Nine-participant reachable-workspace recordings, average percent error per octant: up to 15.45% (frontal camera) and 50.21% (offset camera) in contralateral octants.
clusters.settings: Clinical movement assessment: Parkinson's finger tapping and gait (TULIP, 6 cameras at 80 fps), stroke ARAT grasp tasks (3 webcams at 1280x720, 60 Hz, around the assessment table), upper-extremity reachable workspace (single monocular RGB camera).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Off-the-shelf MediaPipe/MMPose keypoints are triangulated by DLT, with outlier interpolation and smoothing (TULIP, ARAT). A biomechanical model is fit to monocular keypoints for the reachable workspace. A five-camera setup for finger kinematics, single-camera reconstruction, and hardware for small rooms are proposed but untested in clinic.

clusters.name: Monocular depth ambiguity and self-occlusion
clusters.statement: From a single view, or from few views, body parts moving along the optical axis and self-occluded regions cannot be observed. These include a hand hidden by the torso or reaching arm, the back of the body and the mouth interior. Models infer such regions from priors and make large errors there.
clusters.description: The monocular reachable-workspace study names depth ambiguity along the optical axis as unresolved. Posterior targets give large anterior-posterior errors, foreshortening lowers the keypoint signal, and cross-body reaches hide the hand and wrist. The avatar survey and MVP-Human report the same for single-image clothed reconstruction: self-occlusion, depth ambiguity, back-side artifacts and unseen areas. MVHumanNet++ reports DUSt3R depth ambiguity on human point maps before fine-tuning. TULIP reports viewpoint-dependent keypoint occlusion and finds 2D features much weaker than 3D for clinical scoring. NeRSemble says frequently occluded regions such as the mouth interior need a learned prior before monocular capture is possible.

evidence_items.item: Monocular depth ambiguity along the optical axis is unresolved; posterior octants show elevated anterior-posterior errors; movements parallel to the optical axis cause foreshortening and low 2D keypoint signal-to-noise.
PIFu-style single-view methods struggle with complex poses, self-occlusion and depth ambiguity; reconstructing unseen areas from a single image remains a challenge.
Self-occlusion makes image features not describe the 3D point; back-side artifacts in single-image reconstruction remain open.
DUSt3R shows depth ambiguity on human point maps before fine-tuning on human data.
Keypoints can be occluded in specific viewpoints; models using 2D features performed poorly compared with 3D features for both finger tapping and gait.
The occluded mouth interior produces hollow-face artifacts; a learned 4D prior is needed for monocular input and frequently occluded regions such as the mouth interior.

benchmark_evidence: Nine-participant reachable-workspace recordings, average percent error per octant: up to 15.45% (frontal camera) and 50.21% (offset camera) in contralateral octants.
Nine-participant reachable-workspace recordings, octant agreement: offset camera under 40% agreement in the superior-anterior contralateral octant.
MVP-Human canonical shape Chamfer / P2S (cm): single-image PIFu 4.96 / 6.19 and ICON 3.96 / 3.96 versus 1.72 / 1.34 for the multi-frame method.
clusters.settings: Single static calibrated RGB camera for clinical reaching (frontal and offset placements, healthy adults, VR-displayed targets), single-image clothed human reconstruction (PIFu, ICON, MVP-Human), DUSt3R-style point maps on MVHumanNet++, six-camera keypoint triangulation (TULIP), monocular head avatars (NeRSemble future work).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Three approaches reduce the ambiguity but do not remove it: fitting a MuJoCo biomechanical model to monocular keypoints (reachable workspace), fusing multiple unconstrained frames (MVP-Human), and fine-tuning DUSt3R on human data (MVHumanNet++). Implicit-function and SMPL priors fill unseen regions, and errors stay large in contralateral and posterior workspace and on back sides.

clusters.name: Clinical validity of markerless kinematic scores
clusters.statement: Video-based kinematic measures cannot yet be validated as clinical endpoints. Cohorts are small, demographically narrow or healthy-only, and the reference ordinal scores (UPDRS, ARAT) are subjective, with very low inter-rater agreement. Minimal clinically important differences are not estimated, hand-crafted features break across tasks, and the best models match only the weakest clinician.
clusters.description: TULIP's Parkinson's cohort is small relative to disease heterogeneity and has low demographic diversity, and its baselines cover 2 of 25 activities. Clinician agreement on kinetic tremor is as low as ICC 0.1, and the best finger-tapping model only matches the least accurate rater. A deep pose-sequence classifier underperformed, which the authors attribute to dataset size. The ARAT study has longitudinal evidence from only two case studies, a borrowed MCID and no inter-rater data, and its discrimination weakens at the subjective Score 2 versus 3 boundary and where hand-crafted metric domains do not fit a task. The reachable-workspace study tested only nine healthy adults, so validity in patients with tremor or compensatory motion is unknown. The proposed fixes are prospective cohorts, able-bodied reference data, unsupervised signatures beyond UPDRS and movement foundation models.

evidence_items.item: Clinician agreement on kinetic tremor is very low (ICC 0.1 right, 0.4 left), limiting label reliability; the best finger-tapping model is commensurate only with the least accurate clinician; the cohort is small relative to PD heterogeneity with low demographic diversity; a deep pose-sequence classifier underperformed due to small dataset size.

Longitudinal evidence comes from two case studies only; the MCID is borrowed; there are no inter-rater reliability data for ARAT reference scores; hand-crafted metrics assigned to one domain break down for tasks such as Water Pouring; Score 3 is used as a proxy for normal performance.
The cohort is nine healthy adults only; validity in patients with atypical kinematics (tremor, compensatory trunk motion) is unknown.

benchmark_evidence: TULIP finger tapping, UPDRS weighted F1: best 0.69 (MLP, 3D features), commensurate only with the least accurate clinician.
TULIP gait, UPDRS weighted F1: best 0.72 (Random Forest, 3D features); 2D features underperformed.
TULIP clinician labels, ICC: kinetic tremor 0.1 (right hand) and 0.4 (left hand).
Clinical ARAT Tier 2 (Score 2 vs 3), AUC: 0.70-0.84 combined features, 0.59-0.68 compensation-only.
Clinical ARAT Water Pouring, Tier 1 AUC: 0.75, the lowest of seven task groups.
clusters.settings: Parkinson's UPDRS finger tapping and gait scoring (TULIP), stroke ARAT upper-limb assessment in routine clinic (20 patients, 1,174 tasks), reachable-workspace octant scoring in healthy adults (9 participants).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hand-crafted 3D kinematic features are evaluated leave-one-subject-out, with Score 3 used as a proxy for normal motor performance. Prospective cohorts, measure-specific MCIDs, measured able-bodied reference data, networks fit directly to 3D pose time series and movement foundation models are proposed, and none has been done yet.

clusters.name: Measured ground truth missing outside the lab
clusters.statement: Real human captures outside a mocap lab or dome lack measured ground truth for geometry, trajectories and driving signals. Datasets substitute pseudo labels (Sapiens normals, rendered depth, off-the-shelf mask, keypoint and SMPL annotations, cycle-consistency headset targets, pseudo-ground-truth trajectories), and the error bounds of these labels limit both training and evaluation.
clusters.description: MVHumanNet++ has no depth sensor and no measured normals: its normals are Sapiens pseudo labels, and its depth is rendered from normal-refined 2DGS. SmartPortraits has motion-capture ground truth in one lab only. Elsewhere it relies on pseudo ground truth whose no-reference error bound lets only a few methods be ranked. Codec Avatar Studio calls reliable pseudo ground truth from headset images to face deformations a key challenge. MVHumanNet annotates with off-the-shelf matting, keypoint and SMPL-X tools and notes that 3D skeletons are hard to acquire in everyday settings, and RenderMe-360 needed human-in-the-loop labelling when matting failed.

evidence_items.item: No ground-truth normals (pseudo labels from Sapiens) and no depth sensor (depth rendered from normal-refined 2DGS); the field cannot yet obtain measured geometry ground truth at the scale of large real multi-view human datasets.
MoCap ground truth exists only in the lab; other locations rely on pseudo ground truth with a no-reference error bound; ground truth outside the lab is listed as open.
Headset-to-avatar driving depends on pseudo ground truth; obtaining a reliable mapping from headset images to face deformations is called a key challenge.
The headset driver relies on pseudo ground truth from cycle consistency with personalized avatars built from dome captures.
Annotations come from off-the-shelf tools (RVM plus SAM masks, OpenPose, triangulation, SMPL/SMPL-X fitting); acquiring 3D skeletons in everyday settings is hard.
Matting fails on diverse hairstyles and accessories, requiring human-in-the-loop labelling.

benchmark_evidence: SmartPortraits ATE/RPE against pseudo ground truth: only LDSO, OKVIS, PVIO, SVO2 and VINS can be ordered given the pseudo-ground-truth bound.
SmartPortraits MOM no-reference map metric: up to about 2 cm for most locations, comparable to depth sensor noise.
clusters.settings: RGB-only multi-view human rigs (MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++), handheld smartphone plus Azure Kinect in several locations (SmartPortraits), Quest Pro headset face driving (Codec Avatar Studio), studio head matting (RenderMe-360).
clusters.attempted_fixes: The datasets substitute foundation-model pseudo labels (Sapiens normals), depth rendered from fitted Gaussians, cycle-consistency targets, no-reference map metrics (MOM) and manual correction. None of these gives measured accuracy, and each is bounded by its own unknown error.

clusters.name: No comparable benchmarks or task-linked metrics
clusters.statement: Several human-capture tasks lack shared benchmark data, protocols and evaluation criteria. Comparisons run at reduced resolution, and intermediate metrics such as camera trajectory accuracy do not predict downstream reconstruction or synthesis quality.
clusters.description: RenderMe-360 reports no unified data or criteria for talking-head benchmarking and calls its own benchmark coverage incomplete. NeRSemble notes that head NVS lacks comparable benchmarks and plans a public one. HumanRF had to run its comparisons at 4x downscaled resolution because the baselines fail at full resolution. TULIP starts from the absence of benchmark video datasets for Parkinson's symptom scoring, since prior video work is single-camera and covers one or two activities. SmartPortraits finds that trajectory accuracy does not translate into downstream reconstruction and synthesis quality, and leaves the reason as future work.
