evidence_items.item: Lack of unified data and criteria for talking-head benchmarking; benchmark coverage is incomplete.
Comparable benchmarks for human head NVS are lacking; a public NVS benchmark on representative recordings is future work.
There are no benchmark video datasets for PD symptom scoring; prior video work is single-camera and covers one or two activities.
Trajectory accuracy does not translate directly into downstream reconstruction and synthesis quality; investigating why is future work.
Comparisons run at 4x downscaled resolution because baselines fail at full resolution.

clusters.settings: Head NVS and talking-head evaluation (RenderMe-360, NeRSemble), full-body free-viewpoint video (ActorsHQ), clinical video scoring (TULIP), handheld SLAM-to-reconstruction evaluation (SmartPortraits).
clusters.attempted_fixes: New benchmark datasets with fixed protocols (RenderMe-360, NeRSemble, TULIP) and an open community platform proposed by RenderMe-360. No metric linking upstream tracking to downstream reconstruction quality is proposed.

notes:
Reconciled the bottom-up lens (19 clusters) and the capability lens (17 clusters) into 19 clusters. papers_read = 15 records, which are 14 distinct papers: ids 438 and 1430 are two digest records of the same NeurIPS 2024 paper (Codec Avatar Studio, Ava-256 and Goliath). Both ids are kept in paper_ids for traceability, and n_papers counts distinct works.

One-to-one merges, with paper ids unioned: dense-studio/lightweight-sensor avatars; scarce and undistributable data; human-object interaction excluded; SMPL priors vs loose clothing; hair/mouth/eyes; relighting; hands and faces at full-body scale; long or involuntary motion; clinical finger kinematics; clinical validity; measured ground truth; benchmarks. Problem-type conflicts were settled as follows: lightweight-sensor avatars mixed (paired data plus priors), HOI mixed, ground truth mixed.

Finer cuts kept, since each finer cluster has at least 3 distinct papers:
(1) The capability lens's 'Generalization to unseen identities and long-tail' cluster was split into the bottom-up clusters 'Per-identity fitting without cross-identity generalization' (8 papers), 'Cross-dataset domain gap' (4) and 'Object-centric 3D models fail on humans' (4).
(2) The bottom-up 'Upstream pose, mask and landmark errors propagate' cluster was replaced by the capability lens's finer partition. 'Camera and body-pose registration errors propagate' covers 1435, 1442 and 1443, and uses the bottom-up SMPL-X misfit evidence for 1435. The mask-flicker item (1437) and the NHA preprocessing failure (1436) moved to the motion cluster, and the matting human-in-the-loop item (1432) moved to the ground-truth cluster.

Coarser cut kept: the bottom-up 'Out-of-distribution expressions' cluster was folded into the capability lens's 'Driving avatars beyond captured expressions and poses'. An articulation/motion-control-only cluster would have had only 2 papers (1437, 1440).

Offline compute: the bottom-up and capability versions were unioned (8 distinct papers), and per-subject training is kept as evidence in both the compute cluster and the generalization cluster.

Disputed paper ids, settled by re-reading the digest:
- Relighting: dropped 1436. NeRSemble's eye specularities and reflectance are NVS artifacts under fixed diffuse light, not relighting, and they stay in the hair/eyes cluster.
- Monocular depth: kept both 1436 (occluded mouth interior needs a learned prior for monocular input) and 1424 (viewpoint-dependent keypoint occlusion; 2D features underperform 3D). Both are weaker supports than 1427, 1440 and 1443.
- Ground truth: dropped 1427. Its post-hoc alignment to a marker system is an evaluation step, not a stated lack of ground truth. Kept 1432 (failed matting needs manual labels).
- Benchmarks: kept both 1424 (no PD video benchmark datasets) and 1437 (comparisons at 4x downscaled resolution).
- SMPL: kept 1435 (twisted, self-intersecting SMPL-X fits).
- RenderMe-360's accessory drop is a single-ID result, so it sits in the hair/accessories cluster rather than the generalization cluster.

Items left out because each comes from a single work: misuse and impersonation mitigation (438/1430); automatic local 3D editing, SDS noisy geometry, the non-structural nature of 3DGS, and multi-view consistency in generation (1440); uncertain hatch-mounted light positions (1439); therapist-marked trial segmentation (1426).

Relevance for the thesis direction: only 1426 directly states finger and hand-object capture as unmet, and 1434, 1435, 1440 and 438/1430 state HOI exclusion or HOI generation as open. The three clinical papers (1424, 1426, 1427) are the only ones about hand kinematics with few cameras in a compact space. 1442 is the only paper with a depth sensor (Azure Kinect), and 1435 explicitly has none. No paper in this group gives a benchmark number on hand-object interaction.

Benchmark numbers are taken only from the digest's bench_gaps and failures fields. Where a gap is reported only qualitatively (RenderMe-360 tables, HumanOLAT Table 2), the benchmark_evidence entry says so.

clusters.name: Object 6D pose in joint human-object reconstruction
clusters.statement: From a single RGB image, monocular video or sparse consumer RGB-D, the field cannot yet recover the handled object's 6D pose and placement during whole-body interaction to better than several centimetres to decimetres, even when the object template is given, because the body occludes the object, depth is ambiguous or noisy, and contact regions are small.
clusters.description: Papers report that joint human-object reconstruction lags far behind human-only reconstruction: on the same benchmark the object error is roughly 2 to 5 times the body error (BEHAVE: 4.99 cm body vs 21.20 cm object). The causes they name are mutual occlusion, noisy and incomplete depth, monocular depth ambiguity for placement, symmetric objects or parts, the lack of object keypoint detectors and of any statistical object shape model, and contact regions near the image resolution limit. Fitting to noisy point clouds or masks falls into local minima, and the optimization layer that joint methods still need is slow (CHORE about 312 s per frame). Fixes tried are predicted object orientation and contacts as fitting constraints, optimization after regression, IMU initialization of objects, contact-guided placement with retrieved meshes and object-conditioned reconstruction; each leaves centimetre-to-decimetre errors or relies on extra sensors, ground-truth contact or a given object pose.

evidence_items.item: Direct fitting of SMPL and the object template to noisy, incomplete Kinect point clouds gets stuck in local minima (object 26.09 cm v2v); symmetric objects get the right surface fit but the wrong orientation; the proposed tracker still has 21.20 cm object error versus 4.99 cm for the body.

In the RHOBIN challenge the winning joint method still has 87.2 mm object error and object 6DoF average recall of only 0.6, versus 45.1 mm SMPL error; joint reconstruction still needs an optimization layer beyond direct regression.

Coarse in-the-wild reconstruction has collisions, wrong scales and positions and inaccurate object pose, so manual annotation is needed; the best method still has 38.44 cm object translation error and 19.3 cm Chamfer distance.
Without IMU initialization, object rotation cannot be recovered from masks; there are no strong object keypoint detectors, so masks are the main object evidence.
No robust single-image 3D object shape recovery and no statistical object shape model exist; object error rises from 13.34 cm with ground-truth contact to 21.85 cm without.
Part rotation error is still 19.35 deg and translation 66.23 mm even with the known object structure; rotation-symmetric parts get the wrong part rotation.
All monocular capture methods have large object errors on HODome (PHOSA 77.62, CHORE 86.58 Chamfer); the original PIFu fails to predict object depth in human-object scenes.
Directly outputting object pose from images is too hard, so reconstruction is conditioned on a given object mesh and pose.
Estimating rigid object pose given its 3D model while reconstructing the interacting hand and body is stated as open and left as future work.
Reconstruction with interacting objects faces pose-initialisation and sparse object observation problems.

benchmark_evidence: BEHAVE / object v2v: 21.20 cm (PHOSA 34.73 cm) vs SMPL v2v 4.99 cm [1150]
BEHAVE (RHOBIN) / joint reconstruction: winner 87.2 mm object and 45.1 mm SMPL vs human-only PA-MPJPE 18.4 mm; object 6DoF AR-all 0.6 (CHORE 0.3) [1156]
Open3DHOI / object translation 38.44 cm, Chamfer 19.3 cm (PHOSA 77.79 cm / 49.1 cm) [119]
InterCap OOD / PA Chamfer object: 21.85 cm without GT contact vs 13.34 cm with GT contact [120]
HODome / monocular object Chamfer: PHOSA 77.62, CHORE 86.58 [1153]
CHAIRS / part rotation 19.35 deg and translation 66.23 mm even with known structure [1152]
HOI-M3 monocular multi-HOI / PCKabs 5.9%, object V2V 297.8, Chamfer 235.0 [37]
clusters.settings: Single in-the-wild RGB images (Open3DHOI, PICO/DAMON, CHAIRS internet images), monocular RGB on BEHAVE and InterCap (RHOBIN), sparse multi-view Kinect RGB-D (BEHAVE), dense RGB domes evaluated with monocular methods (HODome, HOI-M3); mostly one person with one rigid or articulated object, indoors.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Instance or category template fitting with predicted orientation and contacts (BEHAVE, RHOBIN entrants), optimization after regression (RHOBIN), IMU-initialized object tracking (HOI-M3), contact-guided placement with retrieved Objaverse meshes (PICO), known CAD plus URDF structure (CHAIRS), and object-conditioned reconstruction (F-HOI). All still need a template or a given pose, run slowly through an optimization layer, and leave 5 to 40 cm errors.

clusters.name: Object template dependence and narrow object scope
clusters.statement: Human-object capture and reconstruction still require a pre-scanned or category-level rigid template (or CAD plus URDF), usually for one person with one object, so unseen geometry and articulated, rotation-symmetric, deformable, small, large, multiple or moved objects are not handled or not annotated.
clusters.description: Almost every interaction dataset and method assumes a known rigid mesh, often with markers or IMUs attached, and dataset and challenge papers list the single-person, single-rigid-object setup as a scope limit. Reported failures include wrong orientation for symmetric objects, untracked deformable parts such as backpack straps, large shape error when the kinematic structure is unknown, poor segmentation of small objects such as cups and bottles, degraded contact on unseen objects, missing large objects and multi-object scenes, static-only objects, and no annotation for moved objects. Open-world work substitutes retrieved or generated meshes that need manual repair, and skinning-based avatars cannot represent held objects at all. Proposed fixes (symmetry classification with min-of-N losses, templates built on the fly from video, text-to-3D meshes) are stated as future work.

evidence_items.item: Objects are assumed rigid, so a deformed backpack strap is not tracked with rigid templates; the network predicts the wrong orientation for symmetric objects such as a square suitcase.

Approaches assume a known category-level object template; template-specific pose estimators do not generalize to different object geometry such as different chairs; the challenge covers only one person with one object.

Prior work assumes rigid objects; without the object's kinematic structure shape error stays high (Chamfer 160.2 mm vs 72.3 mm with CAD plus URDF), and rotation-symmetric parts get the wrong part rotation.
A known pre-scanned rigid mesh is assumed; small objects such as bottles or cups are poorly segmented under occlusion; smaller objects and dexterous manipulation are left as future work.
Full object geometry and trajectory are required as input; unseen objects degrade contact F1 from 0.72 to 0.61.
No single statistical object shape model exists, so the object is approximated by a mesh retrieved from Objaverse.
Object meshes come from single-image generation with inpainting and manual repair; in-the-wild 3D HOI benchmarks are limited to few categories with fixed CAD models.
A known 3D object mesh is required as input, and the model is closed-set with no generalization to unseen objects.
Existing HOI datasets and models cover a human with a single object; HIMO itself has no large objects and uses 3D-printed objects with known geometry and markers.
Non-rigid, articulated and deformable objects (cloth, ropes, soft tissue) and multi-object interactions are underexplored.
Interactive objects cannot be modelled by skinning-based avatars and disappear or stretch under large novel poses.
The annotation tool cannot label dynamic, moved objects, so boxes exist only for static objects; most HOI datasets are tabletop-limited.
Despite 217 objects, the aggregated dataset does not cover in-the-wild object diversity; it assumes known object meshes.
Capture relies on known rigid pre-scanned object templates with an IMU embedded in each object.
Objects are rigid bodies tracked with at least four markers and scanned meshes; egocentric hand-object reconstruction with multiple objects is open.
Only static objects are handled (chair 6D pose averaged per session); non-static objects such as lifting a box or opening a door are left for future work.
Objects are treated as rigid pre-scanned templates with at least four glued markers; only single-person, single-object interaction is captured.

benchmark_evidence: CHAIRS / unknown structure Chamfer 160.2 mm and IoU 11.03% vs known structure 72.30 mm and 21.57%; part rotation 19.35 deg even with known structure [1152]
FullBodyManip (OMOMO) unseen objects / contact F1 0.61 (0.72 seen), MPJPE 13.06 cm [1154]
HIMO 3-object partition / method beats baselines only on R-precision and MM-Dist [323]
HOI-M3 / monocular multi-HOI PCKabs 5.9% [37]
NymeriaPlus / only 4547 of 7171 static-object boxes got valid generated meshes [1247]
DNA-Rendering / Interaction-Medium and -Hard novel-pose splits described as insurmountable for current methods [1433]
clusters.settings: Multi-view Kinect RGB-D capture (BEHAVE, InterCap, CHAIRS, COUCH), marker-on-object mocap (OMOMO, HIMO, InterVLA, NeuralDome, HOI-M3), aggregated mocap HOI (InterAct), monocular single-image HOI (RHOBIN, PICO, Open3DHOI, F-HOI), egocentric scene annotation (NymeriaPlus), multi-view neural avatar capture (DNA-Rendering).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Markers or IMUs on every object, URDF kinematic models, mesh retrieval (PICO), single-image 3D generation with inpainting and manual Blender repair (Open3DHOI), generated meshes for static objects (ShapeR), static-object restriction (COUCH), and proposed per-object symmetry classification, on-the-fly templates from video and text-to-3D meshes. All need per-object prior knowledge.

clusters.name: Dense contact inference and contact labelling
clusters.statement: The field cannot yet infer dense 3D contact between the body or hands and objects, scenes or other people from images out of domain, derive it reliably from reconstructed geometry, or detect contact events automatically, so datasets rely on manual annotation or distance thresholds whose labels are unreliable, and methods assume continuous contact.
clusters.description: Contact regions are small, often occluded and near the image resolution limit. Learned dense contact estimators collapse on new interaction types and datasets, and contact computed from current human and object reconstructions is described as very poor. Threshold-based labels inherit pose, shape and scan errors, and models trained on them predict contact almost everywhere. Capture datasets therefore annotate contact frames and vertices by hand, synthetic data lacks non-foot contact labels, and synthesis methods cannot handle intermittent contact. Tactile and pressure sensing does not settle the question: pressure drops are ambiguous between losing contact and applying less force, and insoles give foot contact only.

evidence_items.item: Geometry-based contact from current 3D human and object reconstruction is very poor (CHORE F1 0.08, PHOSA F1 0.18), and DECO itself reaches only F1 0.18 with 44-46 cm geodesic error out of domain on BEHAVE.
Visual threshold contact labels inherit pose, shape and scene-scan errors; estimators trained on them (BSTRO, DECO) predict contact almost always, giving high recall but low precision.
Contact frames and likely contact vertices are annotated manually; automatic contact detection is a stated open problem, and false contacts appear on the dorsal side of the hand.
Incorrect human contact prediction by DECO was the largest failure source (85 of 500 reconstructions); object error rises from 13.34 cm with ground-truth contact to 21.85 cm without.
Contact constraints cannot handle intermittent contact; identifying and predicting contact states for long-term manipulation is open.
Automatic contact-event detection from tactile gloves was ambiguous: thumb-palm contacts came from gripping the wipe, and pressure drops could mean lost contact or lower force.
The dense contact dataset covers only static scenes, not hand-held objects or human-human contact; BSTRO accuracy drops when the interaction type is unseen in training.
Contacts are small image regions close to the resolution limit; contacts are defined by a 2 cm threshold on pseudo ground truth, and contact prediction gave no significant quantitative gain.
Contact signature prediction between people is far below human consistency (IoU 0.082 vs 0.226 at 75 regions), and the contact-consistent optimization uses ground-truth contact annotations.
Contact assignment is ambiguous when body parts occlude each other with the object between them, and adding a contact loss can increase collision in some images.
Synthetic datasets fail to capture dynamic 3D contacts; adding TRUMANS contact data lowers DECO recall from 0.5232 to 0.4806.
Foot sliding is hard to mitigate because foot contact labels are unreliable, and XSens contacts are unreliable on stairs.
Kinect-fitted motion is jittery while IMUs are smooth but miss contacts; predicted contacts more than 10 cm from the chair surface are discarded.
Non-foot body-scene contacts in the synthetic data may be inaccurate (for example hands in cartwheels).
Contact labels for human-scene interaction are not yet included in the synthetic dataset.
Interaction-aware mesh recovery methods depend on pre-defined contact vertices, which limits generalization.

benchmark_evidence: BEHAVE (out of domain) / DECO F1 0.18 and geodesic error 46.33 cm; BSTRO F1 0.04 and 50.45 cm [1155]
DAMON test / best F1 0.55 with geodesic error about 21 cm [1155]
DAMON subsets / contact from reconstructed geometry: CHORE F1 0.08, PHOSA 0.18 vs DECO 0.48 / 0.60 [1155]
MMVP / foot contact best F1 0.532, IoU 0.522 [56]
FlickrCI3D / contact signature IoU_75 0.082 vs human 0.226 [1060]
DAMON + TRUMANS / adding TRUMANS lowers DECO recall 0.5232 -> 0.4806 and F1 0.5115 -> 0.4972 [79]
InterCap OOD / object error 21.85 cm without vs 13.34 cm with GT contact [120]
COUCH test / average contact error 4.73 vs 10.52-12.09 for NSM/SAMP baselines that ignore contact inputs [1151]
clusters.settings: Single in-the-wild RGB images (DAMON, Open3DHOI, PICO-db), BEHAVE out of domain, multi-view Kinect HOI capture (BEHAVE, InterCap, COUCH), static scanned scenes (RICH), RGB-D plus pressure insoles (MMVP), human-human contact (CHI3D, FlickrCI3D), tactile gloves in caregiving, synthetic renders (BEDLAM2.0, SynBody, TRUMANS), contact-conditioned synthesis (COUCH, OMOMO).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Direct dense contact regression (DECO, BSTRO), crowd-sourced contact painting, nearest-neighbour contact lookup (PICO), distance thresholds on pseudo ground truth (BEHAVE), manual contact annotation (InterCap), pressure insoles and mats for foot contact (MMVP), tactile gloves (bathing), and contact-conditioned optimization with ground-truth contact (CHI3D). Learned estimators fail out of domain, threshold and manual labels do not scale, and tactile signals are ambiguous.

clusters.name: Physically implausible reconstructed and generated interactions
clusters.statement: Kinematic reconstruction and generation of human-object and human-scene interaction still produce penetration, floating objects, hovering hands, foot sliding and jitter, and the mocap HOI datasets used for training carry the same artifacts, because methods do not enforce contact, gravity and support beyond a single flat floor.
clusters.description: The papers see these artifacts in three places: monocular, egocentric and sparse-signal pose output (leaning, hovering, ground penetration, foot skating, legs passing through scene geometry), interaction generators (a keyboard floating with no support, bodies passing through bookshelves, hands forced onto objects during intermittent contact), and the training data itself (InterAct reports penetration, floating contacts, inaccurate hands and jitter across seven mocap HOI datasets; CHAIRS needs post-hoc penetration removal). Fixes tried are guidance losses, space occupancy, contact correction, intuitive-physics terms, post-hoc penetration removal, pressure sensing and physics simulators. Each has its own limit: guidance losses add jitter, intuitive-physics terms assume one flat floor and static poses, correction fails on large errors, and simulators are action-specific and fit poorly with diffusion models.

evidence_items.item: MoCap HOI data carry penetration, floating contacts, inaccurate hand poses and jitter; correction fails on severe source noise, and physics imitation succeeds 84.4% on raw vs 90.7% on corrected data.
Generated HOI states ignore gravity (a keyboard floats without contact), and interpenetration persists when actions conflict with objects.

Image-based body estimates lean, hover and penetrate the ground; the intuitive-physics terms handle only body-floor contact on a single flat plane, break on multiple or inconsistent ground planes, and target static poses.
The method is purely kinematic and produces penetration; forcing hands onto the object during intermittent contact causes body-object penetration.
Foot sliding occurs in 8.13% of frames vs 3.36% for ground truth, traded off against penetration avoidance; slight collisions remain in dynamic scenes.
Foot sliding persists in 9.81% of contact frames because foot contact labels are unreliable and lower-body signals are weak.
Reconstructions show ground penetration, foot skating and body leaning; scene-aware methods assume flat floors or pre-scanned static scenes.
Generated motion passes through scene objects (a body through a bookshelf), with feet floating above the ground.
Per-frame separate fitting yields jitter and heavy body-object penetration.
Generated interactions lack physical plausibility in gravity and force interaction; physics-simulator methods are action-specific, generalize poorly and fit poorly with diffusion models.
Vision-based mocap ignores physical interaction with the scene, producing drift, jitter, sliding, floating and penetration.
Prior monocular mesh recovery suffers translation drift, foot sliding and foot-plane penetration in fast large-range motion.
Sparse-signal methods let legs penetrate scene geometry, and the scene-penetration and phase-matching guidance losses that fix this can introduce jitter.
Captured articulated HOI data still contain unrealistic contacts and penetrations because of limited sensor count and limb-length discrepancies, requiring post-hoc penetration removal.

Single head-mounted fisheye methods produce body-environment penetration or floating; an optimization baseline with a contact term forces non-contact joints into contact when the initial pose is wrong.
Prior egocentric methods show floor penetration and foot skating; physics-based modelling is named as future work.
GRAB-trained models show high penetration, and actions outside the training set produce object intersections.
Data-driven interaction generation ignores physical properties and produces sliding, penetration and floating.
sEMG hand-pose predictions can be physically infeasible, and current metrics do not capture plausibility.
Template-free video motion capture works in camera space with no physical or contact constraints such as foot contact.
Most pose methods ignore human interaction with 3D scenes; exploiting human-scene interaction and physical constraints is listed as future work.
Joint multi-person HOI generation has 9.265% penetration versus 1.452% for people alone.
Naive dual-branch multi-object generation produces implausible human-object and object-object contacts.
Synthesized human-chair motion can slightly intersect the chair; collision-avoidance post-processing is future work.

benchmark_evidence: MOB / penetration 15.21 voxels/frame vs GT 0.00; foot sliding 8.13% vs GT 3.36% [328]
HOI-M3 generation / penetration 9.265% joint vs 1.452% for people alone [37]
GRAB-trained models / penetration 34.41 (method), 44.09 (GOAL) [79]
NymeriaPlus / foot sliding 9.81% of contact frames [1247]
InterAct PhysHOI imitation / success 84.4% raw vs 90.7% corrected [1134]
FullBodyManip (OMOMO) / only 31% preferred over ground truth [1154]
I2M / Contact@1 0.672 with intention text vs 0.858 trajectory-only [462]
RICH / MPJPE IPMAN-O 240.9 mm vs SMPLify-X 268.6 mm, errors remain large [1251]
clusters.settings: Monocular and egocentric pose and shape estimation (3DPW, RICH, MoYo, SceneEgo, FRAME, MMVP), sparse HMD signals (CIRCLE, GIMO), mocap HOI datasets used for synthesis (GRAB, BEHAVE, InterCap, CHAIRS, OMOMO, InterAct, HIMO, F-HOI), interaction generation in scanned or synthetic scenes (TRUMANS, MOB, I2M, HOI-M3), sEMG hand pose, template-free video capture.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Scene-penetration and phase-matching guidance (adds jitter), space occupancy (residual collisions), unified contact-threshold correction (fails on large gaps), intuitive-physics terms (flat floor, static poses), post-hoc penetration removal, pressure sensing (confined to a mat), and physics simulators (action-specific, poor fit with diffusion).

clusters.name: Forces, pressure, torques and muscle activity from motion
clusters.statement: The field cannot yet estimate contact forces, ground or object reaction forces, joint torques or muscle activation from vision or kinematics outside instrumented labs, and simulation-derived labels leave out object interaction because object mass and non-foot reaction forces are unknown.
clusters.description: Dynamics ground truth needs force plates, pressure mats or insoles, tactile gloves or EMG, and these confine motion to a mat or a lab. Learned force-from-motion models are not real-time, not validated or do not generalize across activities. Simulation datasets that try to scale (ImDy, Muscles in Time) model only ground reaction forces, assume weightless objects or drop object-interaction motions, and carry a sim-to-real gap. Wearable muscle sensing does not transfer across users or tasks, and its labels still come from occlusion-prone mocap and simulated musculoskeletal hands. Inferring pressure or force from vision is named as the next step, but no paper in the group reports doing it.

evidence_items.item: External force measurement outside mocap labs is unreliable; force-from-motion models are not real-time or not validated, and out-of-distribution multi-activity models exceed 25% body-weight error.
Only ground reaction forces are modelled; hand-object and human-object forces are absent, and torques for a jumping motion are not predicted faithfully.
Object interactions are mostly excluded for lack of reaction forces, and the included object motions assume weightless objects.
Motions with non-foot contact or external objects were excluded because reaction forces are unknown; lifting and throwing assume negligible object mass.
The method depends on specialized pressure sensors and all motion must stay on the mat; inferring pressure from vision is the key next step.
Capacitive gloves cannot separate normal from shear force, mild pressure falls below sensor sensitivity, and tactile data alone cannot tell which bodies are in contact.
There is no one-to-one pose-to-muscle mapping; pose-to-EMG error rises from 0.134 RMSE in distribution to 0.209 cross-user and 0.264 cross-task.
Only relative pressure is recovered because body mass is unknown; estimated pressure IoU is 0.32.
Tendon signals come from a simulated musculoskeletal hand and labels depend on occlusion-prone mocap via inverse dynamics, so real tendon-driven hand testing is required.
Pressure datasets cover only slow, small-range motion; learning body dynamics from pressure alone is future work.

benchmark_evidence: AddBiomechanics / GRF error best 1.17 N/kg, joint torque 1.33 Nm/kg; only 21.2% of data clinical-grade [334]
ImDy on AddBiomechanics / torque mPJE 0.1626 Nm/kg; jumping fails [495]
MinT / Pearson correlation 0.54 lower body, 0.55 upper body; upper-body SMAPE 107.7 [434]
MoYo / pressure IoU 0.32, CoP error 57.3 mm, CoM error 53.3 mm [1251]
PianoKPM / cross-task RMSE 0.264 vs 0.134 in distribution [475]
emg2tendon held-out / tendon RMSE 0.253, angular error 14.7 deg [692]
clusters.settings: Force plates with marker mocap (AddBiomechanics), physics-simulated humanoids and OpenSim musculoskeletal models driven by AMASS (ImDy, MinT), pressure mats and insoles (MotionPRO, MoYo, MMVP), tactile gloves in caregiving, sEMG wristbands and surface electrodes (emg2tendon, PianoKPM).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Physics re-simulation of mocap (ImDy), musculoskeletal simulation (MinT), pressure-RGB fusion (MotionPRO), learning GRF from large lab datasets (AddBiomechanics), and closed-loop summed-pressure tactile control. These suffer sim-to-real gaps, model only foot contact, and confine motion to instrumented areas.

clusters.name: Finger-level grasp lost in whole-body interaction capture
clusters.statement: When the whole body and the handled object are captured together (consumer RGB-D rigs, body mocap, sparse VR trackers, monocular or egocentric video), finger articulation and the hand-object grasp are not recovered: hands jitter, interpenetrate or are omitted, and downstream synthesis and robot transfer fail at precise hand contact.
clusters.description: Body-scale capture leaves the hand at low resolution: consumer depth is too noisy for fingers, body marker sets cannot track most finger articulation, inertial gloves spoil RGB realism, and marker fitting of gloved hands contorts fingers. Datasets therefore paste unrelated hand motions onto bodies or omit hands, and methods trained on them produce implausible grasps and miss hand detail. Errors in predicted hand positions propagate to the full body, whole-body recovery error rises sharply once hands are included, and humanoid or robot policies built from such data fail on hand-precision tasks. Fixes tried are separate hand trackers or wrist-only markers, pasting GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion, glove-specific fitting and manual frame-by-frame hand landmark correction.

evidence_items.item: Kinect noise prevents modeling fine hand interactions, causing interpenetration and unrealistic grasps.
Hand jitter is stronger than body jitter because of low image resolution, motion blur and coarse point clouds; dexterous manipulation and smaller objects are left open.
The dataset does not represent dexterous hand movements; hand-position errors propagate to the full body (MPJPE 12.42 with predicted hands vs 7.01 with GT hands).
Full-body estimation from HMD and controllers fails to capture fine-grained hand-object interactions such as picking up clothes or wiping a blackboard; no hand articulation is modelled.
Inertial gloves were discarded to preserve RGB realism, so finger poses are not captured (three wrist markers only); WiLoR fails to give smooth, accurate hand estimates on egocentric video.
Subtle finger motion capture under severe occlusion is listed as open.
Hands interacting with objects are largely missing from the synthetic data; GRAB hand motions are pasted on without object contact.
Hand motions are sampled from ARCTIC and attached to AMASS bodies without coordination with any object.
Marker-based MoSh++ fitting of gloved hands produces contorted fingers and hand-body gaps.
The best humanoid pipeline reaches only 6/5 percent success lifting a box; retargeting fails on hand-precision tasks and the humanoid has no dexterous hands.
Hand landmarks need frame-by-frame manual correction, and precise gripper finger shaping around small packaging is the dominant robot failure.
Whole-body recovery error rises sharply when hands and face are included.
The headset body network does not predict hand pose; an external hand tracker supplies wrist constraints.
Hand detail is poorly captured; no hand parameters are predicted.
The intention dataset has no hand or finger articulation (body-only kinematics).
Marker placement does not allow tracking most hand articulation during close interaction.
The method does not model hands explicitly, and multi-view reconstruction shows artifacts at hands and feet.
Existing mocap HOI datasets carry inaccurate hand poses.
Monocular depth ambiguity causes implausible hand poses in complex interacting-hands scenarios.
Single-frame vision-based 3D hand annotations (HaMeR) are jittery and erroneous, with missing hand joints under occlusion and rapid motion.
Hand hardcase handling targets wrist rotation only, not precise finger postures; the SMPL body model has no articulated fingers.
Face and finger motion requiring high-resolution capture is listed as open.

benchmark_evidence: FullBodyManip (OMOMO) / MPJPE 12.42 cm with predicted hands vs 7.01 with GT hands; 13.06 cm on unseen objects, 7.73 cm with GT hands [1154]
Mimicking-Bench box lifting / best 6/5% success [1391]
RoboBenchMart non-fridge tasks / mean 13.8% success, dominated by finger shaping failures [1380]
Bathing captures / glove-to-body contact distance median 1.714 cm with MoSh++ vs 0.536 cm with glove-aware fitting [697]
AGORA and EHF / errors much higher when hands and face are included [1264]
Semantic-HOI / authors report the model underperforms on hand details [322]
clusters.settings: Multi-Kinect RGB-D HOI capture (BEHAVE, InterCap), optical body mocap with few hand markers (OMOMO, InterVLA, CHI3D, I2M, bathing), sparse HMD tracking, VR headset cameras (EgoBody3M), synthetic rendering (BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0), monocular sign-language and piano video, multi-view volumetric capture (Hi4D), humanoid and VLA transfer in simulation.
clusters.attempted_fixes: External hand trackers supplying wrist constraints (EgoBody3M), wrist-only markers, inertial gloves (HIMO; dropped in InterVLA for realism), pasting GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion (BEDLAM), glove-aware fitting (bathing), manual frame-by-frame hand landmark correction (SABER), and hand priors with contact constraints proposed (OMOMO).

clusters.name: Wrist, forearm rotation and ankle errors dominate
clusters.statement: Body pose estimators place the distal joints worst: wrist and ankle positions and lower-arm rotations keep the largest errors even when visible, and much larger when out of view, in egocentric, athletic, clinical and occluded settings.
clusters.description: Several benchmarks break errors down by joint and find wrists, ankles and feet highest, with lower-arm rotation not visible in position metrics. Stated causes are high degrees of freedom, near-rest-pose pseudo-labels for hands and feet, out-of-view extremities, close camera distances and training-set bias. The wrist is the anchor of the hand, so these errors bound any hand-object reconstruction built on a body estimate. Fixes tried are hardcase mining and pseudo-label refinement (wrist rotation only), external hand trackers for wrist constraints, and target-domain fine-tuning; ankle and wrist errors remain several centimetres.

evidence_items.item: Wrist joints keep high error despite good visibility in egocentric views of the interaction partner.
Wrists, feet, nose and head show the highest MPJPE under occlusion; distal, high-DoF joints are error-prone even when visible.
Baseline monocular methods fail to capture lower-arm rotations, which MPJPE does not reveal; all methods exceed 23 degrees mean angular error.
Monocular mesh recovery failures concentrate in hand-wrist and foot-ankle misalignment; existing methods recover hands and feet near T-pose in dance and martial arts.
Joints out of view of all four headset cameras give wrist MPJPE of 12.2 cm versus 5.18 cm overall.
Models trained on Human3.6M reach ankle errors up to 560 mm on athletic motion, and about 164-170 mm after fine-tuning.
Wrist distance error is still 5.07 cm including a constant offset (from 14.32 cm).
Foot MPJPE (155.86 mm) and lower-body error (130.97 mm) stay far above upper-body error (77.85 mm) on real head-mounted stereo.
Monocular RGB mesh recovery (WHAM) adds depth and distal-joint error to the clinical gait data.

benchmark_evidence: EgoBody3M / out-of-view wrist MPJPE 12.2 cm vs 5.18 cm overall; 2D-lifting 62.5 cm [329]
EMDB / MPJAE above 23 deg for all methods [1238]
HardMo-Foot / foot MPJPE: ProHMR 213.6 mm, 4DHumans 88.1 mm [1193]
AthletePose3D / ankle error up to 560 mm (H3.6M-trained), 164-170 mm after fine-tuning [1255]
UnrealEgo-RW / foot MPJPE 155.86 mm vs upper body 77.85 mm [1]
NymeriaPlus / wrist distance error 5.07 cm [1247]
clusters.settings: Egocentric HMD and headset cameras (EgoBody, EgoBody3M, UnrealEgo-RW), moving hand-held phone video (EMDB), monocular dance, martial-arts and sports video (HardMo, AthletePose3D), synthetic occlusion lifting (BlendMimic3D), clinical gait (Care-PD), inertial-suit ground truth (NymeriaPlus).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hardcase mining with refined pseudo-labels (HardMo, wrist rotation only), an external hand tracker supplying wrist constraints (EgoBody3M), and fine-tuning on the target domain (AthletePose3D). Distal-joint errors remain the largest.

clusters.name: Body pose under heavy object or person occlusion
clusters.statement: When the handled object, furniture, bedding, an assistive device or another person covers much of the body, monocular and sparse-view body estimators and person detectors fail, with errors of roughly 12 to 33 cm and near-zero detection accuracy in the worst settings, and temporal interpolation breaks once occlusion outlasts the model's window.
clusters.description: Occlusion benchmarks show monotonic degradation with occlusion severity and a large extra error when detected rather than ground-truth boxes are used. Lifting models trained on random masks do not generalize to realistic, prolonged occlusion. Frames with scene contact are markedly worse than frames without, 2D keypoint detectors fail when objects cover the body or hands interact with them, tabletops hide the legs, interacting staff hide clinical subjects, and covered in-bed bodies defeat RGB, depth and pressure. Fixes tried are synthetic occlusion data (sim-to-real gap remains), occlusion-aware lifters (which lose clean-input accuracy), fine-tuned detectors, triangulation from few views, and manual correction of 2D detections.

evidence_items.item: All HPS methods degrade as occlusion severity increases; human detectors struggle under occlusion, and 3DPW MPJPE rises from 71.10 mm with ground-truth boxes to 116.52 mm with YOLO11.
The original DTF collapses to about 302 mm MPJPE when occlusions last longer than its 81-frame interpolation window; masking-trained models do not generalize across occlusion patterns.
Monocular HPS error rises on frames with scene contact (TR-MPJPE 214.0 vs 161.81 mm), attributed to scene occlusion.
OpenPose fails when objects occlude the body or hands interact with them.
For covered in-bed bodies, the pressure map cannot localize limbs out of contact, depth fails when an arm is blocked by the head, and a depth-pretrained 3D model fails most of the time.
Video methods struggle with long-term occlusion; motion priors are needed for temporally consistent tracking under occlusion.
Pose and shape estimation under heavy occlusion by the interacting object is listed as open.
AlphaPose keypoint detection and lifting failed frequently on dense, occluded, object-interacting urban scenes.
All tested monocular methods (HMR, SPIN, HybrIK, PARE, CLIFF) have MPJPE of 309-332 mm on multi-person, multi-object interaction; multi-person pose under object occlusion is open.
Heavy occlusion from close two-body contact, garments and assistive devices drives a pretrained 2D pose detector to about 0.02 mAP.
Strong occlusions such as a tabletop covering both legs increase prediction error considerably.
Object-occluded human pose and shape estimation is listed as open.
Missed 2D keypoints from lower-limb occlusion propagate into mesh regression.
Robustness under heavy occlusion, with multiple plausible reconstructions, is listed as open; severe jitter appears in heavily occluded frames.
Top-down detectors fail to separate largely overlapped bodies under heavy occlusion, and 3D HPE robustness to occlusion in crowded scenes is open.
2D pose detectors are inaccurate under heavy occlusion, requiring a filter and manual correction.
The optimizer fails when body parts severely occlude each other and the object lies between them.
Healthcare staff partially or fully occlude the subject, especially in the sagittal view outside the parallel bars.
The multi-person regressor fails with heavy occlusion and on people with few visible parts.

benchmark_evidence: VOccl3D hard / best fine-tuned MPJPE 136.34 mm and PVE 175.92 mm; CLIFF 192.22 / 247.41 mm [259]
3DPW / VOccl3D-CLIFF 71.10 mm with GT boxes vs 116.52 mm with YOLO11 detections [259]
HOI-M3 / MPJPE 309-332 mm for all tested monocular methods [37]
RICH-test / PIXIE TR-MPJPE 214.0 mm with scene contact vs 161.81 mm without [1252]
OpenRoboCare / pretrained 2D mAP 0.0244 on bathing; 3D MPJPE 119.9-162.7 mm [999]
BlendMimic3D / MixSTE 69.46 -> 175.21 mm under occlusion noise; DTF-GT 301.91 mm [1229]
clusters.settings: Synthetic occlusion video and lifting (VOccl3D, BlendMimic3D), scene contact in scanned scenes (RICH), HOI capture (BEHAVE, InterCap, HODome, HOI-M3, Open3DHOI, RHOBIN), headset views with tabletops (EgoBody3M), in-bed monitoring under covers (SLP), caregiving and clinical video (OpenRoboCare, ProGait), dashcam pedestrians (PVCP), urban blind-pedestrian video, multi-person images (Relative Human).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Synthetic heavy-occlusion training data, occlusion-aware lifting (DTF variant, worse on clean input), masking-based training, fine-tuned detectors, triangulation from three calibrated views (OpenRoboCare), manual correction of 2D detections (FreeMan, EgoBody), and temporal interpolation. Under prolonged real occlusion none of these hold up.

clusters.name: Offline optimisation, no causal real-time capture
clusters.statement: Accurate human and human-object capture still relies on offline whole-sequence or per-frame iterative optimisation that runs far slower than real time, and no causal method of comparable accuracy exists for settings that need live feedback, such as a robot reacting to a moving person.
clusters.description: Joint human-object reconstruction, multi-person global estimation, wearable LiDAR-IMU capture, neural HOI modelling, musculoskeletal simulation and dynamics estimation all report optimisation costs from minutes per frame to hours per sequence, and dataset ground truth is itself built by offline batch optimisation. Regression alone does not reach the accuracy of the optimisation layer. The robot-assisted bathing work states that online pose and shape estimation fast enough for live interaction does not exist and that this perception gap is why the system cannot be used on humans. Surveys list real-time processing on edge devices and the cost of lifting pipelines as open, and diffusion lifters are judged too slow.

evidence_items.item: The system cannot be used on humans; perception is the main bottleneck, and online pose and shape estimation with sub-frame latency during sustained contact does not exist.
The optimization-based baseline CHORE needs about 2000 forward passes (312 s per frame), and joint reconstruction still needs an optimization layer beyond direct regression.
Scene-aware optimization is computationally heavy: 0.73 h and 2.80 h for one 7725-frame sequence, hindering real-time use.
SLAHMR takes 40 minutes per 100 frames with 4 subjects.
Offline trajectory optimization runs at about 0.001x real time and handles only seconds of data.
Diffusion-based lifters are too slow for real-time use.
Real-time processing on edge and ARM platforms is listed as an open challenge.
The instance-segmentation optimization is computationally slow; a faster deformer is future work.
Capture uses offline whole-sequence optimization.
Reconstruction uses offline per-sequence neural optimization.
Capture relies on offline optimization with tedious stages and manual correction.
The pipeline is not real-time and needs pre-selected bounding boxes.
Muscle labels come from offline, compute-intensive simulation that fails to converge on some segments.
Ground truth is built by offline joint optimization with LiDAR SLAM, IMU poses and scene constraints.
Capture uses offline graph-based and joint optimization after offline synchronization and calibration.
Scene depth comes from SfM over 4 s windows of frames, i.e. windowed offline processing.
Computational cost, including that of 2D-to-3D lifting pipelines, and efficiency on resource-constrained devices are listed as open.

benchmark_evidence: BEHAVE (RHOBIN) / CHORE about 312 s per frame [1156]
HiSC4D / optimization 0.73 h and 2.80 h for 7725 frames [1036]
WorldPose / SLAHMR 40 min per 100 frames with 4 subjects [1197]
AddBiomechanics / offline optimization about 0.001x real time [334]
clusters.settings: Monocular and RGB-D HOI fitting (BEHAVE, InterCap, RHOBIN), dense-dome HOI capture (HOI-M3, HODome), multi-person global video optimisation (WorldPose), wearable LiDAR-IMU capture (HiSC4D, HSC4D, SLOPER4D), close-interaction segmentation (Hi4D), musculoskeletal simulation (MinT, AddBiomechanics), robot-assisted caregiving, dashcam video.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Regression networks replacing optimization (RHOBIN entrants still keep an optimization layer), faster deformers (proposed), windowed processing, and lightweight architectures (proposed). No paper in the group reports a causal real-time method that matches offline accuracy.

clusters.name: Jitter, track loss and identity switches over time
clusters.statement: Per-frame and short-window estimators cannot yet track people and their limbs stably over time: outputs jitter, tracks are lost or interpolation collapses when occlusion outlasts the model's window, and identities switch when bodies overlap, exchange positions or the camera moves fast.
clusters.description: Several dataset, benchmark and survey papers report temporal failures separate from per-frame accuracy. Per-frame fitting and single-frame hand or body estimators jitter, worst for hands and in heavily occluded frames, and monocular video methods show high jitter even with ground-truth boxes. Interpolation-based lifters collapse when occlusion exceeds their window, mask and point trackers lose thin or textureless parts and must be re-initialised, and trackers switch identities under overlap, rapid egocentric motion or low light. Offline chunked optimisation leaves gaps between chunks and over-smooths fast motion. Fixes tried are motion priors, forecasting models for occluded keypoints, 3D region proposals, periodic tracker re-initialisation and longer temporal windows; identity switches and jitter remain.

evidence_items.item: Per-frame separate fitting yields jitter; residual jitter from detector sensitivity to occlusion and inter-camera delays remains and is worse for hands; advanced motion priors are future work.
Severe jitter appears in frames with heavy occlusion, and long-term motion jitter in video reconstruction is open.
Monocular methods show high jitter, angular errors above 23 degrees and high standard deviations even with ground-truth boxes.
The original DTF collapses to about 302 mm MPJPE when occlusion outlasts its 81-frame interpolation window; interpolation-based occlusion handling fails for prolonged occlusion.
Frame-based methods cannot maintain identity assignments and coherent trajectories when bodies overlap or exchange positions; temporal reasoning for identity-consistent motion is future work.
Prior trackers suffer person-ID switches from rapid camera motion, occlusion and unconstrained activity; the proposed method still reports 741 ID switches.
Identity preservation is weak (IDF1 at most 22.72), and OC-SORT performs poorly because large motion displacement makes distant frames uninformative.
Distinguishing the subject from healthcare staff and keeping consistent tracking under occlusion is hard; Grounded SAM2 loses track of the prosthetic leg.
STv2-Tracking suffers frequent tracking loss from textureless clothing and thin prosthesis geometry; SAM2 mask tracking must be restarted every 10 s.
Tracking through long occlusions in multi-person video is listed as open.
Video methods help but struggle with long-term occlusion and fast motion; motion priors for temporally consistent tracking are future work.
After contact, occluded keypoints are hard to associate with the correct identity, requiring a forecasting motion model and mask-conditioned pose estimation.
SLAHMR produces overly smooth motion, missing fast movements, with mesh gaps between non-overlapping chunks.
Kinect-fitted motion is jittery under occlusion and drastic movement.
Single-frame HaMeR hand annotations are jittery, with missing and invalid frames under occlusion and rapid motion that need post-hoc refinement.
3D HPE from video is not smooth or continuous.
Self-occlusion leads to incorrect landmarks or frame-to-frame jitter.
SLAM has limits under long-duration occlusion, and the second person is intermittently occluded so sequences are split into visible segments.

EHPT-XC / IDF1 at most 22.72; best MOTA 47.37 [432]
MuPoTS-3D / best HOTA 65.3 [1261]
BlendMimic3D / DTF-GT 301.91 mm under prolonged occlusion [1229]
EMDB / MPJAE above 23 deg with high jitter for all methods [1238]
clusters.settings: Multi-Kinect HOI capture (InterCap, COUCH), monocular HOI video (RHOBIN), moving hand-held cameras (EMDB), occlusion lifting (BlendMimic3D), multi-person RGB-D groups (HUM4D), egocentric multi-human tracking (EgoHumans), low-light multi-person tracking (EHPT-XC), close-contact in the wild (Harmony4D), clinical prosthesis video (ProGait, RSP3D), broadcast sport (WorldPose), wearable LiDAR (HiSC4D), monocular hand video (PianoKPM).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Sequence-level motion priors (InterCap), forecasting motion models for occluded keypoints (Harmony4D), interpolation windows (DTF), 3D region proposals (EgoHumans), periodic re-initialisation of mask trackers (RSP3D), and RGB-event fusion (EHPT-XC, which raises ID switches). Jitter and identity switches remain.

clusters.name: Close multi-person interaction: contact, overlap and identity
clusters.statement: When people touch, overlap or exchange positions, monocular and sparse-view methods cannot yet produce mutually consistent, contact-accurate 3D meshes or keep identities stable, marker mocap itself breaks down under close proximity, and most capture pipelines and benchmarks still track a single person.
clusters.description: Close-contact benchmarks report errors well above 50 mm, contact distances in the hundreds of millimetres, interpenetrating or far-apart meshes, wrong depth ordering and contact-signature prediction far below human consistency. Frame-based estimators lose identity when bodies overlap or swap, top-down detectors fail on overlapped bodies, and point clouds of nearby people merge. Caregiving and assistance scenes add garments and assistive devices, and generic 2D detectors nearly fail there. Several capture systems (SLOPER4D, LIP, RHOBIN, HiSC4D) track only one person or truncate the second, and multi-person extension is listed as future work. The papers blame training data that lacks contact interactions. Fixes tried are contact signatures, personalized avatars with alternating optimization, Kalman forecasting, 3D region proposals and depth-layer weak labels, and these need ground-truth contact, dense rigs or slow optimization.

evidence_items.item: Reconstruction of close interactions remains hard with errors above 50 mm; contact signature IoU 0.082 vs human 0.226; current mocap fails for multiple people in close proximity and occlusion.
Monocular baselines show missing meshes and inaccurate poses under inter-person occlusion (Multi-HMR 93.8 mm vs 61.4 mm on 3DPW); the authors attribute the gap to missing contact data in training.
Monocular SMPL baselines are not robust to strong human-human occlusion (contact distance 295.8-338.0 mm), and 8-view MVPose still has 166.8 mm contact distance with heavy interpenetration.
Frame-based methods cannot maintain identity assignments when bodies overlap or exchange positions; PA-MPJPE rises from about 39-82 mm on 3DPW to 151-180 mm on closely interacting groups.
There is no modelling of contact between people, so contact is missed and meshes interpenetrate; about a third of relative depth relations are still wrong.
Heavy occlusion from close two-body contact, garments and assistive devices causes pose failures; a pretrained 2D detector reaches about 0.02 mAP.
Prior trackers suffer person-ID switches from rapid camera motion, occlusion and unconstrained activity.
Two people in close proximity occlude each other and their point clouds coincide.
Coupled two-person motion prediction in physical assistance degrades on an unseen task (caregiver 154.8 mm at 1000 ms).
Global methods get relative positions between players wrong even with a shared ground plane.
Multi-person pose and shape under object occlusion and monocular multiple-HOI capture are listed as open.
The LiDAR field of view truncates and occludes the second person; capturing human-human interaction from an egocentric view in large scenes is open.
Tactile data alone cannot tell which bodies are in contact, and point or instantaneous contact models cannot represent sustained caregiver-patient contact.
Distinguishing the clinical subject from healthcare staff who occlude them is hard.
Multi-person pose tracking in low light keeps weak identity preservation (IDF1 at most 22.72).
Tracking through long occlusions in multi-person video is open.
The challenge is limited to one person and one object; multi-person, multi-object benchmarks and methods are future work.
Only a single person is captured although multiple people appear; multi-person urban capture is open.
Extending LiDAR-IMU capture to multi-person scenes is future work.
Crowding and occlusion in open-world scenes are open; top-down pipelines fail on detection errors in multi-person scenes.
Top-down detectors fail to separate largely overlapped bodies, and bottom-up keypoint association degrades in occluded scenes.

clusters.attempted_fixes: Contact-signature-guided optimization (CHI3D), personalized implicit avatars with alternating optimization (Hi4D), Kalman forecasting with mask-conditioned pose (Harmony4D), extra marker clusters (HUM4D), 3D region proposals (EgoHumans), and depth-layer weak labels (BEV). These need ground-truth contact, dense rigs or slow offline optimization.

clusters.name: Drift-free world-frame human trajectories
clusters.statement: The field cannot yet recover drift-free, metric world-frame human trajectories over long sequences or large areas, either from moving monocular cameras (human and camera motion entangled, SLAM failing on dynamic or textureless scenes) or from body-worn IMUs, whose integration error grows with time and distance.
clusters.description: Global benchmarks show world-frame errors of metres even when root-relative pose is good. GLAMR and SLAHMR place people on tilted planes, diverge under fast camera motion and long focal lengths, and get relative positions wrong; SLAM fails on textureless pitches and among moving people, and even ground-truth cameras do not remove the error. Camera-space methods and template-free capture output no global trajectory at all, and monocular methods drift in depth during fast motion. Ground-based velocity priors fail for off-ground motion such as climbing. Inertial capture drifts, needs recalibration and needs LiDAR, scene scans or global optimization to correct it, and localization error still grows linearly with distance travelled. Body-worn camera methods accumulate root error without SLAM grounding.

evidence_items.item: GLAMR global predictions drift significantly (G-MPJPE 3193 mm); camera-relative weak-perspective settings are too restrictive for moving cameras.

SLAHMR diverges under fast camera motion and large focal length, DROID-SLAM fails on the textureless pitch, and global methods get relative positions between players wrong even with a shared ground plane.
GLAMR fails worst on high-pace large-area running: ATE RMSE 29.48 m and G-MPJPE 32329.3 mm.
Current methods cannot disentangle human and camera motion in dynamic-camera video; metric world-coordinate motion is left as future work.

Global HMR accumulates errors over long sequences; GVHMR and WHAM are good in camera coordinates but poor in world coordinates, and GVHMR fails in vertical climbing because it predicts horizontal velocity.
Localization error grows linearly with distance travelled for all methods, including the IMU plus LiDAR method.
The IMU-only baseline drifts severely and assumes a horizontal walking plane (569.7 mm pose-to-point-cloud distance).
Root translation errors accumulate because the model predicts frame-to-frame relative transforms and lacks SLAM or SfM grounding.
Camera-space HMR methods fail to recover global trajectories when the camera moves; multi-view SLAHMR is no better when the primary camera moves.
Egocentric global estimators fail when rapid head turns push the person out of view; GLAMR and WHAM lose global orientation.
Vision-only methods (WHAM, TRACE) show vertical root drift and poor global trajectories; without pressure-RGB fusion global accuracy drops.
Monocular RGB methods (CLIFF, TRACE) drift in depth during side-stepping, jumping and throwing, and moving cameras remain hard.
Monocular methods fail on 3D global motion; capturing rapid motion with precise global localization is open.
Global position is not recovered from uncalibrated dashcam video, so non-aligned errors remain large (MPVE 257.75 mm).
Template-free video motion capture outputs camera-space motion with no global trajectory.
World-frame methods trained on BEDLAM2.0 still have W-MPJPE100 of 193.7-284.4 mm on EMDB.
The XSens dead-reckoned trajectory accumulates significant drift, so no static global alignment exists; inertial systems drift.
IMU-only head pose estimation suffers from accumulating drift.
Inertial mocap drifts and requires periodic recalibration.
Weak-perspective single-HOI methods give inaccurate root depth, and IMU drift degrades object tracking over time.

clusters.attempted_fixes: SLAM-initialized optimization (SLAHMR), world motion maps (TRACE), gravity-aligned velocity regression (GVHMR, WHAM), synthetic camera-motion training data (BEDLAM2.0, DynaCam), LiDAR-IMU joint optimization with scene constraints (HSC4D, HiSC4D), LiDAR global position and pre-scanned scenes (ClimbingCap, LEIR), and pressure fusion (MotionPRO). Each fails on fast cameras, textureless scenes or off-ground motion, or leaves drift that still grows.

clusters.name: Close-range body- or robot-mounted views see partial bodies
clusters.statement: From head-mounted, body-worn or close-range robot-mounted cameras, the field cannot yet reconstruct the full body when the wearer's lower body is self-occluded, limbs leave the field of view, or an observed person is truncated and leaves and re-enters the frame, and real annotated data for practical rigs is scarce.
clusters.description: Egocentric papers report that lower-body and foot errors stay far above upper-body errors, that bending, crouching and self-contact fail, and that sparse head, wrist and controller signals leave the lower body under-constrained. Near-field occluders (hair, hats, tabletops) and out-of-view joints raise error sharply, SfM fails when the body fills the frame, and scene depth behind the body is unobservable. For observing others, interaction partners are truncated and blurred, rapid head turns push people out of view so global estimators lose orientation, and low robot cameras see a single limb at close range, which ruins forecasting; wide-FOV distortion adds error at close range. Real data with practical camera placement is scarce, so methods depend on synthetic pretraining with a sim-to-real gap. Fixes tried are stereo fisheye, scene-aware depth inpainting, device-pose floor alignment, multi-camera headsets, imputation models and projection choice.

evidence_items.item: Lower-body (130.97 mm) and foot (155.86 mm) errors remain much larger than upper-body (77.85 mm); SfM fails when the body fills the frame.
Joints out of view of all four headset cameras reach 12.2 cm wrist MPJPE; a tabletop covering both legs and near-field hair or hats raise error; no surface-mounted camera pair covers the full body.
Bending and crouching are reconstructed poorly because the lower body is occluded by the upper body.
Tracking signals come only from the upper body, so lower-body error stays high (107.9 mm vs 23.1 mm hand error on GIMO).
Severe body truncation in the egocentric view raises error, with the lower body most truncated; methods average 77% higher error than on 3DPW.
Egocentric global motion estimators fail when rapid head turns push the person out of view and they re-enter the frame.
Close-range interaction leaves only part of the body (often one limb) visible to low robot cameras; 3D error 168 mm, and forecasting from partial poses reaches 309-333 mm.
Pinhole reprojection error rises rapidly for close-up subjects spanning more than about 120 deg FOV; best absolute error is still about 204 mm.
Lower-body tracking from 3-point inputs is much worse than upper body (16.74 cm lower-body MPJPE with real inputs).
Pose accuracy is bounded by estimated scene depth, especially behind the body where the scene is occluded.
Egocentric body-facing capture struggles with significant occlusion and self-contact; real annotated ego-facing data is scarce.
Head-mounted cameras suffer self-occlusion and poor lower-body resolution; direct sim-to-real training on body-worn cameras gives 0.77 m global MPJPE.
Existing methods are unsuited to rapid wearable camera motion; unreliable 2D keypoints when people are occluded or out of frame degrade triangulation.
Reliable foot contact and lower-body motion from head and wrist signals remain open because lower-body signals are weak.

clusters.attempted_fixes: Stereo fisheye with scene depth, depth inpainting behind the body, floor-aligned frames from device 6D pose, four-camera headset fusion, motion priors, large synthetic pretraining, imputation for incomplete pose sequences, and choice of fisheye projection. Lower-body and out-of-view errors remain large.

clusters.name: Noisy, sparse, device-specific real depth and LiDAR
clusters.statement: Body and body-object recovery from real consumer RGB-D, mobile LiDAR or long-range LiDAR point clouds remains far less accurate than from images, because real depth is noisy at boundaries, sparse at range, misaligned with RGB in fast motion, truncated by the field of view and different across devices, so models trained on one sensor fail on another.
clusters.description: Point-cloud parametric recovery methods depend on synthetic training data and are much worse than image-based HMR on real Kinect clouds; moving from Kinect to iPhone LiDAR raises error sharply. Long-range LiDAR leaves fewer than 30 points on a person, models trained on one LiDAR give the largest errors on another, LiDAR SLAM fails in crowded or narrow spaces, and nearby people merge into one cloud. Kinect noise at boundaries and RGB-depth misalignment limit fine hand capture, depth noise at distance degrades robot-view lifting, body parts blend into the bed in in-bed depth, and naively adding raw depth to a network can hurt when invalid values are present. Robot policies also do worse on raw RGB-D than on structured maps. Fixes tried are multi-view fusion, boundary removal, synthetic LiDAR-IMU data, translation correctors and LiDAR-IMU fusion.

evidence_items.item: Point-cloud parametric recovery performs poorly on real commercial RGB-D clouds because methods depend on synthetic data (VoteHMR 144.99 mm vs image HMR 54.78 mm); Kinect-trained VoteHMR degrades to 255.71 mm on iPhone LiDAR; Kinect depth is noisy at subject boundaries.
Direct fitting to noisy, incomplete Kinect point clouds gets stuck in local minima (SMPL 16.15 cm, object 26.09 cm), and Kinect noise prevents fine hand interaction.
At up to 28 m fewer than 30 points fall on the person; the baseline is not robust to varying point density across distances and devices.
Domain gaps between LiDAR sensors with different point distributions and ranges remain; persons beyond 20 m contain only a few points.
Models trained on another LiDAR dataset give the largest errors on SLOPER4D, indicating a domain gap between LiDAR sensors.
Depth-based 3D lifting is limited by depth-map noise, especially for distant participants; the depth sensor FOV is narrower than the cameras.
Fast motions cause RGB-depth misalignment, and coarse point clouds contribute to hand jitter.
A depth-based pretrained 3D model fails most of the time on in-bed poses because body parts blend and the bed acts as attached background.
RealSense D455 depth accuracy limits capture volume and activity design; depth variation as subjects move creates ambiguity.
Two people in close proximity have coinciding point clouds, and distant, heavily occluded people give sparse points that cause failure.
Naively adding depth to a CNN 3D module does not help, likely because invalid depth values corrupt it.
Multi-view egocentric RGB-D observation collapses to 4/4 percent mean success versus 54/51 percent with an elevation map, attributed to noisy information in the images.
The LiDAR vertical field of view truncates the second person, and low LiDAR resolution prevents texture reconstruction.
LiDAR SLAM fails in crowded places and narrow areas, and LiDAR alone increases local pose errors because of body jitter.
RGB-D has limited range, and LiDAR is sparse with a low frame rate.
LiDAR plus RGB pose fails on long-tail poses such as arm raising and sitting on the ground.
Depth-based 3D pose reaches only 131.4 mm MPJPE in domain, and LiDAR is not covered by the benchmark.
Substituting depth for RGB for privacy degrades joint-level precision and downstream joint angles.

clusters.attempted_fixes: Multi-view RGB-D fusion, aggressive boundary removal and outlier filtering (HuMMan), synthetic LiDAR-IMU training data, translation correctors for partial clouds (LIP), LiDAR-IMU fusion and joint optimization with scene maps, and structured elevation maps instead of raw RGB-D (Mimicking-Bench). Cross-device gaps and sparse-range failures remain.

clusters.name: Wearable and non-visual sensing drifts, transfers poorly
clusters.statement: Non-visual and wearable sensing (body-worn IMUs, wrist sEMG, mmWave, Wi-Fi, thermal and IR arrays, event cameras, pressure mats) cannot yet replace cameras for pose: inertial estimates drift with time and distance, learned models lose much of their accuracy on unseen users, sensor units and scenes, they remain less accurate than RGB or IMU suits, and the privacy they are said to offer is not measured.
clusters.description: Datasets that pair non-visual sensors with mocap labels report large cross-domain drops for new users, new IMU units and new rooms, and drift that grows with time or distance for inertial capture, which needs frequent recalibration and optimization to correct. sEMG relates to pose derivatives, so integrated pose drifts, and EMG models fail across users and tasks. RF and thermal pose errors are several times those of RGB in domain and rise further across scenes, event-only input fails on static hands and adds false positives, and pressure maps cannot see limbs out of contact. A position paper argues that skeletons, depth and RF still leak identity, that obfuscation lowers keypoint accuracy, and that no privacy score is reported anywhere.

evidence_items.item: Wi-Fi pose error rises from 147.3 mm to 399.4 mm across domains because of multipath sensitivity; RGB rises to 473.9 mm cross-scene; IR-array HAR only 25.6%.
mmWave results are worse than RGB or IMUs (MPJPE 163.3 mm vs 80.2 mm IMU), and IMU-based HPE degrades on unseen subjects (147.4 mm).
sEMG models remain less accurate than vision methods; angular drift comes from velocity integration, and accuracy degrades most for held-out user plus held-out gesture combinations.
Non-RGB modalities still leak biometric identity through skeleton, shape and gait; obfuscation degrades joint precision; no standard privacy metric exists.
IMU-only estimation accumulates drift, and transfer to a different IMU cuts the integration-error reduction from about 90-92% to about 53-60%.
RGB is ineffective in darkness and under covers, LWIR heat residue causes labeling ambiguity, and the pressure map cannot localize limbs out of contact.
Event-only input gives the worst results (MPJPE 107.78 mm), and each sensor has its own limits (RGB light-sensitive, LiDAR sparse, IMU worn and drifting).
Adding events to RGB raises false positives and ID switches in low-light multi-person tracking.
Pose-to-EMG models fail across users and tasks (cross-task RMSE 0.264 vs 0.134 in distribution), and EMG sensors detach with perspiration.
sEMG-to-tendon error grows on held-out users and stages (11.3 to 14.7 deg).
The IMU-only baseline drifts severely and assumes a horizontal walking plane.
Localization error grows linearly with distance travelled even with IMU plus LiDAR fusion.
Sparse-IMU methods drift, which motivates adding LiDAR.
Inertial systems drift and XSens quality depends on calibration and body measurements.
IMU-derived labels are inaccurate and translation drifts over long captures, requiring global optimization and manual repair.
The in-the-wild IMU suit needs frequent recalibration and manual filtering of tracking failures.
IMU drift and calibration errors degrade object tracking over time.

RELI11D / event-only MPJPE 107.78 mm [75]
EHPT-XC / adding events raises false positives and ID switches [432]
clusters.settings: Lab multi-modal rigs with mmWave, Wi-Fi, thermal, IR arrays, acoustic and IMU (OctoNet, mRI), in-bed LWIR and pressure (SLP), sEMG wristbands and surface EMG (emg2pose, emg2tendon, PianoKPM), helmet IMUs (HelmetPoser), body-worn IMU suits with or without LiDAR (Nymeria, BlindWays, ClimbingCap, HSC4D, HiSC4D, LIP), object-mounted IMUs (HOI-M3), event cameras (RELI11D, EHPT-XC).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Multi-modal fusion (OctoNet's best fusion keeps 52.7% HAR accuracy cross-scene), LiDAR-IMU fusion (HSC4D, HiSC4D, LIP), RGB-event fusion, personalization, domain adaptation and probabilistic sEMG models (proposed), camera plus sEMG fusion for occlusion (proposed), and privacy risk levels (illustrative only).

clusters.name: Interaction ground truth needs instrumented studios
clusters.statement: Accurate 3D ground truth for people interacting with objects, scenes or each other can still only be obtained with instrumented studios (dense camera domes, marker or inertial suits, markers or IMUs on objects) plus manual correction, and even there markers drop out under contact and alter appearance, inertial suits drift, and markerless pseudo ground truth from fitting is unvalidated, which leaves interaction data small, lab-bound and narrow.
clusters.description: Dataset papers repeatedly state a trade-off between motion accuracy and visual realism. Optical mocap needs suits, markers and gloves that make RGB unnatural and that lose markers under occlusion, clothing, slings and close contact; inertial suits drift and need recalibration; markerless domes need 20 to 76 cameras plus manual correction and are immobile; electromagnetic sensors interfere across people. Markerless and RGB-D pipelines produce pseudo labels from the same detectors being evaluated, often needing manual correction, and several datasets have no independent ground truth at all; true in-the-wild 3D ground truth is called infeasible. Surveys and dataset papers blame this cost for the scarcity of interaction data. Proposed fixes (mobile camera rigs, hybrid IMU-camera capture, smartphone arrays, synthetic rendering on top of mocap, aggregating and correcting existing datasets) trade accuracy for coverage and still need manual work.

evidence_items.item: Accurate capture is still out of reach even with dense multimodal input (42 cinema cameras plus IMUs in each object); extremely occluded cases need manual correction; indoor only.
RGB appearance is unnatural because of mocap suits and markers; 4D HOI capture is hard.
The mocap suit and wristbands make video appearance unnatural and restrict range of motion; optical systems are limited by line of sight and inertial systems drift.
Capture methods force a trade-off between motion accuracy and visual realism; vision and RGB-D capture are less accurate and occlusion-prone, IMU capture drifts.
Accurate ground truth under human-human contact needs RGB-D mocap or 100+ wired cameras; the in-the-wild pipeline needs 20+ synchronized cameras and trades accuracy for mobility.
Inertial gloves were discarded to preserve RGB realism, so finger poses are not captured; about 10 hours of data is still insufficient for generalist models.
RGB-D recorded datasets scale better but give lower-quality pose and object tracking than mocap; mocap needs markers on all movable objects in a dedicated area.
12.7% of emg2pose frames could not be processed because of simultaneous marker occlusions and were interpolated.
Clothing and slings occluded markers, causing mocap failures for manikin pose and caregiver hands.
Large-scale real 3D interaction data are resource-intensive to capture; markerless capture is less robust to lighting and occlusion, and marker systems need controlled environments.
Current mocap fails for multiple people in close proximity and occlusion; only one subject per video is motion-tracked.
Pseudo-annotated test sets contain visible SMPL errors, and error rises sharply when noisy SMPL samples exceed about 50%.
Only pseudo ground truth exists; there is no independent mocap ground truth for evaluation.
True in-the-wild 3D ground truth is infeasible; labels are semi-automatic pseudo ground truth.
Marker-based and commercial capture is expensive, spatially confined and fails under occlusion; BEHAVE ground truth is pseudo ground truth from instance-specific fitting with manual mask correction.
Multiple electromagnetic systems interfere, so no multi-person sequences exist, and in-the-wild ground-truth trajectories drift 23.4 cm over 81 m.
Marker-based MoSh++ fitting of gloved hands produces contorted fingers, and markers that block bathing are temporarily removed.
Ground truth needs a 6-camera OptiTrack system and a 37-marker suit in a lab; occlusions caused missing markers in up to 3% of frames.
Marker-based capture loses markers under occlusion, and IMU calibration error lowers accuracy.
Captured data still contain unrealistic contacts and penetrations because of limited sensor count, and the unclothed SMPL-X annotations misalign with images.
Marker-based object tracking retains bias from camera alignment error, and tracking components have no ground truth.
Pseudo ground truth comes from multi-view triangulated 2D keypoints and SMPL fitting; the mesh toolchain produces shrunk or dilated geometry under self-occlusion.
Ground truth is pseudo ground truth from multi-view triangulation of 2D detector outputs, not marker-based.
Pseudo 3D labels come from 4DHumans plus refinement, and marker or markerless capture of skilled dance and martial arts is prohibitively expensive.
The annotation pipeline needs a calibrated static stadium camera system plus costly manual correction and reaches about 8 cm G-MPJPE against Vicon.
Marker tracking suffers dropout in tight multi-person interactions, so extra marker clusters were added.
Annotation still needs manual intervention and screening (about 25 person-hours), and multi-view configuration and calibration are unwieldy.
Ground truth needs 8-15 static secondary cameras, and in-the-wild capture trails static wired systems in accuracy.
Aligning and annotating data from movable cameras is unsolved; ground truth comes from triangulated detector keypoints with manual correction.
Ground truth requires a 17-IMU suit, LiDAR and a laser scan of each scene, and IMU drift over long captures forces optimization for labels.
Labelled data requires an Xsens IMU suit and manual annotation repair.
In-the-wild motion capture is not solved; the IMU suit needs frequent recalibration and manual filtering of tracking failures, and the hardware is expensive.
Heavy manual annotation in Blender and a web tool is needed, and no ground-truth objects exist.
3D sign language annotation is manual and labour-intensive; the pseudo ground truth is validated only on EHF.
Mocap labels suffer occlusion and lose frames (for example in fist clenching), and the wrist is not tracked.
Mocap requires standardized garments, which attenuate thermal signals and reduce RGB appearance diversity; capture is lab-only.
Heavily occluded takes were dropped after manual inspection, and only joint positions are released.
Ground truth comes from 2D detection, two-camera triangulation and optimization refinement, not marker mocap.
No 3D pose ground truth exists for covered in-bed poses.
3D HPE ground truth depends on mocap, so datasets are constrained and methods degrade in the wild.
Simultaneous capture of humans and 3D scenes is expensive, so paired datasets have limited diversity; MOB derives pseudo-scenes from motion-only mocap.
Existing HOI mocap datasets are small and inconsistent and carry penetration, floating contacts, inaccurate hands and jitter.
Datasets of full-body interaction with moving objects are scarce; capture used 12-camera Vicon with 5 markers per object.
Interaction data are costly to capture, and datasets from controlled settings do not cover real-world interaction diversity.
2D ground truth is derived by projecting mocap data with a simplified pinhole model and tape-measured camera positions.

benchmark_evidence: HOI-M3 monocular HPS / MPJPE 309-332 mm for all tested methods [37]
FreeMan cross-domain / VoxelPose trained on Human3.6M: zero AP below 100 mm [29]
PROX vs TRUMANS / contact 0.723 vs 0.992, much weaker on real scanned scenes [79]

emg2pose / 12.7% of frames lost to marker occlusion [692]
BlindWays / Motion-X-trained text-to-motion FID 11.2-15.0 vs 3.34 trained in domain [436]
