clusters.settings: Optical marker studios for HOI, caregiving and close contact (HIMO, InterVLA, TRUMANS, I2M, HHI-Assist, OMOMO, CHI3D, OpenRoboCare, bathing, HARPER, emg2pose, REHAB24-6), inertial suits in the wild (Nymeria, BlindWays, ClimbingCap, RELI11D), electromagnetic sensors (EMDB), dense RGB domes (HOI-M3, NeuralDome, Harmony4D, EgoHumans), markerless multi-view RGB or RGB-D pseudo ground truth (BEHAVE, InterCap, HuMMan, FreeMan, mRI, WorldPose, FISHnCHIPS, Human-M3), monocular pseudo labels (HardMo, PVCP, SignAvatars, Open3DHOI).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hybrid optical-inertial capture (HOI-M3), electromagnetic sensors (EMDB; interference blocks multi-person), mobile multi-camera rigs (Harmony4D, EgoHumans), smartphone arrays (FreeMan), extra marker clusters (HUM4D), synthetic rendering on top of mocap (TRUMANS), aggregation and correction of existing mocap HOI sets (InterAct), pseudo-scenes from motion-only mocap (MOB), and manual correction and review. Each gives up accuracy or realism, and manual work remains.

clusters.name: Multi-sensor synchronization and calibration
clusters.statement: Multi-sensor capture rigs (multiple Kinects or RealSense, HMD plus external cameras, camera plus LiDAR, mocap plus RGB domes, video plus IMU suits or pressure insoles) still lack hardware synchronization and robust calibration, so pipelines depend on claps, jumps, flashlights and manual alignment, and residual offsets cap accuracy, especially for fast hand motion.
clusters.description: Dataset papers name synchronization and calibration as a source of residual error. Azure Kinect inter-camera delays bound fitting error and produce hand jitter, HoloLens and Kinect show misalignment on fast hand motion, sensors run at different rates and are aligned to the slowest stream, camera and LiDAR frame drops force offline work, and clock drift and non-rigid device mounting break alignment in long recordings. Kinect IR over-exposes on chessboards, chessboard calibration alone is not accurate enough, broadcast cameras lack pre-game scans, and marker-based object tracking keeps camera alignment bias. In-the-wild rigs carry a known accuracy gap to wired static systems from sync and calibration errors. Workarounds are jump, clap or flashlight events, manual start-frame labelling, software TCP sync, PTP hardware sync, dense-matching refinement and 3D poses as extra calibration constraints.

evidence_items.item: Residual jitter comes partly from small inter-camera delays of Azure Kinects; fitting error is bounded from below by Kinect synchronization imperfections.
There is no hardware synchronization between HoloLens2 and Kinect (flashlight alignment); small temporal misalignment is visible on fast hand motions; factory depth calibration is inaccurate.
Hardware-level sync across RGB-D sensors is often missing, and small misalignments cause artifacts.
Camera and LiDAR are not synchronized online, so frame drops cause tedious offline work; online camera-LiDAR sync is future work.
Multi-device alignment lacks universal sync, clock drift appears in long recordings, and glasses slipping breaks the assumed constant head-to-device transform.
The iPhone cannot be hardware-synchronized (software sync leaves up to one Kinect frame of error), and Kinect IR over-exposes on regular chessboards.
Insole and camera cannot be synchronized automatically; synchronization is manual.
In-the-wild capture has an accuracy gap to static indoor wired systems because of sync and calibration errors.
Chessboard calibration alone is not accurate enough and needs dense-matching refinement; synchronization error is under one frame.
Synchronization is by a controlled jump, with manual IMU-camera offset calibration.
Synchronization is by a jump at sequence start.
Calibration needs an A-pose facing a planar marker and a jump-in-place for synchronization.
Hybrid optical-inertial mocap still struggles with cross-modal alignment and synchronization.
Modalities could not be hardware-synchronized, and curves were aligned manually.
Camera and body sensors are synchronized by a clap, and camera trajectory quality is bounded by ARKit.
Multi-view configuration and calibration are unwieldy and time-intensive, with manual camera-LiDAR extrinsic calibration.
Real ground truth from an Xsens suit is synchronized to the cameras by a clap.
Sensors run at different rates because of hardware limits, so all modalities are aligned to the 15 Hz RGB-D stream.
IMU calibration error lowers accuracy when IMUs are combined with Kinects.
RGB-mocap synchronization needs manual start-frame labelling and annotated correspondences for calibration; marker-based object tracking retains bias from camera alignment error.
Broadcast camera calibration normally needs a pre-game scan that was unavailable, so 3D poses were used as extra constraints; calibrating fast-moving broadcast cameras is open.
Synchronization and calibration are done offline from an A-pose start.
Device placement on the body is known only up to calibration error and may drift, and retargeting is brittle under XSens calibration errors.

benchmark_evidence: InterCap / vertex-to-point-cloud distance 20.29 mm body, 18.50 mm object, bounded by Kinect sync imperfections [1563]
EgoHumans / annotation accuracy below static wired systems; improves with more secondary cameras [1248]
HuMMan / software sync error up to one Kinect frame for iPhone [1438]
FreeMan / synchronization error under one frame (33 ms at 30 FPS) [29]
clusters.settings: Multi-Kinect and RealSense rigs (InterCap, HuMMan, HUM4D, OpenRoboCare), HMD plus external Kinects (EgoBody), Aria glasses plus inertial suits (Nymeria, NymeriaPlus), camera plus LiDAR (SLOPER4D, Human-M3, HSC4D, HiSC4D), pressure insoles plus RGB-D (MMVP), IMU suit plus Kinects (COUCH), mocap plus RGB domes (NeuralDome, HOI-M3), body-worn cameras (EgoSim), smartphone arrays (FreeMan), broadcast cameras (WorldPose), clinical multi-modality validation, phone plus EM sensors (EMDB).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Synchronization by jump, clap or flashlight, manual start-frame labelling and curve alignment, software TCP sync, PTP hardware sync (ClimbingCap), light-absorbent chessboards for IR, dense-matching refinement of chessboard calibration, offline per-frame calibration fine-tuning, and 3D poses as extra calibration constraints. Sub-frame offsets remain and limit hand accuracy.

clusters.name: Fast motion, blur and rare dynamic poses
clusters.statement: Under fast, high-acceleration or unusual motion (sports, martial arts, collisions, quick hand movements) and in low light, RGB and RGB-D capture suffers motion blur, low sensor frame rates and RGB-depth misalignment, and estimators trained on daily-activity lab data oversmooth, misplace extremities and get velocities wrong.
clusters.description: Athletic and hardcase benchmarks show models trained on Human3.6M failing on fast or unusual motion, with ankle errors of hundreds of millimetres and near-zero lower-limb velocity correlation. Hand recovery under real blur is temporally ambiguous, and datasets of real blur with 3D ground truth are rare because annotation on degraded frames is unreliable. Low light plus blur causes missed detections and false persons. Capture datasets avoid very fast interactions because of blur and RGB-depth misalignment, 10 fps LiDAR or robot cameras cannot follow fast limbs, and video HOI methods struggle with fast motion. Optimization and learned global methods oversmooth or under-predict jerk, and rare poses (falling, collisions) are poorly covered by training data. Fixes tried are event cameras, domain fine-tuning, hardcase pseudo-labels and beam-splitter rigs for sharp reference frames.

evidence_items.item: Models trained on Human3.6M fail on athletic motion (MPJPE 234-257 mm, ankle up to 560 mm); lower-limb velocity correlation is only r=0.11.
3D hand methods disregard motion blur; a blurry image is temporally ambiguous, deblurring first does not work, and event-only input fails on static hands.
Very fast interactions were avoided because of motion blur and RGB-depth misalignment limits of the sensor.
10 fps LiDAR yields unsmooth results for extremely fast motions.
RGB-only methods misinterpret low-light plus heavy-blur scenes, giving missed and false-positive persons; annotating poses directly on degraded frames is unreliable.
SLAHMR produces overly smooth motion, missing fast movements; fast motion and low player resolution degrade 2D detectors.
Monocular mesh recovery is vulnerable to unusual poses such as dance and martial arts because of a data domain gap.
Predictions are under-active, with lower jerk than ground truth; the largest errors occur on fast-moving limbs.
Existing methods cannot handle rapid complex motion that needs precise location; RGB methods do not model limbs well in rapid taekwondo motion.
Pressure datasets cover only slow, small-range motion, and monocular methods drift in depth in fast large-range motion.
Hands and feet blur at high speed.
Faster-moving joints are harder to forecast (r = 0.79 between joint speed and error), and fast contacts such as kicks and punches are least predictable.
Heavy motion blur degrades methods, and fast hand motions show temporal misalignment.
Models trained on daily-activity data are not robust to pedestrian pre-collision poses.
Capturing rare, safety-critical scenarios such as collisions is costly, and LiDAR plus RGB pose fails on long-tail poses.
Performance is poor on rare poses such as falling because of data imbalance.
Pose estimation produces missing and invalid frames under occlusion and rapid motion.
Video methods struggle with long-term occlusion and fast motion.

benchmark_evidence: AthletePose3D / TCPFormer 234.20 mm trained on H3.6M, 98.26 mm after adding AthletePose3D; velocity r=0.11 lower limb [1255]
EBH / event-only MPJPE 28.6-30.8 mm vs 12.0-16.4 mm with image plus events [308]
EHPT-XC / RGB-only mAP 22.7-25.1 vs RGB+event 37.3 [432]
RELI11D / RGB methods MPJPE 171.97-249.34 mm on rapid motion [75]
PVCP / VIBE official weights MPVE 849.09 mm on pre-collision poses [433]
HardMo / ProHMR MPJPE 113.8 mm; HardMo-Foot ProHMR foot MPJPE 213.6 mm [1193]
HARPER collision prediction / depth baseline 0.49 accuracy on unintended collisions; kick sensitivity 0.52 [929]
clusters.settings: Sports and martial arts (AthletePose3D, RELI11D, HardMo, WorldPose), blurred hands with event cameras (EBH), low-light multi-person tracking (EHPT-XC), dashcam pre-collision pedestrians (PVCP), mixed-reality collisions (PMR), Kinect HOI capture (InterCap), 10 fps LiDAR (LIP), smartphone arrays (FreeMan), HoloLens egocentric video (EgoBody), body-worn cameras (EgoSim), robot-view forecasting (HARPER), piano hand video.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Event cameras fused with RGB (EBH, EHPT-XC), beam-splitter rigs for sharp reference frames, synthetic blur (domain gap), fine-tuning on domain-specific data, hardcase mining with pseudo-label refinement, LiDAR or multi-modal fusion, and filtering out blurred frames during curation. Velocity accuracy and fast-hand capture remain unsolved.

clusters.name: Synthetic humans lack interaction; sim-to-real gap remains
clusters.statement: Synthetic human data cannot yet render people handling objects or touching other people (hand motion is pasted from separate datasets, objects are absent and non-foot contact is inaccurate), and models trained on synthetic or simulation-derived data keep a measurable synthetic-to-real gap, especially for egocentric and occluded views.
clusters.description: The large synthetic datasets (BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0, SynBody, GTA-Human, EgoSim, UnrealEgo, VOccl3D) animate bodies independently from AMASS, paste unrelated GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion on, remove actions that depend on objects such as sitting, and place people to avoid collision instead of interacting. Every paper that trains on synthetic data reports a remaining real-domain gap: real-image backbone pretraining is still needed, CycleGAN-style augmentation does not close the gap, and simulated sensor inputs lack real noise. Simulation-derived dynamics and muscle labels have the same sim-to-real issue, and surveys list the lack of realism in synthetic data as an open problem.

evidence_items.item: Hands interacting with objects are largely missing; motions are random and lack interactions; there is very little mocap with full body plus hands interacting with objects; backbones trained from scratch on BEDLAM are worse than COCO-pretrained ones.
Only human-ground interaction is synthesized, with no objects; realistic synthetic human-object and human-human interaction remains open; a visual domain gap to real video remains.
Simulated avatars are animated independently, so interactions with humans or objects are not modelled; direct sim-to-real gives 0.77 m global MPJPE.
Real-world device-relative MPJPE is 104.14 mm from scratch (72.89 mm with synthetic pretraining) vs 30.53 mm on synthetic UnrealEgo2.
Domain gaps between synthetic GTA-Human and real data persist; CycleGAN-style learned augmentation is not effective for closing them.
A noticeable synthetic-to-real gap remains; gains on real datasets with minimal occlusion are marginal.
Contact labels for human-scene interaction are not included; rendering without cloth geometry or hair degrades performance.
As a simulation dataset a synthetic-to-real gap is unavoidable, and object-related motions assume negligible object mass.
Sensor inputs simulated from mocap lack real noise characteristics; models trained with real device poses perform worse than with synthetic inputs.
Synthetic datasets fail to capture dynamic 3D contacts and object tracking; TRUMANS RGB-D and egocentric views are synthetic renderings.
Prior egocentric work relies on synthetic data and suffers a synthetic-to-real gap.
Synthetic blur (BlurHand) has a domain gap to real motion blur.
There is a significant domain gap between synthetic and real egocentric body data, and synthetic motion sets focus on rare athletic motions.
Simulated muscle activation data carry an unavoidable sim-to-real gap.
Simulated dynamics data can be unnaturally jittery, and the humanoid's physical properties differ from real humans.
Mixed-reality simulated data and VR-glasses egocentric video introduce a domain gap to real data.
The method is trained and quantitatively evaluated only on synthetic renders and is sensitive to domain gaps in real footage.
The dataset is fully synthetic with no real-image evaluation reported.
Synthetic data lack realism, while mocap data are confined to constrained settings.
Synthetic training data suffers a sim-to-real gap.

benchmark_evidence: UnrealEgo-RW / MPJPE 104.14 mm (72.89 with pretraining) vs 30.53 mm synthetic [1]
MultiEgoView real / global MPJPE 0.77 m direct sim-to-real; best fine-tuned 0.33 m [1258]
EMDB / W-MPJPE100: GVHMR trained on BEDLAM2.0 284.4 mm; best PromptHMR 193.7 mm [1240]
AGORA / PARE still 169.93 mm MPJPE and HMR 199.51 mm with SynBody [1259]
Mobjaverse / MPJPE 179.61 seen and 192.04 unseen vs 52.05 on Truebones Zoo [573]
Nymeria 3-point / MPJPE 7.97 cm with real inputs vs 4.20 cm on AMASS [333]
clusters.settings: Unreal Engine and GTA-V renders of single or non-interacting people (BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0, SynBody, GTA-Human, VOccl3D), synthetic egocentric fisheye and body-worn cameras (UnrealEgo, EgoSim), synthetic HSI renders (TRUMANS), synthetic blur (BlurHand), mixed-reality pedestrian capture (PMR), rendered rigged characters (Mobjaverse), simulated sensor inputs (Nymeria), simulated dynamics and muscle labels (ImDy, MinT).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Blending with or fine-tuning on real data, synthetic pretraining before real fine-tuning, 3DGS-reconstructed backgrounds, layered clothing and more realistic rendering, mixed-reality capture, and pasting GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion onto bodies. The gap remains and interaction is still absent.

clusters.name: Atypical bodies and clinical populations
clusters.statement: Pose and mesh estimators built on a fixed complete-limb template and able-bodied data cannot yet represent residual limbs, prostheses, mobility aids or impaired gait, so they mislocalize or hallucinate limbs, fail to jointly recover an attached non-anatomical rigid object, and collapse across clinical sites.
clusters.description: Inclusive-pose datasets show pretrained and fine-tuned estimators placing keypoints on missing limbs, reading prostheses as natural ankles, and propagating hallucinated limbs through time with high confidence. Model-based body estimators cannot represent an attached rigid prosthesis, and model-free reconstruction lacks kinematic priors. Segmenters lose thin prosthetic legs. Motion models pretrained on general data do worse on cane and arm joints for blind pedestrians, and clinical gait models drop sharply across sites, with severe cases scarce. Synthetic datasets list amputees, children and assistive devices as missing, and template-free capture degrades on uncommon topologies. Fixes tried are new keypoint schemas and losses and small population-specific fine-tuning sets; these datasets are too small to train on, so methods are evaluated zero-shot or need manual labels.

evidence_items.item: COCO-trained ViTPose predicts prostheses as natural ankles and puts a missing wrist on the torso; video models hallucinate a complete limb and propagate it across frames.

Pretrained RTMPose and ViTPose place incorrect keypoints on residual limbs; fine-tuned ViTPose predicts both intact and residual keypoints on the same limb while scoring COCO AP 82.6; prosthetics are often hidden by clothing.

Model-based estimators (SAM3D Body) hallucinate amputated-side meshes that do not match the prosthesis; model-free reconstruction lacks kinematic priors and fails under occlusion; jointly recovering body joints and an attached rigid object is open.
Pretrained pose models miss prosthetic knee and foot keypoints; Grounded SAM2 loses track of the prosthetic leg.
Pretraining on Motion-X then fine-tuning underperforms training from scratch on arm and mobility-aid joints for blind pedestrians.
Cross-dataset transfer reduces F1 by 0.2 to 0.4; severe cases are scarce; zero-shot models pretrained on generic motion fail on severe classes.
No children, amputees or atypical morphologies, impaired movement or assistive devices are in the synthetic data.
Body-shape diversity for children, scoliosis and amputees is listed as open.
Template-free motion capture degrades on highly uncommon topologies (MPJPE 192.04 on unseen vs 179.61 on seen topologies).

benchmark_evidence: InclusiveVidPose / residual ArmUp and ArmLow AP almost zero for DCPose and DSTA; LiCC about 60% [521]
LDPose / YOLO-Pose AP 42.6 without fine-tuning; best COCO AP 82.6 with impossible predictions [273]
RSP3D / prosthesis Chamfer 288.44 with F@50 19.92; model-free MPJPE 159.64-174.84 mm [389]
ProGait / gait classification top-1 0.384; Grounded SAM2 mIoU 0.358 [274]
Care-PD / cross-dataset macro-F1 drop 0.2-0.4 [1425]
BlindWays / R Top1 0.060 vs 0.106 for real data [436]
Mobjaverse / MPJPE 192.04 on unseen topologies [573]
clusters.settings: Monocular images and video of people with limb deficiency and prostheses (LDPose, InclusiveVidPose, ProGait, RSP3D), blind pedestrians with canes captured by IMU suits (BlindWays), Parkinson's gait from clinical video (Care-PD), synthetic human datasets (BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0), arbitrary-skeleton characters (TopoCap).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Extended keypoint schemas with residual endpoints, limb-deficiency-aware losses (which trade COCO accuracy), fine-tuning on population data, hybrid model-based and model-free baselines with manual amputation labels, topology-conditioned priors, and proposed synthetic data. The datasets are too small to train on, so these are evaluated zero-shot, and the hybrid baselines need manual labels.

clusters.name: Pseudo ground truth and blind evaluation metrics
clusters.statement: In-the-wild and interaction test sets mostly carry pseudo ground truth from fitting or off-the-shelf estimators and lack temporal tracking ground truth, and standard metrics (PA-MPJPE, COCO AP, ADE/FDE) do not register jitter, limb rotation errors, velocity errors, anatomically impossible poses, physical implausibility, task success or privacy, so method rankings can hide the failures that matter.
clusters.description: Benchmark and dataset papers note that pseudo-annotated test sets contain visible SMPL errors, that HOI capture datasets evaluate tracking only qualitatively for lack of tracking ground truth or have no ground-truth objects, that Human3.6M performance does not predict generalization while 3DPW and other standard sets are saturated, and that a widely used PA-MPJPE function had a bug. Population, plausibility and task papers each say current metrics miss their failure: COCO AP rewards impossible keypoints on residual limbs, MPJPE-PA hides lower-arm rotation and jitter, velocity validity against mocap is poor despite good joint angles, the foot-sliding metric is a heuristic, and no metric exists for intention fulfilment, assistive tasks, sign-language production, physical plausibility or privacy. Validation of markerless capture against biomechanics gold standards is rare.

evidence_items.item: Pseudo-annotated test sets contain visible SMPL errors; H36M performance does not correlate with other test sets; 3DPW is the only large real outdoor set with accurate SMPL ground truth.
MPJPE-PA is forgiving: methods fail on lower-arm rotations that MPJPE does not reveal, all exceed 23 deg angular error, and good MPJPE-PA does not give visually pleasing results.
Fine-tuned ViTPose scores COCO AP 82.6 while predicting intact and residual keypoints on the same limb; COCO metrics do not penalize keypoints on missing limbs.
An evaluation bug was found in a widely used PA-MPJPE function; corrected TRACE 3DPW results are worse than reported.
MPJPE cannot evaluate smoothness or realism, so jitter in video 3D HPE is not measured by current benchmarks.
Tracking components could be evaluated only qualitatively because no tracking ground truth exists.
There is no tracking-specific ground truth, so tracking evaluation is qualitative.
The dataset provides pseudo ground truth only, with no independent mocap ground truth for evaluation.
No metric checks whether the stated intention is fulfilled; ADE/FDE are insufficient.
No HPE benchmark reports a privacy score; privacy-accuracy trade-offs are rarely measured.
Few studies validate markerless methods against biomechanics gold standards; MediaPipe knee angles are offset about 15 deg from IMU and MoCap.
Monocular kinematic estimates have not been sufficiently validated; lower-limb velocity correlation is r=0.11 despite good joint-angle correlation.
Standard datasets (Human3.6M, CMU Panoptic, HUMAN4D) are approaching saturation.
No ground-truth objects exist, so object reconstruction quality cannot be evaluated with standard metrics.
Test labels are semi-automatic pseudo ground truth from existing estimators corrected with an annotation tool.
Test labels are optimized pseudo labels, not marker or multi-view mocap.
The foot-sliding metric is a simple heuristic that differs from real foot sliding.
Metrics do not capture physical plausibility, and the default hand model biases landmark metrics.
There is no standard metric or generic 3D back-translation method for 3D sign language production.
Metrics for assistive tasks (contact sequences, force ranges, kinematic limits) are still needed.
HOI evaluation feature extractors are trained on very limited data, degrading evaluation.
Evaluation is inconsistent across hip keypoint normalization and skeleton formats, and standard benchmarks do not reflect real-world occlusion.
Benchmark comparisons are inconsistent across configurations.
Absolute hand position is not evaluated (root-aligned metrics), and ground truth comes from a network annotator trained on the same data.
Most estimators assign high confidence to anatomically impossible keypoints (LiCC about 60%).
The field lacks a standard, mocap-referenced comparison of off-the-shelf monocular pose frameworks on joint-angle accuracy (abstract-only record).

benchmark_evidence: 3DPW / corrected TRACE PA-MPJPE 50.8 mm vs 42.7 mm for D&D after a metric bug fix [1261]
3DPW / saturation in the 50 mm range, best 47.3 mm [1262]
LDPose / best COCO AP 82.6 coexists with anatomically impossible predictions [273]
InclusiveVidPose / LiCC about 60% for many methods [521]
EMDB / MPJPE-PA above 65 mm and angular error above 23 deg for all methods [1238]
Clinical knee capture / MediaPipe offset about 15 deg vs IMU and MoCap [1231]
AthletePose3D / velocity correlation r=0.11 despite good joint-angle correlation [1255]
HUM4D / PA-MPJPE 151-180 mm vs 39-82 mm on near-saturated 3DPW [1237]
clusters.settings: 3DPW, Human3.6M, EMDB, COCO-style 2D benchmarks, HOI capture sets with fitted pseudo ground truth or no tracking ground truth (BEHAVE, InterCap, HODome, HOI-M3, Open3DHOI), monocular pseudo-labelled sets (PVCP, HardMo, EBH), limb-deficient and clinical pose benchmarks, sports kinematics validation, interaction generation and prediction benchmarks (MOB, I2M, HHI-Assist, InterAct), sEMG and sign-language benchmarks, privacy-sensitive sensing.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Population-specific metrics (LiCC, LD metrics), angular, jitter, standard-deviation and per-meter-drift metrics (EMDB, WorldPose), standardized training setups for fair comparison, mocap-referenced validation studies, and proposed intention-fulfilment, assistive-task and privacy scores. The authors call the privacy levels illustrative, and the other proposals are not yet standard.

clusters.name: Interaction synthesis and forecasting do not generalize
clusters.statement: Models that generate, predict or forecast human-object, human-scene and human-human interaction cannot go beyond the small, mostly single-person, single-object mocap datasets they are trained on: unseen objects, actions, tasks or populations give misaligned contact and large errors, and forecasting from estimated partial poses is several times worse than from ground truth.
clusters.description: Generation and prediction papers trace failures to costly, controlled-setting interaction data. Generators produce intersections for actions outside the training set, dual-branch human and object generation misaligns, closed-set models fail on complex object trajectories, and contact degrades on unseen objects and chair shapes. Interaction and coupled two-person prediction leave large errors and degrade on unseen tasks, semantic conditioning (intention text, RGB) does not improve plausible-future coverage, and models trained on general motion data generate unrealistic motion for blind pedestrians. Forecasting from robot-estimated partial poses is several times worse than from ground truth. Physics-simulator approaches are action-specific, and training on small datasets overfits.

evidence_items.item: The motion generator cannot produce human-object interactions outside the training distribution; climbing off a table yields unrealistic motion and object intersections.
Interaction data are costly and controlled-setting datasets do not cover real-world diversity; physics-simulator methods are action-specific and generalize poorly.
Naive dual-branch generation misaligns human and object motions, and conditioning human motion on generated object motion causes a large performance drop.
Forecasting from robot-estimated partial poses yields about 309-333 mm MPJPE versus 43-70 mm from full ground truth, and existing forecasting methods cannot process incomplete pose sequences.
Interaction prediction leaves significant errors in human motion, object pose and contact (human MPJPE 172.5 mm, object translation 115.6 mm).
Training on limited data (BEHAVE alone) overfits when model size grows.
Coupled two-person motion prediction degrades under distribution shift to an unseen assistance task.
Models cannot ground semantic goals into kinematics; intention text, RGB or MotionCLIP increase diversity but not plausible-future coverage.
The model is closed-set and fails to generate the next state when the object trajectory is complex or highly variable.
Unseen objects degrade contact F1 from 0.72 to 0.61, and the method needs the full object trajectory and geometry as input.
Generalizing contact-controlled synthesis to more chair shapes needs better scene encoding without overfitting.
Limited paired human-scene data restricts diversity; goal-reaching success is 77.91% vs 100% for ground truth, with failures turning in narrow spaces.
Text-to-motion models trained on Motion-X generate diverse but unrealistic blind motion, and rare motion scenarios remain challenging.
Multiple-human and multiple-interaction generation are open, and joint generation has 9.265% penetration.
Few datasets limit interactive entities to a few categories and lack intent annotations; multi-person and multi-object interactions are open.

benchmark_evidence: InterVLA / interaction prediction human MPJPE 172.5 mm, object translation 115.6 mm [251]
HHI-Assist unseen task / caregiver MPJPE 89.3 mm average, 154.8 mm at 1000 ms [813]
HARPER / forecasting 309-333 mm from estimated poses vs 43-70 mm from GT [929]
MOB / goal-reaching success 77.91% vs 100% for GT [328]
FullBodyManip (OMOMO) unseen objects / contact F1 0.61 [1154]
I2M / MMADE@20 1.140 (intention text) vs 0.709 (trajectory) [462]
BlindWays / R Top1 0.060 vs 0.106 for real data; Motion-X-trained FID 11.2-15.0 vs 3.34 [436]
HOI-M3 generation / penetration 9.265% vs 1.452% for people alone [37]
clusters.settings: Mocap-derived HOI and HSI generation (TRUMANS, HIMO, OMOMO, InterAct, COUCH, F-HOI, MOB, HOI-M3), intention-aware prediction (I2M), interaction prediction from egocentric views (InterVLA), robot-view forecasting (HARPER), physical assistance prediction (HHI-Assist), text-to-motion for blind pedestrians (BlindWays), surveys of interaction generation.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Aggregating and correcting datasets (InterAct), occupancy pseudo-scenes from motion-only mocap (MOB), mutual-interaction modules (HIMO), LLM and VLM conditioning, imputation of incomplete pose sequences (HARPER), physics-based imitation, and hybrid simulator plus generative models (proposed).

clusters.name: Transferring human object handling to robots
clusters.statement: Human demonstrations of object handling cannot yet be retargeted into robot or humanoid policies that achieve precise hand contact, even in simulation, and transfer to physical human-robot contact is untested or blocked by human-robot hand and body mismatch.
clusters.description: Benchmarks that learn from human references report near-zero success on hand-precision tasks such as box lifting and grasping small packaged items. Retargeting methods without optimization fail completely, raw egocentric RGB-D observations collapse compared with elevation maps, and humanoids fall on motions they cannot perform. Caregiving and assistance datasets note that transfer to physical human-robot interaction is not tested and that robots need both delicate and high-force contact. Robot-assisted bathing finds a large sim-to-real gap from mannequin-vs-SMPL-X and MANO-vs-robot-hand mismatches, and tendon-control labels come from a simulated hand.

evidence_items.item: The best pipeline reaches only 6/5 percent success on box lifting; copy-rotation and OmniH2O retargeting fail (0 percent) on hand-precision tasks; the humanoid has no dexterous hands.
Non-fridge retail tasks remain at 13.8% mean success after post-training; precise gripper finger shaping around small packaging is the dominant failure; evaluation is in simulation only.
The sim-to-real gap is large because of mannequin-vs-SMPL-X and MANO-vs-robot-hand mismatches; distributed force control is blocked by the mismatch between human and robot hand responses.
In humanoid imitation, more accurate poses make the NAO robot fall on actions it cannot perform.
Transfer to physical human-robot interaction is not tested; using predictions for MPC or policy observations is untested.
Tendon signals come from a simulated musculoskeletal hand, so real tendon-driven hand testing is required.
Bimanual and mobile manipulation of human limbs under safety constraints is open; robots need both delicate (0.1-2 N) and high-force (20-30 N) contact.

benchmark_evidence: Mimicking-Bench box lifting / best 6/5% success; multi-view RGB-D input 4/4% vs elevation map 54/51% [1391]
RoboBenchMart / mean 29.3%, non-fridge 13.8%, Nestle 2% [1380]
Back bathing on mannequin / open-loop pressure significantly higher than human; closed-loop deviates in absolute pressure and spatial distribution [697]
clusters.settings: Simulated humanoids (Isaac Gym Unitree H1), retail VLA in simulation (RoboBenchMart), robot-assisted bathing on a mannequin, NAO humanoid imitation, caregiving and physical-assistance datasets, simulated tendon-driven hands.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Optimization-based retargeting, imitation learning from mocap or synthesized references, robot-native anchor data, closed-loop summed-pressure control, and diffusion-based tendon prediction. Hand-precision success stays near zero and no real-robot validation is reported.

notes:
I re-read all 100 records in G2_body_object.jsonl. There are 100 ids but only 99 newline characters, because the last line has no trailing newline. The result is 23 clusters, and every id is in at least one. Clusters overlap by design, and n_papers counts the distinct papers in each cluster. A scripted check confirmed four things: every paper in a cluster has at least one evidence item, every bracketed id in benchmark_evidence is in that cluster's paper_ids, the output is ASCII only, and every name is 3 to 8 words long.

One-to-one merges, using the union of papers and evidence:
- Object pose: A1 + B1
- Template and object scope: A13 + B2
- Contact: A2 + B5
- Occlusion: A14 + B7
- Close multi-person: A12 + B9
- World-frame trajectories: A10 + B10
- Near-body views: A9 + B11
- Depth and LiDAR: A11 + B12
- Non-visual sensing: A19 + B13
- Ground truth: A5 + B14
- Sync and calibration: A18 + B15
- Fast motion: A15 + B16
- Synthetic data: A6 + B17
- Atypical bodies: A16 + B18
- Evaluation: A7 + B19

Places where I kept the finer cut (each part has at least 3 papers):
- B6 (physical grounding) became A3 (implausible motion) and A4 (forces, torques, muscle). Papers in B6 but in neither A3 nor A4 went to the implausible-motion cluster: 418, 573 and 1266. I also added 56 to that cluster, because its record states foot sliding and penetration.
- A8 (hands and wrists) became B3 (finger-level grasp) and B4 (distal-joint errors).
- B20 became A20 (robot transfer, 7 papers) and the rest of B20 (interaction synthesis and forecasting, 15 papers). 813 sits in both.
- B8 (online tracking through occlusion) became A17 (offline optimisation, no real-time; I added 37) and a temporal-stability cluster covering jitter, track loss and identity switches. The second cluster uses B8's remaining 18 papers. Both lenses state this content: A had it spread across its multi-person, occlusion and plausibility clusters.

Places where the lenses cut along different axes:
- A10 covers drift from both cameras and IMUs; B10 covers cameras only, and B13 holds wearable drift. I kept A10's coarser world-frame scope, unioned with B10 (adding 146), and merged A19 with B13. The IMU-drift papers (1036, 1242, 767, 333) therefore appear in both clusters.
- A put pseudo ground truth with evaluation; B put it with ground truth. I kept two clusters, data ground truth and evaluation, and pseudo-GT papers appear in both.

Disputed papers I removed after re-reading:
- 1563 from object pose: its object statements are about the template assumption, and it stays in the template cluster.
- 1262 from distal joints: its hand and foot item is about training-label noise.
- 1231 from occlusion: it only mentions self-occlusion, cited from prior work.
- 1266 from depth: its statement is about hardware cost, not depth noise.
- 436 from world-frame and from sync: it has no trajectory-drift or multi-device sync statement. It stays in the non-visual sensing and ground-truth clusters.

1444 (REHAB24-6), which lens A left uncategorized, goes into the ground-truth cluster: 2D ground truth is projected through a simplified pinhole model with tape-measured camera positions. So uncategorized_ids is empty.

Caveats:
- Ids 434 and 1562 are the same work (Muscles in Time). Both are kept, so the forces and synthetic-data clusters count that work twice.
- 1080 is abstract-only and supports only the evaluation cluster.
- The ground-truth cluster (45 papers) is broad because nearly every dataset paper states this cost.
- Benchmark numbers are copied from the digest's bench_gaps and failures fields and were not re-checked against the full papers.

Clusters closest to RGB-D tracking of bimanual object handling: object pose, template dependence, contact, finger-level grasp, distal joints, occlusion, offline/no real-time, temporal stability, depth and LiDAR, and sync/calibration.

clusters.name: Metric 3D hand motion from monocular video
clusters.statement: Metric 3D wrist, finger and camera trajectories cannot be recovered from uncalibrated, moving monocular egocentric or internet video accurately enough to serve as fine-grained robot action labels; depth and scale ambiguity leaves errors of tens of millimetres that show up as missed contacts and penetration.
clusters.description: Video-to-robot data engines estimate MANO hands with HaMeR or HaWoR, cameras with DROID-SLAM or VGGT, and metric scale with SLAM or learned monocular depth such as MoGe-2, so hand poses are estimated rather than measured. Depth and scale ambiguity places the hand at the wrong 3D location relative to the object, which after retargeting gives missed contacts, penetration or instability, and segment-wise reconstructions drift in scale. Surveys state that video-to-data engines and model-based pseudo-labels inherit perception errors from pose and depth estimation, occlusion, motion blur and domain shift. As a result, authors use human video only through coarse latent actions, accept noisy labels for pretraining, or defer fine-grained dexterous motion until hand pose estimation improves.

evidence_items.item: Recovering metric 3D hand motion is difficult with single, uncalibrated, moving cameras; noisy labels are accepted for pretraining, and accurate metric 3D hand and camera motion is listed as open.
Monocular hand reconstruction (HaMeR) has depth and scale ambiguity that misplaces hands in 3D, causing missed contacts, penetration or instability after retargeting; depth correction is needed.
3D hand pose comes from HaWoR estimates with a median root-relative 21-keypoint error of 20.4 mm against EgoDex annotations; metric scale is recovered from MoGe-2 monocular depth.
Hand poses are estimated (HaWoR, MANO), not measured; segment-wise reconstructions suffer scale drift and coordinate mismatch that need global bundle adjustment.
Video-to-data engines inherit perception errors from grounding, pose and depth estimation and still struggle with reconstruction noise and action error.

Human videos are used only through coarse latent actions and language, not fine-grained hand motion; obtaining accurate action labels from human video often needs extra sensing such as VR devices or exoskeletons.
Model-based pose pseudo-labels inherit errors from occlusion, motion blur and domain shift.
Hand action labels come from monocular HaWoR reconstruction of generated video, and the method is limited by hand reconstruction accuracy.
3D hand and body pose are estimated, not measured, and automated pose estimates and motion annotations carry errors.
Hand pose comes from HaMeR monocular estimation refined by stereo optimisation, with no ground truth.

benchmark_evidence: HuRo pipeline diagnostics, EgoDex rerun (1381) / hand keypoint error: median root-relative 21-keypoint error 20.4 mm; camera ATE median 4.47 mm.
RoboEdit 300-case benchmark (1382) / decoded robot-hand state error: wrist 42.03 mm, fingertip 43.26 mm, rotation 23.28 degrees in camera space.
Unseen-environment grasping benchmark, 47 environments and 396 objects (1489) / predicted finger-object distance: best model still ends 8.8 cm (average) and 6.2 cm (median) from the target object.

HumanNet (1378) / robot-ready inclusion criterion: clips count as robot-ready only when retargeting error is below 15 mm and valid-frame coverage exceeds 60 percent; the rest lack reliable retargeting.
clusters.settings: Monocular egocentric and internet RGB (EPIC-Kitchens, Ego4D, EgoDex, smartphone capture, generated egocentric video) and lab HOI video (DexYCB, HOT3D, H2O, TACO); MANO hand estimators (HaMeR, HaWoR) combined with monocular SLAM (DROID-SLAM), VGGT or learned metric depth (MoGe-2); outputs used as VLA pretraining action labels or robot-video edits.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Depth regularisation and physics refinement (1382), learned metric depth with masked DROID-SLAM (1381), stereo refinement of HaMeR output (1379), global bundle adjustment with robust kernels (1377), robot-ready filters on retargeting error (1378), and accepting noisy labels for pretraining (1489) or using only coarse latent actions (709). Residual wrist and fingertip errors of roughly 20 to 43 mm remain, and fine-grained dexterous motion is still not used as supervision.

clusters.name: Unverifiable hand annotation accuracy in the wild
clusters.statement: The accuracy of 3D hand, wrist, camera and depth annotations produced at scale from in-the-wild egocentric capture cannot be measured, because ground truth exists only in mocap or calibration rooms, and unverified labels cancel much of the benefit of scale.
clusters.description: Large egocentric datasets check their 3D hand labels by reprojection consistency, qualitative overlay on stereo point clouds, cross-dataset consistency or VLA validation loss, and their authors state that none of these is a controlled accuracy benchmark. Wrist accuracy is validated only on a mocap-room subset, and depth error is measured only in a calibration room, where it grows with distance. One dataset finds that its unverified variant gives little gain over no pretraining, so noisy labels offset scale. Surveys list data quality assessment as open and note that generation scales faster than verification, and dataset authors call for transparent annotation-confidence reporting and for characterising how label fidelity affects policy learning.

evidence_items.item: In-the-wild data lacks motion-capture ground truth and quality is checked by reprojection consistency only; the unverified variant WIYH* gives little overall gain over no pretraining, so noisy labels offset scale.
The annotation-consistency comparison is not a controlled accuracy benchmark; no controlled benchmark of annotation accuracy across datasets exists.
3D hand keypoint accuracy is validated only by qualitative alignment with stereo point clouds, not quantitative ground truth.

Scale introduces label, boundary, metadata and quality noise and automated annotations carry errors; validation is only by VLA validation loss, and transparent reporting of annotation confidence is future work.
The effect of robotization fidelity on downstream policy learning is not characterized.
Model-based pose pseudo-labels inherit errors from occlusion, motion blur and domain shift; data quality assessment is listed as open.
Generation scales faster than grounding and verification.

benchmark_evidence: EgoLive calibration room (1379) / stereo depth mean error: 3.06 mm at 500 mm rising to 13-18 mm beyond 1700 mm; under 80 percent of points within the tightest threshold beyond 900 mm; hand accuracy has no quantitative ground truth.
WIYH RoboCasa pretraining (1376) / task success: the unverified WIYH* variant gives little overall gain over no pretraining (no number in digest).
HumanNet LingBot-VLA post-training (1378) / validation loss: the only validation metric reported; task success is not measured.
clusters.settings: In-the-wild egocentric capture with wearable glove suites (WIYH), head-mounted stereo (EgoLive), commodity smartphones (Open-AoE) and internet-scale video (HumanNet, HuRo); MANO hand estimates from HaMeR or HaWoR used as VLA pretraining labels.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Reprojection-consistency checks plus mocap-room wrist validation on a subset (under 5 mm) and offline SfM refinement (1376), stereo optimisation with qualitative overlay (1379), cross-dataset annotation-consistency comparison (1377), and robot-ready thresholds with validation-loss studies (1378). None measures accuracy against ground truth on the released in-the-wild data.

clusters.name: Hand-object occlusion breaks finger and object recovery
clusters.statement: When the hand hides the held object or the object hides the fingers, especially through large rotations, vision-only pipelines (even with RGB-D) cannot recover the object's 6D trajectory or accurate finger poses, so they fall back on rigid-grasp priors and occlusion-free keyframes or discard occluded segments.
clusters.description: Papers that extract object trajectories or finger actions from human demonstrations report that persistent hand occlusion makes visual object tracking infeasible during manipulation, that point trackers drift when large rotations hide tracked points, and that hand-object occlusion degrades reconstructed finger poses into noisy action labels. Surveys state that vision-only human video remains vulnerable to occlusion and ambiguous interaction states even with RGB-D or metric depth, that headset hand tracking fails under occlusion and fast motion, and that object pose labels become ambiguous under occlusion and symmetry. Dataset pipelines respond by requiring both hands to stay visible, instructing demonstrators accordingly or screening out occluded clips, and evaluators exclude clips whose occlusion prevents judging contact. No paper in the group recovers the object or the fingers through the occluded interval directly.

evidence_items.item: Object visual tracking is infeasible during manipulation due to persistent hand occlusion, so object pose is induced from the hand under a rigid-grasp prior; CoTracker point tracking drifts when large rotations occlude tracked points; registration assumes the first and last frames are free of hand occlusion.
Hand-object occlusion degrades reconstructed finger poses and yields noisy action supervision; accurate finger reconstruction under hand-object occlusion is open.
Even with RGB-D or metric depth, vision-only human video remains vulnerable to occlusion and ambiguous interaction states.

Headset inside-out tracking can fail under fast motion, occlusion or limited field of view; object pose labels can be ambiguous under occlusion and object symmetry; instrumented capture trades accuracy under occlusion against calibration effort and participant burden.
MLLM judgments are uncertain under occlusion or subtle contact, and clips were excluded when occlusion or ambiguous object states prevented assessment.
Both hands must remain clearly visible, and recordings with hand truncation or excessive occlusion are screened out.
Clips with heavy occlusion are discarded.
Demonstrators were told to keep hands visible.

benchmark_evidence: CosmoH2G real-robot test, 186 cases with 40 unseen objects (1390) / success rate and orientation placement error: 70.43 percent success versus 83.87 percent in simulation; orientation error 19.34 degrees on the robot versus 10.27 in simulation, with objects slipping during large rotations.
clusters.settings: Single-hand monocular RGB-D demonstrations with large object rotations and flips (CosmoH2G); generated egocentric video with HaWoR hand reconstruction (Wh0); headset, smartphone and Aria-glasses egocentric capture (EgoDex, HoloAssist, Open-AoE, EgoVerse, HumanNet); MLLM-based evaluation of generated robot video (H2R-Bench).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Object pose induced from the hand under a rigid-grasp prior, with registration on occlusion-free first and last frames (1390); requiring visible hands at capture time or screening out occluded clips (696, 1377, 1378); excluding occluded clips from evaluation (1393); instrumented capture such as gloves and mocap at the cost of calibration and participant burden (1400). Real-robot execution still slips under large rotations.

clusters.name: Aggressive filtering discards most in-the-wild video
clusters.statement: Human-video-to-robot pipelines keep only a small clean fraction of their source footage, discarding clips with occlusion, hand truncation, motion blur, camera shake, static framing or failed reconstruction and retargeting, so long-tail real interactions are filtered out rather than recovered.
clusters.description: Dataset papers that convert egocentric or web video into robot supervision report heavy screening: recordings with hand truncation, excessive occlusion, severe blur, static framing, low hand valid-frame ratio or high IK failure are discarded, and only 6.9 to 17.3 percent of large corpora survive as manipulation segments. A human-to-robot editing benchmark rejects about a third of its lab-video candidates, mostly because retargeting fails. Capture protocols instruct demonstrators to keep hands visible and keep only manipulation-dense segments. A survey names this dependence on curated or aggressively filtered data as a limitation and proposes uncertainty-aware supervision and robust pseudo-labelling for low-quality video.

evidence_items.item: Low manipulation-segment yield from in-the-wild video: 17.3% of EPIC-Kitchens and 6.9% of Ego4D frames retained.
Current pipelines depend on curated or aggressively filtered data, discarding low-quality, occluded or blurred videos and long-tail interactions; use of low-quality video is open.
Recordings with residual third-person views, hand truncation or excessive occlusion are screened out, and parts with low hand-reconstruction valid-frame ratio or high IK failure rate are discarded.
Clips with severe motion blur, heavy occlusion or static framing are discarded; only clips with retargeting error below 15 mm and valid-frame coverage above 60% count as robot-ready.
Demonstrators were told to keep hands visible, and manual quality control kept only manipulation-dense segments.
About 33 percent of ARCTIC candidates are rejected during pseudo-ground-truth curation, with hand retargeting the dominant cause.

benchmark_evidence: EPIC-Kitchens and Ego4D robotization (1381) / retained frames: 17.3 percent and 6.9 percent.
HumanNet robot-ready subset (1378) / inclusion criteria: retargeting error below 15 mm and valid-frame coverage above 60 percent.
HandEdit ARCTIC curation (1394) / non-kept rate: about 33 percent of candidates rejected.
clusters.settings: Monocular egocentric and internet RGB video (EPIC-Kitchens, Ego4D, smartphone capture, HumanNet, Aria glasses) and lab HOI video (ARCTIC) processed with MANO hand estimators, SLAM, IK retargeting and image editing into VLA pretraining data.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Threshold-based filtering, manual quality control and capture instructions to keep hands visible (696, 1377, 1378); human screening of converted samples (1394). Proposed but not demonstrated: uncertainty-aware supervision and robust pseudo-labelling for blurred, occluded and failed executions (1399).

clusters.name: Object pose and state labels missing or template-bound
clusters.statement: Egocentric and human-video manipulation datasets release no object 6-DoF pose or object-state labels, and pipelines that need object motion depend on scanned, multi-view or generated rigid templates tracked by model-based trackers, so object-centric supervision is unavailable at scale.
clusters.description: Several egocentric datasets state that object poses are not annotated (masks only, or nothing), and leave object pose annotation and object-centric affordance and manipulation models to future work. Pipelines that do use object motion require a known mesh from a 3D scanner, multi-view capture or a generative model, tracked with FoundationPose or registered to CAD models, while kinematic robotization pipelines use no object pose at all. Surveys and the position paper state that video-to-data engines and object-centric world models assume reliable object mesh, 6D pose and tracking, that object pose labels are ambiguous under occlusion and symmetry, and that inferring object-state changes from partially labelled episodes is unsolved. A benchmark paper lists translating human video into robot demonstrations via explicit 3D hand-object pose estimation as future work.

evidence_items.item: Object poses are not annotated; object-centric affordance and manipulation models are left to future work, and annotating object poses is listed as future work.
No object pose annotation; objects get masks only.
No object pose annotation is released; object 6-DoF must come from downstream tools.
Large human activity datasets (Ego4D, HOI4D, EgoExo4D, Epic-Kitchens) lack manipulation-relevant annotations such as precise hand poses or object interactions.
Videos only; no 3D pose or object annotations are used in the benchmarks.
The rigid object mesh is reconstructed by TRELLIS and 6D-tracked by FoundationPose (model-based tracking of a reconstructed template).
Known object mesh assumed: real objects are 3D-scanned and posed with FoundationPose.
Object meshes are reconstructed from multi-view captures and tracked with FoundationPose++; reliable extraction of object-centric trajectories in cluttered environments is open.
Retargeting is kinematic only, with no object pose or physics.
Translating human video, especially bimanual and deformable manipulation, into robot demonstrations via explicit 3D hand-object pose estimation is not yet possible and is listed as future work.
Object pose annotation often relies on CAD-model registration and can be ambiguous under occlusion and object symmetry.
Video-to-data engines assume reliable hand pose, object mesh and 6D pose and depth reconstruction from video.
Inferring events, contacts and object states from partially supervised episodes is open; object-centric world models assume reliable perception and tracking of objects.

benchmark_evidence: CosmoH2G real robot (1390) / orientation placement error: 19.34 degrees on the robot versus 10.27 in simulation, with object pose induced from the hand rather than tracked.
HoloAssist, Open-AoE and EgoLive (1397, 1377, 1379) / object pose annotation: none released, so no object-pose accuracy number exists for these datasets.
clusters.settings: Egocentric headset, head-mounted stereo, smartphone and gaze-glasses datasets (HoloAssist, EgoLive, Open-AoE, EgoExoLearn, EgoVerse); human-to-robot pipelines on rigid objects with scanned, multi-view or generated meshes (UniFucGrasp, RoboEdit, CosmoH2G); kinematic robotization (HuRo); simulated twins with scanned objects (RoboTube).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Template meshes from 3D scanning, multi-view capture or TRELLIS with FoundationPose or FoundationPose++ tracking (891, 1382, 1390); CAD-model registration (1400); object pose induced from the hand under a rigid-grasp prior (1390); masks in place of pose (1379); scanned digital twins (1389). These restrict pipelines to rigid objects with templates and do not annotate pose or state at dataset scale; physical data engines with object-state estimation are proposed (1402).

clusters.name: Kinematic retargeting yields non-executable robot motion
clusters.statement: Retargeting reconstructed human hand motion to robot hands or grippers by kinematic or pose matching yields trajectories that look plausible but are not physically executable, with self-collision, joint-limit violations, floating or penetrating fingers and lost functional contact, and mappings are tied to one robot hand.
clusters.description: Papers that convert human demonstrations into robot actions report retargeting as a dominant failure. Kinematic IK without self-collision or contact terms leaves almost half of audited trajectories with non-grasp self-contact and many with joint-limit violations, pose matching alone produces floating or penetrating fingers, and retargeting causes most rejected pseudo-ground-truth samples in an editing benchmark. Rule-based retargeting cannot grasp under natural hand grasps, learned mappings are calibrated per robot hand, simple nearest-joint mappings avoid pose transfer altogether, and functional actions such as pressing a button often fail. Surveys call this mis-grounding, and the position paper argues that pose matching should give way to task-preserving retargeting that keeps contact and object-state transitions.

evidence_items.item: Kinematic retargeting models neither self-collision nor physical contact; only 55.2% of audited trajectories were free of non-grasp self-contact and 62.5% free of joint-limit violation, so outputs are not executable demonstrations.
Kinematic matching alone produces floating or penetrating fingers; without depth regularisation and physics refinement the retargeted robot hand is displaced.
Hand retargeting causes 63.46 percent of sampled pseudo-ground-truth rejections on ARCTIC, the dominant failure in the conversion pipeline.

Action-level transfer fails through mis-grounding: extracted trajectories or contact cues look plausible in video but violate robot kinematics, control frequency, collision constraints or contact dynamics.
Retargeted human hand motions can look plausible yet fail on real robot hands.
Pose-matching retargeting is insufficient; the effect on the object must be preserved, so task-preserving retargeting that keeps contact and object-state transitions is proposed.
Rule-based retargeting cannot even grasp objects under natural hand grasps, and the computed (non-learned) variant always fails on flipping motions.
MANO-based synthesis lacks physical embodiment and must be post-processed to map to real robot hands; human-to-robot mapping methods are designed for a single hand and a single mapping paradigm.
The human hand is treated as the robot end-effector with a simple nearest-joint mapping to the robot hand, with no direct pose transfer.

benchmark_evidence: HuRo five-source audit, 288 trajectories (1381) / fraction free of non-grasp self-contact: 55.2 percent; free of URDF joint-limit violation before clamping: 62.5 percent.
HandEdit ARCTIC curation (1394) / non-kept rate: about 33 percent of candidates rejected, retargeting causing 63.46 percent of sampled rejections.
RoboEdit Genesis simulation, 512 environments (1382) / trajectory-reproduction success: 71 percent (Panda) and 62 percent (XHand).
UniFucGrasp UFG test split in IsaacSim (891) / grasp success: mean 0.6955; real UR5 press button 4/10 (InspireHand) and 2/10 (HnuHand), totals 37/70 and 39/70.
clusters.settings: Human hand (MANO or MediaPipe keypoints) retargeted to parallel grippers and dexterous hands (Panda, XHand, InspireHand, HnuHand, Inspire on Unitree G1, ALLEX, ShadowHand) in simulation (IsaacSim, MuJoCo, Genesis) and on real robots; sources include EgoDex, ARCTIC, DexYCB, HOT3D and in-the-wild video.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Depth regularisation and physics refinement (1382), post-hoc joint-limit clamping (1381), per-hand mapping matrices calibrated by fingertip alignment (891), learned hand-to-gripper transfer from paired data (1390), human screening of retargeted samples (1394), and a nearest-joint mapping that avoids pose transfer (1489). Self-collision, contact and functional success are still not guaranteed; task-preserving retargeting is proposed but not built (1402).

clusters.name: Embodiment and strategy gap across robot hands
clusters.statement: Human manipulation strategies, grasps and workspaces do not transfer directly to heterogeneous robot embodiments (parallel grippers, larger or differently actuated dexterous hands, smaller arm workspaces) because the robot must act differently, and human-to-robot methods and action spaces are tied to one hand or robot.
clusters.description: Beyond reconstruction error, papers report that the human strategy itself can be wrong for the robot: a two-handed bag-holding strategy versus a one-gripper prop, sanding directions that suit human anatomy rather than robot performance, demonstrations outside a small robot's workspace, and a robot hand larger than the human hand that disturbs objects. Functional grasp datasets support only ShadowHand, learned human-to-robot mappings show strong hand-type dependency, and robotization methods are tied to grippers or single platforms. Action and state spaces differ across robots and datasets, and end-effector poses defined in different frames give conflicting supervision. Large-scale and survey papers state that the embodiment gap remains despite scale and list cross-embodiment state-action alignment as open.

evidence_items.item: On bag-grocery, Robot B performance dropped with human co-training because its demonstrations used one gripper to prop the bag open, unlike the two-handed human strategy; embodiment factors need deeper analysis.

Existing functional grasp datasets support only ShadowHand; learned human-to-robot capture tied to one hand type generalises poorly to other hands, and differences between robot hands limit broader generalisation.
The robot hand is larger than the human hand and can disturb objects during execution.
Human-collected data may exceed small robot workspaces; Wash Clothes lies fully outside the Xarm6 workspace.
Human surface-processing strategies are optimised for human anatomy and ergonomics, not robot performance; the human-preferred working direction conflicts with an optimal robot strategy.
The human-hand to gripper embodiment gap remains unsolved and is left for future work.
The embodiment gap between human and robot dexterous hands spans appearance, geometry, articulation and kinematics; existing robotization methods are tied to grippers or single platforms.
End-effector poses defined in different frames give conflicting supervision across datasets; cross-embodiment state-action alignment with consistent geometric semantics is open.
The embodiment gap between human and robot control spaces remains despite scale.
Action and state spaces are heterogeneous across robots and datasets, and learning from human video faces embodiment mismatch.
Naively added human video degrades in-domain policy performance due to embodiment and viewpoint mismatch, which is listed as open.
Rule-based retargeting and object-trajectory methods break under the hand-gripper morphology gap on movements with rotations or flips.

benchmark_evidence: UFG IsaacSim test split (891) / grasp success: flashlight 0.7037 versus DFG baseline 0.9103; real-world totals 37/70 (InspireHand) and 39/70 (HnuHand).
EgoVerse-A bag-grocery co-training (696) / robot task success: decreased for Robot B, whose one-gripper strategy differed from the two-handed human strategy, while Robots A and C improved.
clusters.settings: Human-to-gripper and human-to-dexterous-hand transfer (InspireHand, HnuHand, Inspire on Unitree G1, ShadowHand, xArm parallel gripper); bimanual mobile manipulators co-trained on egocentric data; UMI-style handheld data replayed on small arms (Xarm6); robotic surface finishing from hand-held tool demonstrations; human-to-robot image editing.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Co-training with task- and scene-aligned anchor data (696), per-hand mapping matrices (891), paired human and UMI re-enactment with learned transfer (1390), URDF-conditioned image editing (1394), embodiment-aligned generated data (1482), and recording coordinate conventions as metadata (1400, proposed). Papers state that embodiment factors still need deeper analysis (696) and that the gap remains despite scale (1378).

clusters.name: Human video does not reliably improve policies
clusters.statement: Adding human manipulation video as pretraining, co-training or latent actions does not reliably raise robot policy success: without task- and scene-aligned robot or human-robot anchor data it gives no gain or lowers in-domain success, and the benefit fades as robot data grows.
clusters.description: Benchmarks and datasets that measured robot outcomes report weak or negative returns from human video: human-video pretraining lowered in-domain success on all three bimanual tasks of one study, neither diverse nor aligned human data alone gave significant gains in another, and latent actions and discrete tokens from human video gave no significant improvement and helped only when robot data was scarce. Positive results still need hundreds to thousands of teleoperated robot demonstrations or a large human-video-pretrained backbone, and 1,000 h of egocentric pretraining roughly matches only 100 h of robot data. Action decoders conditioned directly on human video produce jittery executions. Surveys explain the failures as under-grounding, mis-grounding and false visual equivalence, and one dataset states that the effect of robotization fidelity on policies is not characterized.

evidence_items.item: Naively added human video degrades in-domain policy performance; human-video pretraining reduces in-domain success on all three tasks (Pick Dual Bottles 0.70 to 0.45), and its positive effect on unseen positions diminishes as data grows.
Neither 8 h of diverse human data nor domain-aligned human data alone produced significant gains; scaling with diverse human data works only when task- and scene-aligned human-robot data is included.

Latent-action pre-training helped only when target-robot data was scarce and the benefit faded as robot data grew; no discrete-token variant, including latent actions from human video, gave statistically significant gains.
Human pretraining alone gives zero task success; generated human data gives little benefit without a human-video-pretrained backbone, and 400 real teleoperated demonstrations are still required.
1,000 h of egocentric pretraining only matches or slightly surpasses 100 h of real-robot data and does not match the 20,000 h robot baseline.
Task-matched co-training with 200 robot clips plus 800 egocentric clips reaches only 23.3 percent success on single-object tasks.
Task-level transfer fails through under-grounding and observation-level alignment fails through false visual equivalence: aligned images or embeddings do not imply aligned actions.
An action decoder conditioned directly on human video produces jittery executions and misses grasps, with 23 percent average success.
The latent-action pretraining baseline fails completely in unseen environments, and the method still requires 1.2K teleoperated robot fine-tuning trajectories.
Learning from human video faces embodiment mismatch, lack of action data and train-test environment mismatch.
Robotized trajectories serve only as pretraining supervision, not executable demonstrations, and the effect of robotization fidelity on downstream policy learning is not characterized.

benchmark_evidence: Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 (224) / success rate: Pick Dual Bottles in-domain 0.70 teleoperation only versus 0.45 after human-video pretraining; Rank RGB Blocks unseen position 0.17 versus 0.13 with human video.
TRI-Ramen simulation tasks (709) / task success: latent actions, FAST and VQ-VAE tokens give no statistically significant improvement; FAST lowers unseen-task success.
WIYH task-matched co-training on a real robot (1376) / success rate: 23.3 percent with 200 robot plus 800 egocentric clips.
Wh0, 18 real dexterous tasks on Unitree G1 (1482) / zero-shot unseen-task success: best 38.9 percent (robot-only VITRA baseline 8.3 percent).
Real-robot unseen objects and categories (1489) / success rate: VPP, latent-action and OXE-pretraining baselines reach 0 to 8.3 percent.
HumanNet LingBot-VLA post-training (1378) / validation loss: 1,000 h egocentric pretraining roughly equals 100 h robot data, short of the 20,000 h robot baseline.
EgoVerse-A bag-grocery (696) / robot task success: decreased for Robot B with human co-training while Robots A and C improved.
Human2Robot ablation (1495) / success rate: action decoder conditioned directly on human video averages 23 percent, with jittery executions and missed grasps.
clusters.settings: Bimanual and single-arm tabletop policies (Aloha-Agilex, ARX-R5, Franka, xArm, Unitree G1 with Inspire hands, bimanual mobile robots) co-trained or pretrained on chest-mounted, head-worn, smartphone, web or generated human video, with MediaPipe, Aria MPS or MANO hand keypoints as action proxies; VLA, large-behaviour-model and diffusion policies.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Task- and scene-aligned human-robot anchor data (696), pretrain-then-fine-tune with end-effector deltas (224), latent actions and discrete action tokens (709), robotized human video (1381), human-video-pretrained VLA backbones plus 400 to 1.2K teleoperated demonstrations (1482, 1489), and paired human-robot video with video-generation pretraining (1495). Gains appear only with aligned or substantial robot data or in low-robot-data regimes, and embodiment-forced strategy differences can still make co-training harmful.

clusters.name: Paired human-robot demonstrations cannot be captured at scale
clusters.statement: Frame-aligned human and robot demonstrations of the same task cannot be captured at scale: current pairing needs VR teleoperation in mirrored workspaces, handheld-gripper re-enactment of each human demonstration or synthetic pseudo-references, and is restricted to simple pick-and-place.
clusters.description: Papers that learn from paired human-robot data state that existing pairs are only coarsely aligned, so methods learn global or task-level features and fail on unseen tasks. Capturing fine alignment needs VR teleoperation with anchor-based coordinate alignment in two mirrored workspaces, or a UMI re-enactment of every human demonstration with manual start and end annotation. Pixel-aligned human-robot image pairs cannot be captured at all, so editing benchmarks build pseudo-references that keep an appearance and contact gap, and paired human demonstrations recorded on a lab platform went unused. Harder tasks such as screwing cannot be collected with these setups, and a dataset paper calls for methods that ground weakly aligned human data through limited aligned supervision.

evidence_items.item: Paired-video teleoperation cannot collect difficult tasks such as screwing, so training and testing focus on pick-and-place; fine-grained frame-level human-robot alignment datasets are lacking.
Pixel-aligned human-robot image pairs cannot be physically captured, so the dataset relies on edited pseudo-references that keep a gap from real-robot observations in appearance and contact dynamics.
Paired data needs UMI handheld gripper re-enactment of each human demonstration, with manual annotation of start and terminal frames and click-based SAM2 masks.
Aligned human-robot data with the same task semantics and scene context is needed to anchor transfer; methods that use weakly aligned data grounded through limited aligned supervision are needed.
Paired human demonstrations were recorded on the same lab platform, not in the wild, and were not exploited in the experiments.

benchmark_evidence: HandEdit pseudo-pair curation on ARCTIC (1394) / non-kept rate: about 33 percent of synthesized human-robot candidates rejected.
clusters.settings: Third-person static RealSense views with Meta Quest 3 VR teleoperation of a parallel-gripper xArm in mirrored workspaces (1495); RGB-D hand demonstrations re-enacted with UMI grippers (1390); MANO-annotated egocentric and lab HOI datasets edited into robot images (1394); fixed calibrated multi-camera lab platform (1388); egocentric co-training with aligned anchor data (696).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Mirrored workspaces with anchor-based VR coordinate alignment (1495), UMI re-enactment with manual start and end annotation (1390), segmentation-inpainting-retargeting-compositing pseudo-pairs with human screening (1394), and same-platform human recordings (1388). These remain lab-bound, labour-intensive, limited to pick-and-place, or synthetic with a residual appearance and contact gap to real robot observations.

clusters.name: Human demonstrations lack measured contact force
clusters.statement: Human demonstration and human-video datasets carry no measured contact force or full-hand tactile signal; where contact appears it is a geometric proxy, and force sensors cannot be added to hand-held tools without disturbing natural use, so contact-rich skills cannot be supervised from human data.
clusters.description: Dataset papers and surveys state that tactile and force data are small, narrow in contact coverage and not a standard modality, leaving a missing contact layer, and that contact-rich behaviours are underrepresented. Human-video pipelines provide only visual and kinematic supervision, and the position paper says latent actions, progress signals and representations learned from passive video miss contact dynamics and force constraints. Where human tactile labels exist they are binary per-vertex contact from hand-object mesh distance, simulation benchmarks substitute proprioception for touch, and no powered hand-held tool with integrated force sensing exists because a force-torque sensor would impair grasp ergonomics. Contact-intensive tasks such as plug insertion remain mostly unsolved, and several papers list tactile or inferred force cues as future work.

evidence_items.item: Tactile datasets remain small and narrow in contact coverage; HOI-Tac tactile labels are binary per-vertex contact from hand-object mesh distance thresholding, not measured force; human demonstration datasets largely omit the tactile modality.
No force or tactile signals are captured, only visual and kinematic action supervision; augmenting robotized videos with inferred contact or force cues is future work.
Tactile sensing is not a standard modality in robot datasets, leaving a missing contact layer.
Contact-rich behaviours with force or tactile signals are underrepresented.
Learning from passive video does not solve grounding; latent actions, progress signals and representations still miss contact dynamics and force constraints.
Vision-driven demonstrations lack robot actions and force/contact data.
No tactile sensing; full-hand tactile sensing is future work.
No powered sanding tool design with integrated force sensing exists, and adding a force-torque sensor would impair grasp ergonomics.
Over-reliance on visual guidance; multimodal tactile, force and audio perception is needed.
Adding audio, gaze and tactile (including pseudo-tactile) signals to human video is future work, and integrating streams with differing rates and noise is open.
Integrating multi-view visual inputs and tactile feedback is listed as open.

benchmark_evidence: Real robot PlugIn with visual defects (1385) / success rate: 20 percent (gripper) and 10 percent (DexBotic) in-distribution, 20 percent out-of-distribution; all baselines 0 percent.
RoboCasa (1385) / average success: 55.1 percent; Pick and Place only 35 percent.
clusters.settings: Egocentric RGB human video and glove-based datasets used for VLA pretraining; contact-rich tasks such as plug insertion and wiping; hand-held powered tool use (sanding); handheld UMI-style capture; haptic teleoperation platforms; simulation benchmarks without a tactile modality.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Mesh-distance contact labels, a tactile glove with three calibrated RealSense cameras and a MoCap glove, and simulated tactile projected onto a shared MANO surface (1385); haptic teleoperation with a force-torque sensor on a fixed lab platform (1388); a force-torque sensor under a fixed workpiece fixture (998); proposed inferred or pseudo-tactile cues (1381, 1399) and full-hand tactile sensing (1376). None yields measured, scalable full-hand force for natural human manipulation.

clusters.name: Demonstration interfaces fail on force-rich, fine tasks
clusters.statement: Robot-side and handheld demonstration interfaces (kinesthetic teaching, teleoperation without force feedback, paired VR teleoperation, UMI-style grippers) cannot record clean demonstrations of force-rich skills or fine manipulation of thin flexible objects.
clusters.description: Studies comparing demonstration modalities report that kinesthetic replay becomes jerky and misaligned under strong contact force when no force sensor is present, and that teleoperation struggles with force-involved skills because of dynamic delay and limited feedback transparency. Teleoperation without force feedback is called inefficient and unsafe in contact-rich tasks, with emergency stops from hard collisions, and paired VR teleoperation cannot collect tasks such as screwing. Handheld grippers designed for rigid pick-and-place cannot open thin flexible packaging, and adding a force-torque sensor to a hand-held powered tool would impair ergonomics while robot-mounted tools bias demonstrations through inertia. The fixes reported are task-specific: post-hoc force compensation, haptic rendering, redesigned fingers or fixtured workpieces.

evidence_items.item: Kinesthetic replay fails on contact-force tasks; on Push Sanitizer replay actions are highly jerky and misaligned, and with no force sensor the force-induced error is compensated only after the fact, doubling replay time.
Teleoperation-based data collection cannot readily capture subtle force-involved interaction skills because of dynamic delays and feedback transparency.

Original UMI hardware could not open sterile bandage packaging at all; compliant fingers do not deform on flexible planar packaging, and tools built for rigid pick-and-place fail on thin, flexible materials.

No powered sanding tool with integrated force sensing exists and a force-torque sensor would impair grasp ergonomics; kinesthetic teaching or robot-mounted force-sensing tools would bias demonstrations through robot inertia and kinematic limits.
Teleoperation interfaces without force feedback are inefficient and unsafe in contact-rich tasks; failures include emergency stops from hard collisions.
Paired-video VR teleoperation cannot collect difficult tasks such as screwing.
Teleoperation for contact-rich tasks is labour-intensive and hard to scale.

benchmark_evidence: Bandage-opening user study (854) / bandages opened within 2 minutes: distributed-load grippers 65.8 percent versus 100 percent for bare hands; hands significantly faster than both gripper designs.
Push Sanitizer (782) / policy success rate: kinesthetic data underperforms teleoperation and was excluded from the mixed-data scheme for low quality.
RH20T (1388) / success-to-failure ratio: about 10:1, with failures including emergency stops from hard collisions during teleoperation.
clusters.settings: Single 7-DoF Franka with impedance control under kinesthetic, VR and spacemouse demonstration (782); handheld UMI grippers on flexible sterile packaging (854); simulation versus teleoperation interfaces for plane cutting, tight peg-in-hole and deformable pipe plugging (919); haptic teleoperation with force rendering (1388); powered hand-held sander with a Vive tracker (998); paired VR teleoperation (1495); tactile dexterous VLA tasks (1385).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Post-hoc force-compensation heuristic that doubles replay time (782), haptic teleoperation with force rendering (1388), a simulation interface rendering high stiffness to the operator (919), redesigned concentrated-load fingers (854), and a force-torque sensor under a fixed workpiece fixture (998).
