These remain task-specific, slow or limited to fixtured workpieces, and 854 states that gripper hardware limits cannot be overcome by learning algorithms alone.

clusters.name: Demonstration collection is costly and physically burdensome
clusters.statement: Robot-side and wearable demonstration interfaces remain costly, slow or physically burdensome per demonstration: kinesthetic teaching is too demanding, teleoperation is expensive, hardware-coupled and unintuitive, handheld grippers are slow and heavy, and wearables need fitting, calibration and synchronisation.
clusters.description: A modality study finds kinesthetic teaching too physically demanding for large-scale collection, VR rotation control unintuitive and teleoperated trajectories widely spread near joint limits, yet users still prefer teleoperation despite its lower data quality. A handheld gripper study reports that demonstrations need at least 200 per task at roughly twice bare-hand time, with a 780 g tool causing fatigue. Dataset papers describe teleoperation as costly, hardware-coupled, labour-intensive for contact-rich tasks and poorly extensible, and specialised head-mounted or AR/VR capture hardware as a barrier to access. A survey states that wearable head and hand tracking is not mature for large-scale deployment because gloves, tactile sensors and EMG need fitting, calibration and synchronisation.

evidence_items.item: Kinesthetic teaching is too physically demanding for large-scale collection; VR rotation control is unintuitive, and users prefer teleoperation despite its lower data quality.
Demonstrations are time-consuming, at least 200 per task at roughly twice hand time, and the gripper weight of about 780 g causes fatigue.
Teleoperation is costly and hardware-coupled.
Data collection is expensive, and failures include emergency stops from hard collisions during teleoperation.
Wearable head and hand tracking is not mature for large-scale deployment; gloves, tactile sensors and EMG need fitting, calibration and synchronisation, trading accuracy against participant burden.
Specialised head-mounted or AR/VR capture hardware limits accessibility.
Teleoperation for contact-rich tasks is labour-intensive and hard to scale.
Teleoperation and UMI collection have poor extensibility and limited scalability.
Robot data is expensive to scale.
Teleoperation is aligned with deployment but expensive.
Teleoperation data is costly to collect at scale.
Lab-based teleoperation limits scene diversity, and hardware engines face calibration and embodiment constraints.

benchmark_evidence: Bandage-opening user study (854) / time to open: bare hands significantly faster than both gripper designs; at least 200 demonstrations per task at roughly twice hand time.
clusters.settings: Franka kinesthetic, VR and spacemouse teleoperation (782); UMI and FastUMI handheld grippers (854, 1369); haptic and VR teleoperation rigs (1388, 1385); smartphone, head-mounted stereo, AR/VR and glove-based wearables (1377, 1379, 1400); generated data positioned as an alternative to teleoperation (1482).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Mixing modalities (782), redesigned gripper fingers (854), handheld UMI-style collection (1369), commodity smartphone capture (1377), a custom head-mounted stereo device (1379), generated egocentric data (1482), and proposed lighter wireless wearables with automatic cross-device calibration (1400). Collection stays slow or burdensome per demonstration.

clusters.name: Manipulation datasets are narrow, static and unevenly covered
clusters.statement: Robot and human manipulation datasets remain narrow in scene and task diversity (mostly simple tabletop pick-and-place), small relative to vision-language corpora, released as one-off static corpora with fragmented processing pipelines, and unevenly covered.
clusters.description: Dataset papers state that lab-collected robot and egocentric datasets have restricted environmental and scenario diversity, focus on simple push or pick-and-place tasks, and are small relative to large robot or vision-language corpora. Most human datasets are one-off static releases that are hard to extend, processing pipelines are dataset-specific rather than shared infrastructure, and large human activity datasets include tasks beyond robot capability. Functional grasp datasets cover only one costly robot hand, and no large-scale dexterous hand action dataset existed before the paper that built one. Web-scale corpora bring uneven geographic, socioeconomic and body-type coverage plus privacy and licensing issues, and surveys describe a fidelity-versus-scale trade-off in which aggregated corpora lose interface consistency.

evidence_items.item: Most human datasets are one-off, static releases that are hard to scale or extend, and large human activity datasets include tasks beyond robot capability.
Existing robot datasets have restricted environmental diversity.
Lab-collected datasets have limited scenario diversity.
Dataset-specific processing pipelines are fragmented rather than unified infrastructure.
Coverage is uneven, with geographic, socioeconomic and body-type bias, plus privacy, safety and licensing issues of human-centric video.
Large diverse robot manipulation datasets are lacking because of data acquisition barriers, so one-shot imitation focuses on simple push or pick-place tasks.
Human-video datasets for robot learning focus on simple tasks and fall short of in-the-wild settings; balancing diversity and relevance is open.
Large-scale annotated functional grasp datasets are lacking, and existing ones support only the costly ShadowHand.
Robot VLA data are lab-collected, costly and scarce, and no large-scale dexterous hand action dataset existed.
Benchmark data scale is small relative to large robot datasets, and the benchmark is tabletop only.
Datasets trade fidelity against scale; aggregated corpora gain volume at the cost of interface consistency.

clusters.settings: Teleoperated multi-camera lab platforms (RH20T), UMI-style tabletop benchmarks (UMI-Bench), wearable, smartphone and head-mounted egocentric capture (WIYH, Open-AoE, EgoLive, EgoVerse), internet-scale and real-life activity video (HumanNet, 1489), functional grasp datasets (UniFucGrasp), simulated twins (RoboTube).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Community-extensible releases and unified toolchains (696, 1377), large-scale wearable or web collection (1376, 1378, 1379, 1489), multi-hand functional grasp annotation (891), and licence review, redaction and access controls (1378). Each trades scale against fidelity and robot alignment, as the VLA survey states (1401).

clusters.name: Portable capture tracking drifts under motion
clusters.statement: Wearable and handheld capture (VIO trackers on handheld grippers, Vive trackers on powered tools, headset inside-out tracking, IMU or magnetic gloves, head-mounted stereo, smartphone and monocular SLAM) loses pose accuracy under fast motion, vibration, occlusion, camera shake or distance, showing jumps, drift and scale distortion, and needs per-session calibration and synchronisation.
clusters.description: Papers using portable capture report sudden jumps and global scale distortion in VIO pose, tracking interruptions and variable sampling rates under tool vibration and occlusion, headset tracking failures under fast motion or limited field of view, IMU drift and magnetic distortion near metal, VR coordinate frames that shift between sessions, stereo depth error that grows with distance, and eye-tracking glasses whose frame rate varies from overheating. Monocular SLAM on smartphone or internet video needs re-tuned robust kernels under camera shake and is run only on stable, high-parallax clips. Affected trajectories are typically flagged and deleted. A survey states that wearable sensing is not mature for large-scale deployment and that UMI-style pose tracking and synchronisation degrade in hard visual conditions.

evidence_items.item: T265 tracking can show sudden jumps or global scale distortion and such trajectories are auto-flagged and deleted; SLAM drift from operator anomalies leads to discarded trajectories.
Vive motion tracking was interrupted by occlusions and tool vibrations, with the rate varying from 83 to 470 Hz; robust, low-cost, portable capture under vibration and occlusion remains unsolved.

Headset inside-out tracking can fail under fast motion, occlusion or limited field of view; IMU-based tracking accumulates drift and magnetic fingertip sensors are distorted by nearby metal; UMI-style pose tracking and synchronisation degrade in hard visual conditions.
Coordinate systems of the VR headset vary slightly each session, requiring object position adjustments.
Stereo depth error grows with distance, from about 3 mm at 500 mm to 18.0 mm at 3500 mm; low error is claimed only within the typical human operation range.
Severe camera shake and torso motion require re-tuned robust kernels in DROID-W, and segment-wise reconstructions suffer scale drift.
Monocular SLAM camera trajectories are produced only for first-person clips that meet stability and parallax requirements.
Egocentric gaze glasses recorded variable frame rates due to overheating, requiring resampling to 25 fps.

benchmark_evidence: SURP sanding capture, 21 users (998) / Vive tracker rate: varied from 83 to 470 Hz (median 127 Hz) under vibration and occlusion.
EgoLive calibration room (1379) / stereo depth mean error: 3.06 mm at 500 mm rising to 13-18 mm beyond 1700 mm.
clusters.settings: Handheld UMI-style grippers with RealSense T265 VIO (1369); hand-held powered tools with Vive trackers (998); headsets with inside-out tracking and IMU or magnetic gloves (1400); smartphone and internet video with DROID-W or monocular SLAM (1377, 1378); head-mounted stereo with learned stereo depth (1379); Meta Quest VR teleoperation (1495); eye-tracking glasses (23).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Auto-flagging and deleting bad trajectories (1369), a damper on the tracker and suggested passive optical markers that may not solve vibration (998), re-tuned robust kernels and global bundle adjustment (1377), stability and parallax gating of SLAM clips (1378), anchor-based coordinate alignment with per-session object adjustment (1495), resampling variable frame rates (23), and proposed lighter wireless wearables with automatic cross-device calibration (1400).

clusters.name: Task phases and events need human labelling
clusters.statement: Atomic action boundaries, contact events, task phases, object-state changes, mistakes and task completion cannot yet be inferred automatically and reliably from unscripted manipulation video or asynchronous multimodal streams, so pipelines rely on human verification.
clusters.description: Datasets that segment human video into atomic actions report that VLM-generated labels hallucinate and need human-in-the-loop correction, that task boundaries are inconsistent, that captions omit or alter steps, and that no existing temporal action segmentation method meets their needs. Fine-grained action recognition and mistake detection remain low under skewed classes, cross-view action segmentation is open, and VLM completion verification is near chance. The position paper names embodied autolabelling, meaning temporal alignment of video, mocap, tactile and robot logs to a common event timeline and joint inference of phase, contact, object state, action and reward, as the core missing mechanism. A survey adds that failure and recovery data are scarce and that binary success labels are insufficient.

evidence_items.item: Multimodal streams (video, mocap, tactile, logs) are asynchronous and aligning them to physical events is itself unsolved; inferring events, contacts and object states from partially supervised episodes is open.
Temporal action segmentation remains an open problem with no existing method meeting the authors' needs; fixed-interval segmentation degrades grasp prediction.
Model hallucinations in atomic-action labels require human-in-the-loop correction, and passive video lacks action boundaries.
Atomic segmentation needs human verification; VLM completion verification is only slightly above random, and progress modelling in VLMs is open.
Noise comes from ambiguous labels, inconsistent task boundaries and missing metadata, and automated captions carry errors.
Mistake detection is difficult under highly skewed classes (about 6 percent mistakes), and fine-grained action recognition is around 35 percent top-1.
Predicted captions omit or alter steps compared with ground truth.
Failure and recovery data are scarce and poorly organised; binary success labels are insufficient.
Cross-view action segmentation and cross-view referenced video captioning are listed as open benchmarks.

benchmark_evidence: WIYH human-centric vision-language benchmark (1376) / completion verification: only slightly above 50 percent random for all VLMs.
HoloAssist (1397) / fine-grained action recognition top-1: around 35 percent (coarse around 50 percent).
HoloAssist (1397) / mistake detection: best 40.19 (hands only), RGB 35.11.
EgoLive (1379) / caption quality: predicted captions omit or alter steps relative to ground truth (examples only, no number).
clusters.settings: Unscripted egocentric video segmented into atomic actions with VLM or GPT captioning (WIYH, Open-AoE, HumanNet, EgoLive, real-life activity video); HoloLens 2 instructor-performer sessions (HoloAssist); asynchronous ego-exo procedural video (EgoExoLearn); multimodal capture with mocap, tactile and robot logs (position paper).
clusters.attempted_fixes: VLM-generated labels with human-in-the-loop verification (1376, 1377), fixed-interval segmentation, which degrades grasp prediction (1489), and gaze and hand cues for cross-view tasks (23). Proposed: physical data engines with embodied autolabelling and wearable sensing suits as labelling instruments (1402), and failure-centric datasets with onset, cause and recovery labels (1400).

clusters.name: Single-hand assumption blocks bimanual and multi-agent transfer
clusters.statement: Human-to-robot data and transfer pipelines mostly assume one hand (often the right), one demonstrator and one arm, so two-handed coordination, handovers and contacts on shared objects cannot be extracted or transferred, and bimanual tasks are untested or perform worst.
clusters.description: Most papers in this group restrict human-to-robot experiments to the right hand, single-hand to single-gripper transfer, single-arm parallel grippers, or one hand at a time, and list bimanual or dual-arm extension as future work. Where bimanual tasks are tested they are the hardest (pot-lifting, cloth folding), degrade more out of distribution than single-hand versions, or reveal handover difficulty and strategy mismatches. The human-video survey states that nearly all methods assume one demonstrator and one robot, and that multi-agent settings need agent correspondence, disentangled overlapping motions and contact tracking across agents and shared objects, which current pipelines do not do. Handheld grippers also block the demonstrator's view in bimanual use.

evidence_items.item: Nearly all learning-from-human-video methods assume one human demonstrator and one robot; multi-agent settings require resolving agent correspondence, disentangling overlapping motions and tracking contacts across agents and shared objects, which current pipelines do not do.
Experiments cover only single-arm pick-and-place and the policy action space handles only the right hand; bimanual extension is future work.
Robot experiments are primarily single-handed, with bimanual shown only by a simple hand-over demo; bimanual manipulation transfer is open.
The dataset covers single-arm robots with parallel grippers only; extension to dual-arm and multi-finger dexterous manipulation is future work.
Bimanual pot-lifting and cloth folding are the hardest tasks: reward learning remains hard, TCN fails on bimanual pot-lifting, and RL success is lowest.
Bimanual VaseWiping drops to 80 percent out of distribution while the single-hand version reaches 100 percent.
In bimanual use the handheld grippers block the demonstrator's view, making placement hard.
Object handover in cup-on-saucer was difficult, and a robot's one-gripper strategy for bag-grocery conflicted with the two-handed human strategy.
Human hand input comes from a single RGB-D camera with MediaPipe keypoints, one hand at a time.
Transfer is single-hand to single-gripper from monocular RGB-D input.
Demonstrations are right-hand only, with a parallel-gripper xArm.
Scalable collection of complex, fine-grained, dual-arm, long-horizon data is open, and dual-arm collaborative manipulation is future work.

benchmark_evidence: Real robot VaseWiping (1385) / out-of-distribution success: bimanual 80 percent versus single-hand 100 percent.
RT-sim bimanual pot-lifting and cloth folding (1389) / RL success and reward prediction: hardest tasks, with poorly predicted learned rewards and the lowest RL success (no number in digest).
Bandage-opening user study, bimanual (854) / bandages opened within 2 minutes: 65.8 percent for distributed-load grippers versus 100 percent for bare hands.
EgoVerse-A bag-grocery (696) / robot task success: decreased for Robot B with human co-training because of a one-gripper versus two-handed strategy mismatch.
clusters.settings: Egocentric and RGB-D human demonstrations transferred to single-arm grippers and dexterous hands (Unitree G1, xArm, UR5, Franka); bimanual mobile manipulators (EgoVerse); bimanual simulated twins (RoboTube); handheld bimanual grippers (UMI, FastUMI); tactile bimanual wiping; multi-agent handovers and joint transport named by the survey.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Dual-arm UMI-style collection (1369), a simple hand-over demo (1489), and co-training with aligned bimanual robot data (696); bimanual extension is deferred to future work in 1482, 1388 and 1489. Single-hand assumptions remain in 891, 1390 and 1495, and no paper in the group reports a method for two-hand or multi-agent correspondence and shared-object contact tracking (1399).

clusters.name: Human-to-robot visual conversion loses embodiment and contact
clusters.statement: Converting human manipulation video or images into robot-embodiment video, by rendering, inpainting, image editing or video world models, does not reliably replace the human actor or preserve hand-object contact and action events, and generic visual-quality and VLM metrics do not detect these failures.
clusters.description: H2R-Bench finds actor leakage (the human stays the manipulator), contact-region and contact-mode mismatch, end-effector mismatch for gripper targets and omitted action events in generated robot videos, with weak rank association between generic video quality and transfer correctness. HandEdit reports that general image editors give plausible-looking edits that fail embodiment and interaction preservation, that VLM judges miss fine-grained morphology and contact, and that retargeting dominates rejected pseudo-references. Render-and-inpaint pipelines ignore robot-scene occlusion, leave artifacts near the edit boundary and take tens of minutes per clip, and robot-hand editing of generated video fails to preserve posture or alters scene objects. A survey states that embodiment-aware inpainting yields interactions that are not physically grounded.

evidence_items.item: Frame-conditioned models often keep the human as the active manipulator (actor leakage), show contact-region or contact-mode mismatch and omit required action events; generic video quality metrics do not reflect valid robot transfer.
General image editors produce visually plausible edits that fail target embodiment and interaction preservation; VLM-based judgment misses fine-grained morphology and contact.
Robotized observation fidelity is bounded by reconstruction and visual conversion; the robot overlay ignores occlusion with scene geometry and leaves inpainting and rendering artifacts.
Robot-hand editing fails to preserve hand posture or unintentionally modifies scene objects; without embodiment alignment, grounding degrades under robot-hand appearance.
Embodiment-aware inpainting produces interactions that are not physically grounded.
Background SSIM is lower near the edit-mask boundary because robot and human hands differ in extent, and curation takes about 20 minutes per clip on an H100.

benchmark_evidence: H2R-Bench, 240 transfer cases (1393) / H2RCore 0-100: scores span 30.0 to 84.6 across 11 models while video quality spans only 0.73 to 0.81, with weak rank association.
H2R-Bench (1393) / embodiment correctness: HunyuanVideo 1.5-I2V near zero despite the highest video quality, contact score near 0.185; Veo 3.1 embodiment 0.100 and 0.227 for parallel-jaw targets.
H2R-Bench (1393) / H2RCore with nine-frame conditioning: drops by 27.6 (gripper) and 41.4 (hand) points.
HandEdit ARCTIC curation (1394) / non-kept rate: about 33 percent of candidates rejected.
clusters.settings: EgoDex, ARCTIC, OakInk2, HOI4D, HO-Cap and lab HOI sources (DexYCB, HOT3D, H2O, TACO) converted to parallel-jaw grippers and dexterous robot hands by video world models, image editors and render-and-inpaint pipelines; robot overlay on EPIC-Kitchens and Ego4D; robot-hand editing of generated egocentric video.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Hand-crafted segmentation, inpainting, retargeting and compositing pipelines with human screening (1394); depth-corrected, physics-refined compositing (1382); MLLM judges over sampled frames (1393); scene and embodiment alignment for generated data (1482). Proposed: end-to-end embodiment-aware editing (1394) and fine-grained 3D reconstruction for geometry diagnostics (1393); physical executability and downstream policy value remain unevaluated (1393).

clusters.name: World models predict physically invalid interactions
clusters.statement: Video and world models learned from human manipulation cannot predict physically consistent interaction futures: generated rollouts show interpenetration, contact without force, deforming rigid objects, object fragmentation and inconsistent long-horizon states.
clusters.description: The surveys and the position paper agree that world models trained on human video optimise visual similarity without physical constraints, so their rollouts become physically invalid in contact-rich, long-horizon tasks: objects interpenetrate, contacts occur without force and rigid objects deform. Generative egocentric data shows hands passing through objects, unexpected objects and inconsistent pre- and post-interaction states, and untextured video-generation baselines show object fragmentation. The position paper adds that point clouds, meshes, neural fields and Gaussian splats may struggle with contact, force and material response, while mechanics-based models are brittle in unknown or deformable environments. Interactive world models also have limited temporal context, high compute cost and a sim-to-real discrepancy.

evidence_items.item: Purely learned predictors produce futures where objects interpenetrate, contacts occur without force, or rigid objects deform; 3D representations may struggle with contact, force and material response, and mechanics-based models are brittle when the environment is unknown or deformable.
Human-video world models emphasise visual similarity and impose no physical constraints, producing physically invalid rollouts in contact-rich, long-horizon tasks.
The generator can produce physically implausible interactions such as hands passing through objects, unexpected objects, or inconsistent pre- and post-interaction states and long-horizon videos.
Untextured video generation baselines show object fragmentation and physically implausible hand-object interactions.
Interactive world models have limited temporal context, high compute cost and sim-to-real discrepancy.

benchmark_evidence: Wh0 user study, 72 AI practitioners (1482) / perceived realism: only 37.7 percent (134/355) of generated videos judged real; participants used physics, layout and contact cues to spot fakes.
clusters.settings: Egocentric video generators and world models for hand manipulation (Wh0, WIYH generation baselines); world models trained on human video for contact-rich, long-horizon tasks (surveys); deformable and unknown environments (position paper).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Scene- and embodiment-aligned generation (1482) and textured generation (1376). Proposed but not validated: hybrid physics-grounded world models combining 3D scene, object-centric structure, physics constraints and residual dynamics (1402), physically grounded world models learned from human video (1399), and high-fidelity real-scene reconstruction in simulation (1401).

clusters.name: Viewpoint mismatch between demonstration and execution
clusters.statement: Demonstrations recorded from a different viewpoint or place than execution (exocentric versus egocentric, chest camera versus robot camera, asynchronous recordings, new deployment views) cannot be reliably associated or transferred, so working methods assume the deployment camera viewpoint.
clusters.description: An ego-exo dataset shows that models trained on one view show a large gap on the other, that zero-shot cross-view association is barely above random, that an exocentric reference adds little to skill assessment, and that zero-shot recognition is worse on egocentric video. Robot-learning papers attribute part of the harm from human video to viewpoint and spatial-domain mismatch, and report a high-error tail in camera-robot alignment under viewpoint inconsistency. Surveys list device-dependent viewpoints and viewpoint imbalance as noise sources and state that aligned images do not imply aligned actions. Methods that work assume identical static cameras, background images taken by the deployment camera, or an operator-selected camera-relative virtual robot base.

evidence_items.item: Models trained on a single view struggle with cross-view association and show a large gap on the other view; zero-shot cross-view evaluation gives the lowest anticipation and planning performance; cross-view association from unpaired samples is open.

Naively added human video degrades in-domain performance due to embodiment and viewpoint mismatch; with pi0 on ARX-R5 human video was uniformly detrimental in unseen positions, attributed to spatial domain mismatch.
Observation-level alignment fails through false visual equivalence: aligned images or embeddings do not imply aligned actions.
Egocentric human data suffers device-dependent viewpoints and is not equivalent to robot experience.
The method requires background images captured by the deployment camera at the same viewpoint and resolution; without scene alignment generated videos drift from the target workspace.
Paired data requires third-person static cameras with identical viewpoints and two mirrored workspaces.
Hand-arm consistency with target morphology and camera viewpoint is open; the hand-arm virtual base cannot be observed and requires operator selection.
Camera-robot alignment has a high-error tail with large viewpoint or robot-placement inconsistency.
Noise sources include viewpoint imbalance across clips.

benchmark_evidence: EgoExoLearn test (23) / cross-view association accuracy: best co-trained model with gaze 55.3 (Ego2Exo) and 51.1 (Exo2Ego); zero-shot models 21.7 to 33.3 versus random 13 to 14.
EgoExoLearn (23) / cross-view anticipation Top-5 recall: mostly 25 to 56, with zero-shot cross-view transfer lowest.
EgoExoLearn (23) / skill assessment ranking accuracy: exocentric reference gives only marginal gains (about 79 to 84 percent).
Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 Rank RGB Blocks unseen position (224) / success rate: 0.17 teleoperation only versus 0.13 with human video.
clusters.settings: Asynchronous egocentric executions versus exocentric demonstrations in different environments (EgoExoLearn); chest-mounted human video versus robot cameras (224); generated or edited robot video from a fixed deployment camera (Wh0, HandEdit); robot overlay on egocentric video (HuRo); third-person static cameras with identical viewpoints (Human2Robot).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Co-training with gaze cues (23), recording human video in the same environment as teleoperation (224), deployment-camera background images with a hand scale anchor (1482), identical static cameras in mirrored workspaces (1495), and an operator-selected fixed virtual robot base per sequence (1394). These avoid the mismatch by construction rather than solving cross-view transfer, and unpaired cross-view association is left open (23).

clusters.name: Long-horizon multi-stage tasks fail
clusters.statement: Policies trained from human, handheld or teleoperated demonstrations cannot complete long-horizon multi-stage manipulation: they lose the stage estimate under ambiguous wrist-only views and accumulate small errors until tight final tolerances fail, while human-video data covers only short atomic skills.
clusters.description: Real-world benchmarks of UMI-style policies report zero full success on multi-stage and long-horizon rearrangement tasks: policies complete intermediate steps, then lose track of the stage because wrist observations look alike across stages, or accumulate small early placement deviations until a tight final tolerance fails. Diffusion Policy could not handle long horizons, so tasks were split into subtasks, and chained-instruction benchmarks cited by a survey drop to near-zero success. A survey attributes this to compounding errors that push the robot into states absent from demonstrations, and chain-of-thought conditioning gave no benefit. Human-video and generated-data pipelines target only short-horizon atomic skills and short clips, and longer horizons are left as future work.

evidence_items.item: All three evaluated policies get 0% full success on T3 (multi-stage) and T9 (long-horizon rearrangement); on T3 they lose the stage estimate under an ambiguous single wrist view, and on T9 small early placement deviations fail the tight final tolerance.

With no fixed third-person view, similar wrist observations across stages confuse long-horizon inference; Diffusion Policy cannot handle long-horizon tasks, so tasks were split into subtasks, and errors accumulate over stages.
CALVIN success drops sharply for five sequential instructions, and multi-step logical tasks fail systematically on VLABench.
Compounding errors in sequential decisions push the robot into states absent from demonstrations; solving arbitrary long-horizon tasks remains open.
Data construction and training target only short-horizon atomic skills; long-horizon task structure from human video is open.
Planning with more steps remains weak, with edit distances around 0.75 to 0.85.
Conditioning actions on chain-of-thought gave no benefit in simulation; richer forms such as hierarchical plans are left open.
Scope is limited to three rigid-object tasks; long-horizon manipulation is left to future work.
Long-horizon tasks are left to future work, and the generator can produce inconsistent long-horizon videos.
The benchmark is limited to short clips; extending to longer demonstrations is future work.

benchmark_evidence: UMI-Bench 1.0 T3 tool-mediated stamping (1372) / full success rate: 0 percent for all three models; best progress score 34.30.
UMI-Bench 1.0 T9 long-horizon rearrangement (1372) / full success rate: 0 percent for all models; progress scores 10.6 to 26.4.

FastUMI-100K Heat Food, Flexiv Rizon4 with pi0 (1369) / stage success: put bread into microwave 0.00 percent and close door 0.00 percent after 100 percent door opening; Wash Clothes close washer door 60.00 percent.
CALVIN, as cited by the survey (1401) / success for five sequential instructions: drops to 0.08 percent.
EgoExoLearn (23) / multi-step planning edit distance: around 0.75 to 0.85.
clusters.settings: Real tabletop and household tasks with UMI-style wrist-fisheye observations and VLA or diffusion policies (UMI-Bench, FastUMI-100K); simulated chained-instruction and multi-step benchmarks (CALVIN, VLABench); egocentric procedural planning (EgoExoLearn); short-clip generated or human-video data (Wh0, H2R-Bench, real-life activity video); large behaviour models with chain-of-thought (709); dual-arm data-utilisation tasks (224).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Splitting tasks into subtasks (1369); chain-of-thought conditioning, which gave no benefit (709); proposed LLM planning grounded in low-level skills (1028), fusion of UMI-style and conventional data for long-horizon reasoning (1369), organising human video into higher-level task structures (1489), and longer-horizon extensions listed as future work (224, 1393, 1482).

clusters.name: Policies degrade under geometric and dynamics shifts
clusters.statement: Policies learned from demonstrations rely on demonstration-aligned motion priors and fail when object position, layout, pose, dynamics, camera or clutter change, and robustness to one shift does not extend to combined shifts.
clusters.description: A real-world UMI benchmark finds larger drops under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts than under object or appearance shifts, and still larger drops when shifts combine, concluding that policies rely on demonstration-aligned motion priors. Surveys cite degradation under combined perturbations, spurious correlations learned from small datasets, distribution shift between demonstration and deployment, and a density-estimation objective that does not match task success. Robot-only training fails in cluttered multi-object scenes, tactile pretraining is weak under camera and robot perturbations, baselines reach near-zero success on unseen objects or environments, and functional grasps generalise to unseen instances only within some categories. Open-loop execution without error correction lets objects slip under shifted conditions.

evidence_items.item: Performance drops more under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts than under object and appearance shifts (mean 59.62 seen/seen to 45.33 Factor-B and 40.19 combined); policies rely on demonstration-aligned motion priors.
Performance degrades under combined perturbations (THE COLOSSEUM); single-axis robustness does not extrapolate.

With small datasets policies learn spurious correlations, distribution shift between demonstration and deployment causes generalisation failures, and the density-estimation objective does not match task success.
Robot-only training in cluttered multi-object scenes reaches 0.0 percent (200 clips) and 8.0 percent (500 clips) success.
On LIBERO-plus camera and robot perturbations the tactile-pretrained model scores 48.9 and 49.5, below some baselines.
Policies pretrained on small subsets show unstable grasps, off-center contacts, slipping and stacking failures under shifted placement and a checkered tablecloth.
The framework runs open-loop with no real-time error correction or collision avoidance, and objects slip during large rotations on the real robot.
Generalisation to unseen instances is claimed only within some categories, and differences between robot hands limit broader generalisation.
The latent-action pretraining baseline fails completely in unseen environments.
Most zero-shot trials on unseen tasks still fail, with best success 38.9 percent.
With pi0 on ARX-R5, human video was uniformly detrimental in unseen positions, attributed to spatial domain mismatch.

benchmark_evidence: UMI-Bench 1.0 all tasks (1372) / progress score: mean 59.62 seen/seen, 45.33 under Factor-B (position, layout, pose, dynamics) shifts, 40.19 under combined unseen object and position.
LIBERO-plus (1385) / zero-shot success under camera perturbation: 48.9 percent versus OpenVLA-OFT 56.4 and pi0-Fast 65.1.
WIYH real robot cluttered scenes (1376) / success rate: 0.0 percent (200 robot clips) and 8.0 percent (500 robot clips).
HuRo ALLEX four tasks (1381) / OOD completion: 72.2 percent with full pretraining (34.9 percent without) versus 80.3 percent overall.
Real-robot unseen objects and categories (1489) / success rate: VPP, latent-action and OXE-pretraining baselines 0 to 8.3 percent.
Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 Rank RGB Blocks unseen background (224) / success rate: 0.13 teleoperation only, 0.20 with simulation.
clusters.settings: Real tabletop policies trained on UMI data, teleoperation, human-video or tactile pretraining under unseen object, position, layout, background, camera and clutter conditions (UMI-Bench, WIYH, HuRo ALLEX, Aloha-Agilex, Unitree G1, UR5 with dexterous hands, CosmoH2G); simulation robustness suites (LIBERO-plus, THE COLOSSEUM).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Large-scale human-video or robotized pretraining (1376, 1381, 1482, 1489), simulation co-training (224), tactile pretraining (1385), proposed closed-loop feedback and collision-aware planning (1390), and proposed structured priors and 3D feature fields (1028). Gains are partial and the drop under combined shifts persists.

clusters.name: Robot-learning evaluation is fragmented and non-diagnostic
clusters.statement: Human-to-robot transfer and the contribution of data cannot be compared or diagnosed reliably: benchmarks are fragmented across robots, tasks and video sources, many results rest on offline losses or visual metrics rather than robot rollouts, real-world evaluation carries reset and calibration noise, and success-only scores do not locate the failing component.
clusters.description: The human-video survey states that methods are evaluated on different robots, tasks and video sources, so it is unclear which transfer choices cause better results, and that most cannot be benchmarked in simulation alone. A real-world benchmark argues that differences in hardware, camera placement, reset and action interfaces show up as performance differences, with residual noise from resets, calibration drift, lighting and timing. Several dataset papers validate only by offline action-prediction error or VLA validation loss, evaluate no robot learning, or score only visible evidence rather than physical executability, and generic image, video and VLM metrics miss embodiment and contact fidelity. The VLA survey and the position paper add that success-only benchmarks cannot attribute failures to planning, memory, recovery or a specific component.

evidence_items.item: Benchmarking is fragmented across robots, tasks and video sources, and most methods cannot be benchmarked in simulation alone, so which transfer choices cause better performance remains unclear.

When hardware, camera placement, reset and action interfaces differ, performance differences reflect evaluation variation rather than model capability; residual noise remains from operator reset, calibration drift, lighting and hardware timing.
Benchmarks report overall success without diagnosing whether failures come from planning, memory, composition or recovery.
Diversity effects are measured only with offline action-prediction error, which does not directly measure robot performance; robot rollouts are still needed.
Validation is only by VLA validation loss, not task success, and no new human-to-robot transfer experiments are reported.
The benchmark evaluates only visible evidence of transfer, not physical executability or downstream policy performance.

Without component-level credit assignment, deployment failures cannot be routed to the faulty component; evaluation should test whether a system can infer contacts, object-state changes and task phases.
There is no standard test environment for reproducible comparison of methods that learn from human video.
The grippers lacked the sensors of a full pipeline, so no robot learning was evaluated; full demonstration-to-robot pipeline evaluation is still missing.
Policy-level evaluation of egocentric datasets is insufficient.
Robotic foundation models were not evaluated on the dataset because attempts failed on compute limits.
Generic image-quality and VLM metrics miss embodiment and contact fidelity.

benchmark_evidence: UMI-Bench 1.0 overall (1372) / overall score: best model averages 55.84 of 100 across ten tasks.
H2R-Bench (1393) / H2RCore versus video quality: weak rank association (30.0 to 84.6 versus 0.73 to 0.81).
EgoVerse-A fold-clothes diversity experiments (696) / offline Avg-MSE: diversity effects measured only offline, not by robot success.
HumanNet LingBot-VLA post-training (1378) / validation loss: the only reported validation metric; no task success.
clusters.settings: Real-robot policy evaluation across heterogeneous labs, embodiments and operator resets; egocentric dataset releases validated offline (action-prediction error, validation loss); simulated twins (RoboTube); MLLM and VLM judges for generated robot video and edited images; handheld-gripper user studies without robot learning.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Standardised UMI hardware with released protocols, rubrics, runners and rollout audit packages (1372), simulated twin environments (1389), policy-level evaluation in dataset papers (1376), and diagnostic H2R metrics (1393). Proposed: 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions of capture scenes as benchmarks (1399), benchmarks built on high-fidelity data engines (1401), and evaluation of contact, object-state and phase inference with component-level credit assignment (1402).

clusters.name: No principled valuation or mixing of data
clusters.statement: The value of teleoperation, simulation, human-video, kinesthetic and handheld data for a given policy cannot be predicted in advance: exchange rates are task-dependent, mixing ratios are set empirically, heterogeneous action spaces and frames give conflicting supervision, and claimed diversity benefits are mostly unvalidated on robots.
clusters.description: A data-utilisation study derives local exchange rates between teleoperation, simulation and human video and finds them task- and goal-dependent rather than universal, so mixing must be tailored per task. A modality study leaves the optimal mix of demonstration modalities to future automatic methods, and a co-training study chose a 9:1 ratio empirically and found that raising the co-training share degraded in-distribution performance. Surveys state that optimal mixtures are unknown with few compute-matched ablations, that action and state spaces differ across robots and datasets, and that aggregated corpora gain volume at the cost of interface consistency. Dataset papers add that diversity and relevance are hard to balance and that the benefits of scene, demonstrator or camera diversity are unvalidated on robots.

evidence_items.item: Utilisation ratios are task- and goal-dependent rather than universal; data mixing must be tailored per task, and principled valuation of heterogeneous data sources is open.
The optimal mix of demonstration modalities is unknown and should be determined automatically.
A 9:1 robot to co-training data ratio was chosen empirically, and raising the co-training loss weight or data ratio degraded in-distribution performance.
Optimal data mixtures across pyramid layers are unknown and compute-matched ablations are limited; end-effector poses defined in different frames give conflicting supervision.
Action and state spaces are heterogeneous across robots and datasets.
Datasets trade fidelity against scale; aggregated corpora gain volume at the cost of interface consistency.
Balancing dataset diversity and relevance in robot-oriented video datasets is an open problem.
The downstream benefit of camera-domain diversity is unvalidated, with statistics from a 100-hour sample.
Embodiment factors need deeper analysis to guide data selection, curriculum and architectures, and when pre-training on human data yields transferable structure is open.
1,000 h of egocentric pretraining only matches or slightly surpasses 100 h of real-robot data.

benchmark_evidence: Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 Pick Dual Bottles unseen background (224) / success rate: 0.20 teleoperation only versus 0.30 with a budget-aware simulation mix.
Flip Glass mixed data (782) / success rate: 75 percent with 100 mixed demonstrations, only 5 percent above the best single-modality model.
TRI-Ramen simulation tasks (709) / task success: latent actions, FAST and VQ-VAE co-training tokens give no statistically significant improvement; FAST lowers unseen-task success.
clusters.settings: Dual-arm tabletop imitation learning (Aloha-Agilex, ARX-R5), single-arm modality studies (Franka), large behaviour model co-training with VLM backbones, egocentric dataset curation (EgoVerse, Open-AoE, HumanNet), simulated twins (RoboTube), and survey analyses of aggregated corpora.
clusters.attempted_fixes: Locally linear utilisation-ratio models with power-law optimality gaps (224), mixed-modality training (782), empirically tuned co-training ratios (709), and the data-pyramid taxonomy (1400). Proposed: automatic modality mixing (782), architecture-aware stage-dependent recipes with compute-matched ablations and coordinate conventions recorded as metadata (1400), and robot-rollout validation of diversity effects (696, 1377). No universal recipe is reported.

clusters.name: Simulation data does not substitute for real
clusters.statement: Simulation-generated manipulation data cannot yet substitute for real data: sim-to-real artifacts make it hurt simple in-domain tasks, generators cannot create new physics and repeat trajectories, simulators lack touch, and building high-fidelity simulated twins of real scenes and objects from human capture remains open.
clusters.description: A data-utilisation benchmark finds that simulation data hurts simple in-domain tasks, attributed to sim-to-real artifacts, and that neither simulation-only nor human-video-only training suffices. Surveys note that trajectory-reuse generators assume known subtask structure, that visual augmentation cannot create new physics, that LLM-driven generation stays inside simulation, and that skill-constrained generation produces repetitive trajectories despite scale. Simulation benchmarks lack a tactile modality, simulated assistant agents transfer poorly to real interaction, and digital twins required scanning every object. Proposed directions are reconstructing real scenes in simulation at high geometric and physical fidelity and learning to simulate objects from human video.

evidence_items.item: Simulation data hurts simple in-domain tasks, attributed to sim-to-real artifacts; neither simulation-only nor human-video-only training is sufficient.

Trajectory reuse assumes known subtask structure, visual augmentation cannot create new physics, and LLM-driven generation remains simulation-bound; bridging the gap via high-fidelity real-scene reconstruction in simulation is open.
Learning from synthetic data must address the sim-to-real gap for policies trained on synthetic data.
Simulation suffers a sim-to-real gap, while real egocentric video scales but is misaligned with robot deployment.
Simulation benchmarks have no tactile modality, so a proprioceptive proxy replaces tactile input there.
Learning to simulate objects from human videos is open; the digital twins required scanning 60 objects.
Skill-constrained simulation generation produced trajectories whose action keypoints concentrate in a small region, indicating repetition despite scale; sim-to-real transfer is listed as open.
Simulated assistant agents transfer poorly to real interaction, and transferring them to real-world human interaction is open.
Sim-to-real generalisation is named as an open problem in the introduction.

benchmark_evidence: Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 Rank RGB Blocks unseen background (224) / success rate: 0.13 teleoperation only, 0.20 with simulation.
Real Aloha-Agilex-2.0 Pick Dual Bottles unseen background (224) / success rate: 0.20 teleoperation only, 0.30 with a budget-aware simulation mix.
InternData-A1 simulation (1400) / action keypoint spatial spread: concentrated in a small region despite scale.
clusters.settings: Dual-arm simulation co-training (Aloha-Agilex), simulated digital twins of household tasks (RoboTube), large simulated data generators (InternData-A1, MimicGen family), tactile VLA training with simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-plus, RoboCasa), simulated assistant agents (HoloAssist), and generated egocentric data positioned against simulation (Wh0).
clusters.attempted_fixes: Budget-aware simulation mixing (224), digital twins from 60 scanned objects (1389), a projected shared-MANO tactile proxy for simulation (1385), and generated egocentric data as an alternative (1482). Proposed: high-fidelity real-scene reconstruction in simulation (1401) and learning to simulate objects from human video (1389). Simulation data still hurts simple in-domain tasks (224).

notes:
Inputs: a bottom-up clustering (20 clusters) and a capability clustering (20 clusters), both over all 33 records in G4_robot_learning.jsonl. I re-read all 33 records (problem, cannot_yet, limitations, failures, assumptions, future, open_problems, bench_gaps) to settle membership. Paper 1544 (Observe, Retarget, and Distill) has no accessible full text and only one inventory-derived assumption, so it stays uncategorized. Every other paper supports at least one cluster. Result: 24 clusters. Clusters overlap: a paper is listed wherever one of its own items states the pain point.

Merged one-to-one (both lenses name the same pain point; paper ids unioned, then checked against the records): metric monocular hand motion (bottom-up 3 + capability 1), unverifiable annotation accuracy (4 + 2), hand-object occlusion (5 + 3), object pose labels (7 + 4), kinematic retargeting (8 + 6), portable capture tracking drift (11 + 16), event and phase labelling (12 + 12), single-hand assumption and bimanual transfer (13 + 15), viewpoint mismatch (15 + 18), long-horizon failure (16 + 13), shift generalization (17 + 14), evaluation (18 + 19), data valuation and mixing (19 + 9).

Finer cut kept (the lenses disagree and each finer cluster has at least three papers):
(a) Bottom-up 'Unaligned human data does not improve robot policies' is split into capability 'Embodiment and strategy gap' (12 papers) and 'Human video does not reliably improve policies' (11).
(b) Bottom-up 'Generated robot videos are physically implausible' is split into capability 'visual conversion loses embodiment and contact' (6) and 'physically grounded world models' (5).
(c) Capability 'Contact force and tactile capture' is split into bottom-up 'Human demonstrations lack measured contact force' (11) and 'Demonstration interfaces fail on force-rich, fine tasks' (7).
(d) Bottom-up 'Low usable yield from in-the-wild video' stays separate from occlusion (6 papers). The capability lens had folded it into occlusion.
(e) Bottom-up 'Paired human-robot demonstrations cannot be captured at scale' is kept (5 papers). The capability lens had spread it over visual conversion and interfaces.
(f) Capability 'Simulation data does not transfer to real' is kept (9 papers). The bottom-up lens has no such cluster.
(g) Bottom-up 'Manipulation data costly, narrow and non-extensible' and capability 'Demonstration interfaces trade effort for quality' cut the same material differently. I kept the common refinement: 'Demonstration collection is costly and physically burdensome' (12 papers, interface level) and 'Manipulation datasets are narrow, static and unevenly covered' (11, corpus level).

Membership settled by re-reading the records:
- 1369 was dropped from data mixing. Its item is about fusing UMI and conventional data for long-horizon reasoning, so it stays in long-horizon.
- 1385 was dropped from object pose. Its mesh-distance contact label is a force item and stays in the force cluster.
- 1389 was added to object pose, because its cannot_yet names explicit 3D hand-object pose estimation. It also stays in bimanual.
- 1489 was dropped from annotation verification, because its items are about label noise; it stays in metric hand. It was also dropped from embodiment; its nearest-joint mapping stays in retargeting.
- 1482 moved from retargeting to embodiment, because a robot hand larger than the human hand is a morphology mismatch.
- 1376 and 1372 were dropped from capture drift. 1376 has no drift item. 1372's calibration drift is evaluation noise and stays in evaluation.
- 1381 moved from capture drift to viewpoint (camera-robot alignment tail under viewpoint inconsistency).
- 998 was kept out of hand-object occlusion, because its occlusion blocks the Vive tracker's line of sight; it stays in capture drift. It was added to the force-data cluster (no powered tool with integrated force sensing).
- 709 was dropped from world models. It only says that world-model co-training is unexplored.
- 1399 was dropped from long-horizon. Its long-horizon item concerns world models and stays there.
- 224 was dropped from bimanual. It evaluates three dual-arm tasks and states no single-hand assumption. 1369 was added (dual-arm data collection is open).
- 1397 was added to sim-to-real (simulated assistants transfer poorly).
- 1394 was added to filtering yield (about 33 percent of candidates rejected).
- 696, 1377 and 1378 stay in occlusion as well as filtering, because their items say that visible hands are required or that occluded clips are discarded.
- 3D hand pose forecasting (1397) was dropped from event inference because it is a different task.

Items left unassigned (fewer than three papers, or already spread across clusters):
- Deformable and flexible objects: 224 future work, 854 flexible packaging, 1389 cloth folding hardest, 1402 mechanics models brittle for deformables, 919 deformable pipe plugging as an assumption. This is close to a cluster, but its items already sit in the interface, bimanual and long-horizon clusters.
- 3D hand pose forecasting error that grows with horizon (1397).
- Multimodal fusion that does not help (1397) and integrating streams with different rates (1399).
- VLM backbone language erosion (709).
- Train versus evaluation objective mismatch and online exploration (1028); the objective mismatch is cited in the shift cluster.
- Continual learning from new video (1399).
- Reward grounding and credit assignment (1402); credit assignment is cited in evaluation.
- VLM spatial referring and spatial deictics (1376, 1397).
- Skill assessment with an exocentric reference (23), cited in viewpoint.
- Privacy and dual use (1378), cited in the narrow-datasets cluster.
- When to learn strategies from humans versus using pre-programmed ones (998).
- Intervention type prediction (1397).

Problem types where the lenses differed: data mixing = research (bottom-up research, capability data); force data = data (bottom-up data, capability mixed); object pose = mixed (bottom-up data, capability mixed).

Benchmark numbers are copied from bench_gaps and failures as recorded. The CALVIN 0.08 percent figure is the survey's citation (1401), not its own measurement.

Clusters closest to RGB-D bimanual hand-object tracking and reconstruction: metric monocular hand motion, unverifiable annotation accuracy, hand-object occlusion, object pose labels, portable capture tracking drift and the single-hand assumption. Retargeting and missing contact force come next.
